===The Gothic Revival===
Birmingham lay at the heart of the mid-19th century [[Gothic Revival]], being closely associated with its two most influential early pioneers: [[Thomas Rickman]] and [[A. W. N. Pugin]]. [[Gothic architecture]] had been used for picturesque decoration in England throughout the 17th and 18th centuries, a practice that continued into the early 19th century, with notable examples in Birmingham including [[Metchley Abbey]] in [[Harborne]] of ca. 1800; and [[Francis Goodwin (architect)|Francis Goodwin]]'s [[Holy Trinity Church, Bordesley|Holy Trinity, Bordesley]] – a [[commissioners' church]] of 1822, "far from correct and far from dull".{{sfn|Hickman|1970|p=6}} The mid 19th century however saw a conscious and far-reaching revival in the use of Gothic as a complete and rigorous system of construction, encompassing both structure and decoration and involving a renewed emphasis on historical authenticity.

[[File:St Augustine Edgbaston.jpg|left|thumb|upright|[[St Augustine's Church, Edgbaston]], by [[J. A. Chatwin]], 1868.]]
The first notable figure of this architectural revolution was [[Thomas Rickman]], who was based in Birmingham for 21 of the 23 years he practiced as an architect.{{sfn|Ballard|2009|p=xii}} Although he worked in a wide variety of architectural styles Rickman's understanding of Gothic was far more thorough and learned than that of most other architects of his time,{{sfn|Little|1971|p=20}} and his [[Quaker]] background gave him a systematic and objective view of Gothic styles free from the complications of the [[Church of England]]'s search for [[Sacred architecture|liturgical meaning]].<ref>{{Citation|last=Aldrich|first=Megan|year=2009|contribution=Rickman, Thomas (1776–1841), ''architect''|contribution-url=http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/23607|title=Oxford Dictionary of National Biography|edition=Online|location=Oxford|publisher=Oxford University Press|url=http://www.oxforddnb.com|access-date=2013-05-10}}</ref> His earliest Birmingham church [[St George-in-the-Fields]] of 1819 (demolished) was a remarkably correct Gothic structure for its date,{{sfn|Hickman|1970|p=5}} and moved away from the economical but historically inauthentic use of [[cast iron]] detailing of his earlier churches in [[Liverpool]].{{sfn|Little|1971|p=20}} It was followed by a series of  other notable works in the Birmingham area, including [[St Barnabas' Church, Erdington]] of 1824; the Watt Memorial Chapel of 1826 at [[St Mary's Church, Handsworth]]; [[All Saints Church, Ladywood]] of 1834 (demolished); and the [[Bishop Ryder Church, Birmingham|Bishop Ryder Church]] of 1836 (demolished).{{sfn|Little|1971|p=21}} Rickman's longest-lasting influence on the course of  the Gothic revival however was his book ''An Attempt to Discriminate the Styles of English Architecture, from the Conquest to the Reformation''; the first study of Gothic architecture designed to guide architects towards historically authentic styles and the first to establish a convincing classification and chronology of [[English Gothic architecture]], defining the four principal periods – [[Norman architecture|Norman]], [[Early English Period|Early English]], [[Decorated Period|Decorated]] and [[Perpendicular Period|Perpendicular]] – that still frame the understanding of Gothic styles today.<ref>{{Citation|last=Mallgrave|first=Harry Francis|year=2005|title=Modern Architectural Theory: A Historical Survey, 1673-1968|location=Cambridge|publisher=Cambridge University Press|page=86|isbn=0521793068|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iK7ld8-oYswC&pg=PA86|access-date=2013-05-10}}</ref>

The most influential figure of the most important phase of the Gothic Revival, however, in Birmingham and worldwide, was [[Augustus Pugin]].<ref>{{Citation|last=Véliz|first=Claudio|year=1994|title=The New World of the Gothic Fox: Culture and Economy in English and Spanish America|publisher=University of California Press|page=98|isbn=0520914031|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PMFK2h1lVvAC&pg=PA98|access-date=2013-05-15}}</ref> Pugin first became involved with Birmingham in 1833, designing the Gothic detailing for [[Charles Barry]]'s rebuilding of [[King Edward's School, Birmingham|King Edward's School]] (demolished) in [[New Street, Birmingham|New Street]].{{sfn|Foster|2005|p=11}} This was the first secular building in Birmingham to demonstrate the emerging, more scholarly use of gothic,{{sfn|Hickman|1970|p=6}} being designed in a [[Tudor architecture|Tudor]] style to reflect the school's 16th century foundation.{{sfn|Little|1971|p=24}} It was also the first work of the partnership between Barry and Pugin that would later design the [[Palace of Westminster]] in [[London]], and it established the pattern that Westminster was to follow, with gothic detailing on a fundamentally classical, symmetrical composition.{{sfn|Little|1971|p=24}} As a centre of industrial manufacture, with a reputation for religious [[Nonconformist (Protestantism)|non-conformism]] and a largely [[Georgian architecture|Georgian]] streetscape, Birmingham was anathema to Pugin's craft-based, high-church, medievalist outlook, and in 1833 he condemned it as "that most detestable of detestable places - Birmingham, where Greek buildings and smoking chimneys, Radicals and Dissenters are blended together".{{sfn|O'Donnell|2002|p=6}} However Birmingham's ferment of religious diversity also placed it at the heart of the mid-19th-century English [[Catholic Revival]],<ref>{{Citation|year=2010|title=St. Mary's College, Oscott|series=Pope Benedict XVI in the United Kingdom|location=London|publisher=Catholic Communications Network|url=http://www.thepapalvisit.org.uk/2010-Visit/Visit-Event-Information/Itinerary/19-September-2010/St.-Mary-s-College-Oscott|access-date=2012-06-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120309072313/http://www.thepapalvisit.org.uk/2010-Visit/Visit-Event-Information/Itinerary/19-September-2010/St.-Mary-s-College-Oscott|archive-date=2012-03-09|url-status=dead}}</ref> and after his conversion to Catholicism in 1834 Pugin quickly became associated with Birmingham's [[Oscott College]], where he was to live from 1837 as college architect and Professor of Ecclesiastical Art and Architecture.<ref>{{Citation|title=The College Museum|publisher=St. Mary's College, Oscott|url=http://www.oscott.net/museum---history.html|access-date=2013-05-18|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304030755/http://www.oscott.net/museum---history.html|archive-date=2016-03-04}}</ref> During this period he built a series of buildings in Birmingham that marked the turning point in the use of Gothic as a functional, honest expression of the form and function of building.{{sfn|Hickman|1970|p=6}}

The first of these, completed in 1838, was the chapel of Oscott College itself – alongside [[Scarisbrick Hall]] one of the two major works of Pugin's first years as an architect.<ref name="Atterbury">{{Citation|last=Atterbury|first=Paul|year=1995|contribution=Pugin and Interior design|contribution-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RfBpd-OZ7e4C&pg=PA189|editor-last=Atterbury|editor-first=Paul|title=A. W. N. Pugin: Master of Gothic Revival|location=New Haven, CT|publisher=Yale University Press|pages=189–190|isbn=0300066562|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RfBpd-OZ7e4C|access-date=2013-05-06}}</ref> This was Pugin's first large-scale work of ecclesiastical gothic, and the freedom he had at Oscott gave him his first opportunity to achieve his vision of a complete, integrated medievalist world, with his Gothic design work extending from the building's architecture to its furnishings and metalwork and even the [[vestments]] of its clergy.<ref name="Atterbury" /> In 1840 he designed [[St Mary's Convent, Handsworth]], a small and unobtrusive building that is nonetheless exceptional for its date in its explicit medievalism.{{sfn|Little|1971|p=25}} The major work of this period, and one of the most important buildings of Pugin's career,{{sfn|Hickman|1970|p=6}} was [[St Chad's Cathedral, Birmingham|St Chad's Cathedral]], the first new cathedral to be built in England since London's [[St Paul's Cathedral|St Paul's]],<ref>{{Citation|last=Hill|first=Rosemary|year=2008|title=God's Architect: Pugin and the Building of Romantic Britain|location=Harmondsworth|publisher=Penguin|page=24|isbn=978-0140280999|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ufTvr_GTtH4C&pg=PA24|access-date=2013-09-23}}</ref> and the first Roman Catholic cathedral to be built in England since the [[reformation]].<ref>{{Citation|editor-last=Belcher|editor-first=Margaret|year=2001|title=The Collected Letters of A.W.N. Pugin: 1830-1842|volume=1|location=Oxford|publisher=Oxford University Press|page=117|isbn=0198173911|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ypn5FmpS-3sC&pg=PA117|access-date=2013-09-23}}</ref> Opposite St Chads stood the [[Bishop's House, Birmingham|Bishop's House]] (demolished). Austere and tightly composed, with ornamentation limited to decorative brickwork and a small number of stone dressings, this was the most influential building Pugin ever designed.<ref>{{Citation|last=Saint|first=Andrew|year=1995|contribution=Pugin's Architecture in Context|contribution-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RfBpd-OZ7e4C&pg=PA95|editor-last=Atterbury|editor-first=Paul|title=A. W. N. Pugin: Master of Gothic Revival|location=New Haven, CT|publisher=Yale University Press|pages=95–96|isbn=0300066562|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RfBpd-OZ7e4C|access-date=2013-09-23}}</ref> Its simple unpretentious style based on the honest use of traditional materials marked the birth of the spirit of the [[Arts and Crafts movement]],<ref>{{Citation|year=1984|contribution=Red House and the founding of the Firm|contribution-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=thW8AAAAIAAJ&pg=PA111|editor1-last=Banham|editor1-first=Joanna|editor2-last=Harris|editor2-first=Jennifer|title=William Morris and the Middle Ages: A Collection of Essays, Together with a Catalogue of Works Exhibited at the Whitworth Art Gallery, 28 September - 8 December 1984|location=Manchester|publisher=Manchester University Press|page=111|isbn=0719017211|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=thW8AAAAIAAJ|access-date=2013-09-23}}</ref> and its exceptional originality and adventurousness marked the birth of the idea of rational construction that was to dominate the architecture of the 20th century.<ref>{{Citation|last=Saint|first=Andrew|year=1995|contribution=Pugin's Architecture in Context|contribution-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RfBpd-OZ7e4C&pg=PA99|editor-last=Atterbury|editor-first=Paul|title=A. W. N. Pugin: Master of Gothic Revival|location=New Haven, CT|publisher=Yale University Press|page=99|isbn=0300066562|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RfBpd-OZ7e4C|access-date=2013-09-23}}</ref>

[[J. A. Chatwin]] became one of the most prolific architects involved in the construction or alteration of churches in Birmingham. Some of his most significant works include the [[Birmingham Orthodox Cathedral|Greek Orthodox Cathedral]] in Birmingham, which was completed in 1873,<ref>{{Harvnb|Hickman|1970|page=36}}</ref> [[Church of SS Peter & Paul, Aston|Aston Parish Church]] in 1879, and [[St Martin in the Bull Ring]] in 1873. As well as designing churches, he designed the [[King Edward VI High School for Girls]] on [[New Street, Birmingham|New Street]] in 1866 and [[Bingley Hall]] in 1850.<ref name=little /> His son [[P. B. Chatwin]] also became an architect, designing [[King Edward VI Handsworth]] in 1911 and [[St Mary the Virgin, Acocks Green]] Church and Church Hall, [[Acocks Green]] which opened around 1908.<ref name=pevsner />

===High Victorian architecture===
The early and dramatic advent of [[High Victorian Gothic|High Victorian architecture]] in Birmingham took place in 1855 with the completion of 12 Ampton Road in [[Edgbaston]] by [[John Henry Chamberlain]].{{sfn|Foster|2005|p=11}} [[Martin & Chamberlain]] were prolific architects in Birmingham during the Victorian era, having designed 41 [[Birmingham board schools]]. John Henry Chamberlain, who was not of local descent, was part of Martin & Chamberlain. His works in Birmingham include [[Highbury, Birmingham|Highbury Hall]] and [[Birmingham School of Art]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://icbirmingham.icnetwork.co.uk/expats/pastpres/tm_objectid=11996804&method=full&siteid=50003&headline=man-who-built-city-s-civic-pride-name_page.html |title=Man who built city's civic pride |publisher=icBirmingham |access-date=2007-09-23}}</ref> which was completed by his son Frederick Martin following his sudden death in 1883. The cutting of [[Corporation Street, Birmingham|Corporation Street]] through slums in the city centre began in 1878<ref name=corporationstreet>{{cite web|url=http://www.birmingham.gov.uk/GenerateContent?CONTENT_ITEM_ID=87359&CONTENT_ITEM_TYPE=0&MENU_ID=10277 |publisher=Birmingham City Council |title=Corporation Street |access-date=2007-09-23}}</ref> and much of the work for designing the buildings that were to line the street was given to Martin & Chamberlain. Numerous buildings, which had leases of 99 years, were demolished in the [[post-war]] period, however, the street has retained many of its fine Victorian buildings above modern ground-floor façades, providing an insight into how the city once looked.<ref name=corporationstreet />

[[File:Birmingham - Lawcourt 2.JPG|left|thumb|The [[Architectural terracotta|red brick and terracotta]] [[Victoria Law Courts]] by Sir [[Aston Webb]] and [[Ingress Bell]], on [[Corporation Street, Birmingham|Corporation Street]], 1891.]]
The use of [[Architectural terracotta|red brick and terracotta]] was pioneered during this period. Red terracotta was useful as a substitute for natural stone, which Birmingham lacked, and it also was resistant to soot and smoke which was prevalent in the city due to the heavy industrial presence.<ref name=birmterra>{{cite web |url=http://www.birmingham.gov.uk/ELibrary?E_LIBRARY_ID=74&a=1199241745519 |title=Birmingham Terracotta |author=Nicola Coxon (Birmingham City Council Planning Department) |publisher=Ibstock Hathernware (republished by Birmingham City Council) |year=2001 |access-date=2008-08-18}}</ref> Birmingham's importance as a growing town encouraged the construction of municipal buildings which were designed by some of the most prominent architects of the time. Sir [[Aston Webb]] and [[Ingress Bell]]'s [[Victoria Law Courts]] were completed in 1891 and feature extensive use of terracotta on the exterior. The ornamentation on the exterior, which includes a statue of [[Queen Victoria]], is carried on inside the building.<ref name=pevsner>{{cite book|author=Andy Foster|title=Pevsner Architectural Guides - Birmingham|year=2005|isbn=0-300-10731-5|publisher=Yale University Press|location=New Haven}}</ref> Webb was not the only major architect to make an impact on Birmingham.

Wealthy landowners saw business opportunities as a result of the arrival of the railways in Birmingham. One such land owner, Isaac Horton, commissioned [[Thomson Plevins]] to design a hotel for [[Colmore Row]]. The result was the Grand Hotel which was completed in 1875 in the French Renaissance-style. The hotel was altered and extended in 1876, 1891 and 1895 but is now empty, and was saved from demolition when it was granted Grade II listed status in May 2004. Another Plevins hotel for Isaac Horton is the Midland Hotel (now the Burlington Hotel) on New Street. Horton constructed hotels next to railway stations to maximise trade and made them attractive to visitors decorating them lavishly on the inside as well as on the exterior.<ref name=Tappenden>{{cite web |url=http://www.24hourmuseum.org.uk/birmingham/trails/TRA25212.html?ixsid=wAV7QjG0WKI |title=Birmingham's Buildings In Danger |last=Tappenden |first=Roslyn |date=2004-12-14 |work=City Heritage Guides |publisher=24 Hour Museum |access-date=2008-08-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110519030809/http://www.24hourmuseum.org.uk/birmingham/trails/TRA25212.html?ixsid=wAV7QjG0WKI |archive-date=2011-05-19 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Other transport improvements in the town improved the quality of life as well as the provision of commercial space in the town. 
The city has several Victorian [[Green Man]] (or foliate heads) sculptures which consist of unusual human heads, carved of stone with vegetation growing out of their faces.<ref>{{cite book |author=George Noszlopy |author2=Jeremy Beach |title=Public Sculpture of Birmingham |year=1998 |publisher=Liverpool University Press |isbn=0-85323-692-5}}</ref>

In the late 19th century, [[James & Lister Lea]] became prolific designers of [[public house]]s in Birmingham. They designed The Woodman (1896-97),<ref>{{NHLE |num=1234088 |access-date=2007-09-23}}</ref> the Swan and Mitre (1899),<ref>{{NHLE |num=1234169 |access-date=2007-09-23}}</ref> The White Swan (1900),<ref>{{NHLE |num=1276272 |access-date=2007-09-23}}</ref> [[Anchor Inn, Birmingham|The Anchor Inn]] (1901)<ref>{{NHLE |num=1234167 |access-date=2007-09-23}}</ref> and The City Tavern (1901).<ref>{{NHLE |num=1376199 |access-date=2007-09-23}}</ref> Many of these pubs are now listed buildings and were built of red brick and terracotta.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.imagesofengland.org.uk/default.aspx |title=Main page |publisher=Images of England |access-date=2007-09-23| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20070915095329/http://www.imagesofengland.org.uk/default.aspx| archive-date= 15 September 2007 | url-status= dead}}</ref>

</gallery>

===The Arts and Crafts Movement===
The early 1890s saw a sudden change in Birmingham's dominant architectural style, as [[High Gothic]] gave way to a distinctive local school of [[Arts and Crafts Movement|Arts and Crafts]] architecture.{{sfn|Granelli|1984|p=41}} Buildings came increasingly to be designed in an understated style that limited ornament and was based on traditional forms of local [[vernacular architecture]], in Birmingham largely [[brick]], [[roughcast]] and [[half-timbering]].{{sfn|Foster|2005|pp=20-21}} Design emphasised the simple and honest expression of the building's construction, highlighting structural elements such as the [[brickwork#Load bearing brick bonds|bonds]] of the brickwork, and often emphasising differences in the function of elements of the building through the deliberate creation of awkward juxtapositions and contrasts.{{sfn|Foster|2005|p=21}} Buildings often featured decorative elements such as furnishings, friezes or paintings by local artists and craftsmen{{sfn|Granelli|1984|p=43}} – particularly by the [[Birmingham Group (artists)|Birmingham Group]] which formed around the [[Birmingham School of Art]] in the 1880s – considering these to be integral to the design of the building to form a "total work of art".{{sfn|Granelli|1984|p=44}}  The Arts and Crafts philosophy was an approach to design rather than a defined style, however,{{sfn|Granelli|1984|p=42}} and the work of Arts and Crafts architects within Birmingham ranged from the eclectic and spectacular [[Tudor Revival architecture|Elizabethan revival]] work of [[Crouch and Butler]]{{sfn|Granelli|1984|p=44}} to the [[Methodist]] purism of [[Joseph Lancaster Ball]];{{sfn|Granelli|1984|pp=48-49}} and from the politically radical austerity of [[Arthur Stansfield Dixon]];{{sfn|Foster|2005|p=23}} to the mystically charged symbolism of the work of [[William Lethaby]].{{sfn|Foster|2005|p=93}}

[[File:21-Yateley-Road,-Edgbaston,-Birmingham---Herbert-Tudor-Buckland.jpg|thumb|left|[[21 Yateley Road, Edgbaston]], Grade I listed<ref>{{NHLE |num=1076073 |desc=21 Yateley Road |access-date=2015-04-23}}</ref> designed by [[Herbert Tudor Buckland]] in 1899 as his own home.]]
Birmingham's existing visual culture made it highly receptive to Arts and Crafts thinking.{{sfn|Foster|2005|p=21}} The Arts and Crafts Movement itself had been born out of the [[Birmingham Set]]: a group of undergraduates, most of whom were from Birmingham, that formed at Oxford University in the 1850s and whose members included [[William Morris]] and [[Edward Burne-Jones]].<ref>{{Citation|last=Naylor|first=Gillian|year=1971|publication-date=1990|title=The arts and crafts movement: a study of its sources, ideals and influence on design theory|location=London|publisher=Trefo|pages=97–101|isbn=0-86294-058-3}}</ref> The direct relevance of the practice of design and production to the Birmingham economy gave such issues a high-profile within the town, and the aesthetic and social philosophy of the key Arts and Crafts influence [[John Ruskin]] was well established among Birmingham's governing [[Liberal elite]] by the 1870s.{{sfn|Foster|2005|p=21}} It was on a trip to Birmingham in 1855 that Morris had decided to pursue architecture as a career, and he was to maintain close links with the town over following decades, serving as President of the [[Royal Birmingham Society of Artists|Birmingham Society of Artists]] in 1878.{{sfn|Foster|2005|p=21}} By the 1890s Arts and Crafts architects dominated the [[Birmingham Architectural Association]] and architectural teaching at the [[Birmingham School of Art]],{{sfn|Granelli|1984|p=43}} and the Movement provided the first two Directors of the [[Birmingham School of Architecture]] from its foundation in 1905.{{sfn|Granelli|1984|p=44}}

The first sign of this newly-simple and free approach to architecture was a series of buildings in the [[Queen Anne style architecture|Queen Anne revival]] style by Ball and by [[Arthur Harrison (architect)|Arthur Harrison]] in the 1880s.{{sfn|Foster|2005|p=21}} The most influential early Arts and Crafts domestic work was Lethaby's ''The Hurst'' in [[Four Oaks, Birmingham|Four Oaks]] of 1892 (since demolished),{{sfn|Foster|2005|p=21}} with major surviving works including [[Herbert Tudor Buckland]]'s 1899 and 1901 houses in Yateley Road, Edgbaston;{{sfn|Foster|2005|p=22}} J. L Ball's ''[[Winterbourne Botanic Garden|Winterbourne]]'' of 1903, also in Edgbaston;{{sfn|Granelli|1984|p=49}} and [[C. E. Bateman]]'s ''Redlands'' of 1900 in Four Oaks.{{sfn|Granelli|1984|p=50}} The dominance of Arts and Crafts culture among Birmingham's growing manufacturing, commercial and professional classes saw the development of a wide variety of detached suburban houses in upmarket districts such as [[Edgbaston]], [[Moseley]], [[Four Oaks, Birmingham|Four Oaks]], and [[Yardley, Birmingham|Yardley]], and outside the city boundaries in areas such as [[Barnt Green]], [[Olton]] and [[Solihull]], designed both by celebrated local Arts and Crafts architects and by less well-known but prolific local figures such as [[Owen Parsons]], [[Thomas Walter Francis Newton]] & [[Alfred Edward Cheatle]] and [[William de Lacy Aherne]].{{sfn|Ballard|2009|p=xviii}}

Notable commercial buildings in Arts and Crafts styles included Lethaby's [[122-124 Colmore Row]] of 1900 – a building of European importance in its break with revivalism{{sfn|Hickman|1970|p=7}} – and Arthur Dixon's 1898 [[Birmingham Guild of Handicraft]] in Great Charles Street, whose "virtually styleless"{{sfn|Hickman|1970|p=6}} design reflected his radical socialist views by using round arched windows in an explicit rejection of the Gothic Revival.{{sfn|Foster|2005|p=23}} The most important church architecture of the movement was that of [[William Bidlake]], culminating in his [[St Agatha's Church, Sparkbrook|St Agatha's, Sparkbrook]] of 1899, whose inventive but restrained design had a national influence, maintaining the close relationship between function and decoration that was important to the Gothic revival, while moving away from the straightforwardly [[Historicism (art)|historicist]] imitation of medieval precedent.{{sfn|Hickman|1970|p=7}}

The most comprehensive expression of the Arts and Crafts spirit within Birmingham however was the suburb of [[Bournville]], which was developed from 1894 by [[George Cadbury]] as a [[model village]] for workers from his nearby factory,  and was largely designed by the architect [[William Alexander Harvey]], a pupil of Bidlake appointed at the young age of  22.{{sfn|Foster|2005|pp=22-23}} Harvey designed over 500 houses in Bournville between 1895 and 1904{{sfn|Little|1971|p=36}} – simple but exceptionally varied cottages built in pairs in brick, timber and stone – and a few public buildings clustered around a central village green.{{sfn|Granelli|1984|p=57}} Bournville was most influential in its [[urban planning]], however, where its layout of cottages set in substantial gardens, on roads lined with fruit trees, moved beyond the 19th century model of the company village towards the [[garden city movement|garden cities]] of the early 20th century.{{sfn|Foster|2005|pp=22-23}}

The Arts and Crafts Movement marked a golden age of Birmingham architecture,{{sfn|Hickman|1970|p=7}} placing the city at the forefront of English architecture{{sfn|Little|1971|p=11}} at a time when English architecture was leading the world. Its influence was international: Lethaby was the most important architectural theorist of the whole movement, and built over half of his work in Birmingham or for Birmingham clients,{{sfn|Foster|2005|pp=20, 21}} while the buildings of Birmingham architects such as [[William Bidlake]] and [[William Alexander Harvey]] were to feature prominently in [[Herman Muthesius]]'s 1905 book ''[[The English House]]'',{{sfn|Foster|2005|p=23}} which was to be revolutionary in its introduction of the Arts and Crafts philosophy into [[Germany]], and a pivotal influence on the later birth of the [[modern movement]].<ref>{{Citation|last=Jensen|first=Finn|year=2012|title=Modernist Semis and Terraces in England|location=Farnham|publisher=Ashgate Publishing|page=80|isbn=978-0754679691|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2tOa9xOxzQkC&pg=PA80|access-date=2013-05-01}}</ref>

<gallery class="center">
</gallery>

==Edwardian and interwar architecture==
[[File:Hall of Memory Birmingham.jpg|left|thumb|The [[Hall of Memory (Birmingham)|Hall of Memory]] in [[Centenary Square]], 1925.]]
The late-Victorian era of [[red brick and terracotta]] gave way to coloured [[Glazed architectural terra-cotta|glazed terracotta]] – faïence: examples being the [[Trocadero, Birmingham|Trocadero]] in Temple Street, completed around 1902,<ref name=pevsner /> and the Piccadilly Arcade, completed in 1909 as a cinema, on New Street.<ref name=pevsner /> Glazed brick was also used with examples including [[Birmingham Moor Street railway station|Moor Street station]] (1909–1914). Terracotta still remained in use, for example, in the [[Methodist Central Hall, Birmingham|Methodist Central Hall]] (1903-4) on Corporation Street.<ref name=pevsner /> [[Classical architecture]] made a return as a preferred choice of architecture during the 1920s and 1930s as well as [[Art Deco]], which was pioneered during the latter decade.

The original buildings of the [[University of Birmingham]], including its clock tower and [[The Barber Institute of Fine Arts]] (opened 1939), and the large [[Council House, Birmingham|Council House]] Extension and bridge housing the [[Birmingham Museum & Art Gallery]] (1911–1919) are from this period. [[S. N. Cooke]] and W.N. Twist's [[Hall of Memory (Birmingham)|Hall of Memory]] (1922–25)<ref name=pevsner /> and T. Cecil Howitt's [[Baskerville House]] on [[Broad Street, Birmingham|Broad Street]] (1938) were part of a large civic complex scheme designed by [[William Haywood (architect)|William Haywood]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.birmingham.gov.uk/GenerateContent?CONTENT_ITEM_ID=91618&CONTENT_ITEM_TYPE=0&MENU_ID=10277 |publisher=Birmingham City Council |title=Baskerville House |access-date=2007-09-23| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20070930225212/http://www.birmingham.gov.uk/GenerateContent?CONTENT_ITEM_ID=91618&CONTENT_ITEM_TYPE=0&MENU_ID=10277| archive-date= 30 September 2007 | url-status= live}}</ref> The Trinity Road Stand at [[Aston Villa F.C.|Aston Villa's]] [[Villa Park]] ground was completed in 1924,<ref name=trinityroad>{{cite web|url=http://www.apwj49.dsl.pipex.com/lost/trinity.htm |title=The Trinity Road Stand |publisher=Internet Football Ground Guide |access-date=2007-09-23| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20070912201635/http://www.apwj49.dsl.pipex.com/lost/trinity.htm| archive-date= 12 September 2007 | url-status= live}}</ref> and was considered the grandest in the land, complete with stained glass windows, Italian mosaics and sweeping staircase, it was thought of as architect [[Archibald Leitch]]'s masterpiece<ref>{{cite web|url=http://astonvilla.blogfootball.com/theAlmanac/park |publisher=Heroes and Villains |title=Villa Park |access-date=2007-09-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070929101911/http://astonvilla.blogfootball.com/theAlmanac/park |archive-date=29 September 2007 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and was described as "the St Pancras of football" by a ''[[The Sunday Times|Sunday Times]]'' reporter in 1960. It was demolished in 2000.<ref name=trinityroad /> The [[Birmingham Blue Coat School|Blue Coat School]] in [[Harborne]] dates from 1930, the [[King Edward's School, Birmingham|King Edward VI boys']] and [[King Edward VI High School for Girls|girls']] schools in Edgbaston from 1840, and the [[Queen Elizabeth Hospital, Birmingham|Queen Elizabeth Hospital]] from 1933 to 1938. A distinctive [[Art Deco]] cinema is the [[Odeon, Kingstanding]] (1935).<ref>{{cite book |author=Jane Turner |title=The Dictionary of Art |year=1996 |publisher=Grove |isbn=1-884446-00-0}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author=Anne Massey |title=Hollywood Beyond the Screen: Design and Material Culture |year=2000 |publisher=Berg Publishers |isbn=1-85973-321-2}}</ref> Many cinemas were constructed by [[Oscar Deutsch]] who commissioned Birmingham-born architect [[Harry Weedon]] to design many of these cinemas. Weedon's designs also extended to industrial buildings and he designed the [[Typhoo|Typhoo Tea]] factory in [[Digbeth]] in 1936.

[[File:Odeon-Sutton-Coldfield.jpg|thumb|left|The former [[Odeon Cinema, Sutton Coldfield]] by [[Harry Weedon]] and [[Cecil Clavering]], 1936.]]
Art-Deco architecture became popular in the design of cinemas, however, it was not so widespread in other buildings and its use was very limited in Birmingham. In 1933, the new Kent Street Baths, operated by the [[Birmingham Baths Committee]], was completed to a design by [[Archibald Hurley Robinson|Hurley Robinson]]. This is one of the first non-cinema buildings in Birmingham to feature this style of architecture. Another prominent building exhibiting this style is the former Times Furnishing Company store on the High Street in Birmingham, now a [[Waterstone's]] store. The building was completed in 1938 to a design by Burnett and Eprile.<ref name=hickman65>{{Harvnb|Hickman|1970|page=65}}</ref>

The [[Bournville Village Trust]] was set up in 1900 to manage the [[Bournville]] estate and public buildings growing around [[Cadbury Schweppes|Cadbury's]] in Bournville.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bvt.org.uk/history/george.html |publisher=Bournville Village Trust |title=George Cadbury |access-date=2007-09-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070922174920/http://www.bvt.org.uk/history/george.html |archive-date=22 September 2007 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Much of the planning was done by [[William Alexander Harvey]].<ref>{{Harvnb|Hickman|1970|page=57}}</ref> In addition, the Birmingham-born architect, Town Planner and Secretary of the [[Birmingham Civic Society]], [[William Haywood (architect)|William Haywood]], did much to raise the profile of the improvement of Birmingham in the inter-war years.

The ''reformed pubs'' started just after 1900 - large 'family' pubs intended to replace the workers' and drinking men's pubs of the previous century. Such pubs included ''[[Black Horse, Northfield|The Black Horse]]'' on the Bristol Road in [[Northfield, Birmingham|Northfield]] which was completed in 1929.

Birmingham's first multi-storey block of flats was built in 1937 on the Bristol Road. The building, called Viceroy Close, was designed by Mitchell and Bridgwater in partnership with Gollins and Smeeton. It also features sculptures by [[Oliver O'Connor Barrett]]. In the same year, the Art Deco "Petersfield Court" in [[Hall Green]] was completed. The building contains 14 flats and consists of large curved corner windows.<ref name=hickman65 />
{{Clear}}

==Post-World War II architecture==
[[File:The Rotunda, Birmingham.jpg|thumb|[[Jim Roberts (architect)|James A. Roberts]]' iconic [[Rotunda (Birmingham)|Rotunda]] prior to renovation, 1965.]]
Birmingham's industrial importance in [[World War II]] led to heavy and destructive bombing raids during the [[Birmingham Blitz]]. This claimed many lives and many buildings too, but the planned destruction that took place in post-war Birmingham was also extensive. The Public Works Department of Birmingham City Council established a city engineer and a city architect position within the department to aid the design and construction of new housing and public facilities in the city. Therefore, Sir [[Herbert Manzoni]], City Engineer and Surveyor of Birmingham from 1935 until 1963, became profoundly influential in changing the city. His view was "there is little of real worth in our architecture", and in any case, conservation of old buildings was merely sentimental.<ref>Quoted in Andy Foster, Birmingham, Yale University Press, London, p.197</ref> At the end of war, Birmingham again began to expand and reached a peak in its population in 1951. This produced a demand for new housing to replace that lost in the bombing raids over Birmingham upon the housing needed to meet the requirements for the growing population. As well as this, the increased use of public facilities encouraged their reconstruction and improvement by the city council.

This public demand for modern buildings, combined with Victorian architectural styles falling out of fashion, resulted in dozens of fine Victorian buildings like the intricate glass-roofed [[Birmingham New Street railway station|Birmingham New Street station]],<ref name=aerialnewstreet>{{Cite web|url=http://www.birmingham.gov.uk/GenerateContent?CONTENT_ITEM_ID=89806&CONTENT_ITEM_TYPE=0&MENU_ID=10277 |publisher=Birmingham City Council |title=Aerial View of New Street Station 1963 |access-date=2007-09-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930221007/http://www.birmingham.gov.uk/GenerateContent?CONTENT_ITEM_ID=89806&CONTENT_ITEM_TYPE=0&MENU_ID=10277 |archive-date=30 September 2007 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and the old Central Library being destroyed in the 1950s and 1960s by the city planners.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.birmingham.gov.uk/GenerateContent?CONTENT_ITEM_ID=46357&CONTENT_ITEM_TYPE=0&MENU_ID=260 |publisher=Birmingham City Council |title=Central Library - from old to new |access-date=2007-09-23 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070702174842/http://www.birmingham.gov.uk/GenerateContent?CONTENT_ITEM_ID=46357&CONTENT_ITEM_TYPE=0&MENU_ID=260 |archive-date=2007-07-02 }}</ref> These planning decisions were to have a profound effect on the image of Birmingham in subsequent decades, with the mix of concrete [[ring road]]s, [[shopping mall|shopping centres]] and [[tower block]]s giving Birmingham a '[[wiktionary:Concrete jungle|concrete jungle]]' tag.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/england/2701829.stm |title=Tackling congestion in Birmingham |work=BBC News |date=2003-02-13 |access-date=2007-09-23}}</ref> Manzoni's work included the construction of the [[A4400 road|Inner Ring Road]], [[A4540 road|Middle Ring Road]] and the [[A4040 road|Outer Ring Road]], which necessitated the purchase and clearance of vast areas of land. As well as this, he designated large areas of land redevelopment areas and set about clearing large areas of slums. Several architects were made the [[city architect of Birmingham]], with the first being [[Alwyn Sheppard Fidler]] who held the position from 1952 to 1964, when he walked out following disagreements over his design for the [[Castle Vale]] housing estate.<ref name=jones>{{cite web|url=http://www.gees.bham.ac.uk/research/cpp/membersfiles/phil/biggerbetter.pdf |title=Bigger is Better? Local authority housing and the strange attraction of high-rise, 1945-70 |author=Phil Jones, Urban Morphology Research Group |year=2002 |publisher=University of Birmingham |access-date=2007-09-23 }}</ref>

The architecture produced following World War II has been met with mixed reaction. Many of the buildings constructed in this period have since been heavily criticised and refused listing whilst others have been praised and listed. The past decade has seen the demolition of many postwar buildings and more are set to be replaced in the coming years, some controversially such as [[John Madin]]'s [[brutalist]] [[Birmingham Central Library]].<ref>{{cite magazine |url=http://www.architectsjournal.co.uk/news/dailynews/2008/08/birminghams_brutalist_library_to_be_demolished.html |title=Birmingham's Brutalist library to be demolished |magazine=[[Architects' Journal]] |date=2008-08-15 |author=Richard Vaughan |access-date=2008-08-18}}</ref>

===Commercial buildings===
[[File:Alpha Tower 2014.jpg|thumb|left|upright|[[Alpha Tower]], designed by Birmingham-born [[George Marsh (architect)|George Marsh]] of [[Richard Seifert|R. Seifert and Partners]], 1973.]]
Demand for offices had changed since the Victorian era with large office blocks being preferred by companies over small office buildings. Highrise office blocks offering large floorplates were constructed in city centre in the form of basic shapes such as cuboids. 'Big Top' was completed in the late 1950s and became the city's tallest office building and the first shopping centre in Birmingham.<ref>{{cite book|author=Chris Upton|title=A History of Birmingham|year=1993|isbn=0-85033-870-0|publisher=Phillimore|location=Chichester, Sussex}}</ref> This was followed by Laing's nearby [[Bull Ring, Birmingham|Bull Ring Shopping Centre]], which included plans for a large cylindrical office tower, in the 1960s. In 1964, [[Rotunda (Birmingham)|The Rotunda]], by [[Jim Roberts (architect)|James A. Roberts]] was completed as a separate development to the Bull Ring Shopping Centre, and although the building failed as an office tower, it became a landmark and received Grade II listed status in 2000, before being renovated into apartments by [[Urban Splash]] between 2006 and 2008.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.emporis.com/en/wm/bu/?id=streetrotunda-birmingham-unitedkingdom |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070309220721/http://www.emporis.com/en/wm/bu/?id=streetrotunda-birmingham-unitedkingdom |url-status=usurped |archive-date=9 March 2007 |publisher=Emporis |title=The Rotunda |access-date=2007-09-24}}</ref> Other postwar office highrises constructed in the city centre include [[The McLaren Building]] and [[Centre City Tower (Birmingham)|Centre City Tower]], which were constructed towards the end of the 1960s and in the early 1970s. The tallest office building constructed in Birmingham at the time was [[Alpha Tower]], and it remains so today at {{convert|100|m|ft|0}} in height.  In recent years Birmingham has seen the regeneration of a number of previously disused industrial buildings within the city, an example of which is the Walker Building, a previously disused Nautical Equipment factory the building has been refurbished to provide modern office space<ref>{{cite web|author=The Walker Building |url=http://www.thewalkerbuilding.co.uk/ |title=Walk this way |access-date=2012-08-09}}</ref>
{{clear}}

===Domestic architecture===
[[File:Nechells Flats.jpg|thumb|Birmingham's first post-war multi-storey flats in [[Nechells]].]]
[[Slum clearance in the United Kingdom|Slum clearance]], the increase in the population of Birmingham and the destruction of housing during the Birmingham Blitz led to the council constructing thousands of housing units all over the city. Mostly designed by the [[City Architect of Birmingham]] and the Public Works Department at the council, the schemes focussed on high-density housing in low-cost builds.

The immediate need for housing straight after the war was tackled by constructing [[Prefabricated buildings|prefabricated bungalows]]. Initially, the city council resisted constructing them due to the lack of materials and labour. However, the council eventually constructed 2,500 whilst a further 2,000 were constructed on private plots. They were provided initially to those who were displaced by the destruction of their homes.<ref name=a&a>{{cite web|url=http://www.birmingham.gov.uk/ELibrary?E_LIBRARY_ID=61&a=1080741348832 |title=Architecture & Austerity - Birmingham 1940-1950 |date=February 1995 |author=Birmingham City Council Department of Planning and Architecture |publisher=Birmingham City Council |access-date=2008-08-23 |format=pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080609091753/http://www.birmingham.gov.uk/ELibrary?E_LIBRARY_ID=61&a=1080741348832 |archive-date=2008-06-09 }}</ref> These structures were intended to be temporary, although many lasted longer than they were intended. A row of sixteen listed single storey Phoenix prefabs, built 1945 under the Housing (Temporary Accommodation) Act still exist on [[Wake Green#Wake Green Road|Wake Green Road]] and a 1940s Arcon V prefab was disassembled from Moat Lane in Yardley and transported to [[Avoncroft Museum of Historic Buildings]] in 1981 where it remains on display.<ref>{{Cite book| last=Stratton |first=Michael |title=Twentieth Century Industrial Archaeology |year=2000 |publisher=Taylor & Francis |isbn=0-419-24680-0 |page=36}}</ref> Following the provision of these temporary structures, the local authority looked to providing permanent housing units.

[[File:Coppice House, Hollypiece House and Homemeadow House.jpg|thumb|left|1960s flats in [[Hall Green]].]]
In July 1949, the city council approved a plan by the Birmingham COPEC Housing Improvement Society Ltd. to construct twenty flats for single women in Cob Lane. The council had been against flats initially as they had seen them as being unnecessary for their cost. However, as Birmingham's population expanded and the demand for housing increased, the idea of building flats and maisonettes across the city became more popular. Eventually, the city council acknowledged that there was a need for flats and started a programme to provide such properties for Birmingham's citizens.<ref name=a&a/>

Starting in the 1950s, a total of 464 [[tower block]]s above six storeys were built in Birmingham, 7% of all the tower blocks constructed in the United Kingdom,<ref>{{cite book |author=Michael Stratton |title=Twentieth Century Industrial Archaeology |year=2000 |publisher=Taylor & Francis |page=141}}</ref> with the first Birmingham tower blocks being built in [[Duddeston]], part of the Nechells and Duddeston Redevelopment Area, in the late-1950s. They were designed by S.N. Cooke and Partners and proved to be extremely costly for the city council.<ref name=jones /> In 1960, the Lyndhurst estate in [[Erdington]] was completed and the entire estate won a Civic Trust award in 1961.<ref name=jones /> The main tower block on the estate, the 16&nbsp;storey Harlech Tower, became the tallest tower block in the city, although it was later surpassed by many more tower blocks including the 32&nbsp;storey [[The Sentinels|Sentinels]] in the city centre, which were inspired by the [[Marina City]] complex in [[Chicago]].<ref name=jones /> Stephenson Tower was another city-centre tower block, located on top of [[Birmingham New Street railway station|New Street station]],<ref name=aerialnewstreet /> although the [[Gateway Plus|refurbishment]] of New Street station saw the demolition of the tower.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://80.249.57.22/vault/XDDocStore_5/0186408_FINAL.New%20Street%20Station.C0506606OUT.pdf |title=Birmingham Gateway committee brief |publisher=Birmingham City Council |access-date=2007-09-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071010041752/http://80.249.57.22/vault/XDDocStore_5/0186408_FINAL.New%20Street%20Station.C0506606OUT.pdf |archive-date=10 October 2007 |url-status=dead }}</ref> A group of four tower blocks located behind [[Birmingham Repertory Theatre|The Rep Theatre]] on Broad Street have also undergone an extensive renovation to improve their insulation and appearance.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.wates.co.uk/living_space/living_space_projects/bconst_partner/ |title=Birmingham Construction Partnership |publisher=Wates |access-date=2008-03-23 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080509092232/http://www.wates.co.uk/living_space/living_space_projects/bconst_partner/ |archive-date=2008-05-09 }}</ref>

The largest high-rise housing estate in Britain was constructed at [[Castle Vale]] with 34 tower blocks on the site of [[Castle Bromwich Aerodrome]]. This became an unpopular area as it began to suffer from social deprivation and crime whilst the buildings were poorly constructed leading to maintenance issues. To tackle the downward spiral of the estate, one of the largest tower block demolition and renovation programmes anywhere in Europe began in Castle Vale, with the construction of new buildings, squares and green public open spaces.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cvhat.org.uk/ |title=Castle Vale HAT |access-date=2007-09-23}}</ref>

===John Madin and Brutalism===
[[File:Chamberlain Square Birmingham 14-08-83.jpg|thumb|[[Birmingham Central Library]], before mid-1980s alterations.]]
[[John Madin]] and his architecture firm made an impact on the city, from the 1960s through to the late-1970s, comparable to that of Martin & Chamberlain in the 19th century.<ref name=Tappenden/> His best known buildings included [[Birmingham Central Library]], an inverted concrete ziggarat in the brutalist style, in Chamberlain Square.<ref>{{Harvnb|Hickman|1970|pages=93–4}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.birmingham.gov.uk/ELibrary?E_LIBRARY_ID=59&a=1134944545704 |publisher=Birmingham City Council |title=Shaping the Seventies - 1970s Architecture in Birmingham |format=pdf |access-date=2007-09-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930181807/http://www.birmingham.gov.uk/ELibrary?E_LIBRARY_ID=59&a=1134944545704 |archive-date=30 September 2007 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Built in 1974, it was once described as "''looking more like a place for burning books, than keeping them''" by [[Charles, Prince of Wales|Prince Charles]]. Madin's work was not highly regarded by the early-21st century political leadership within Birmingham. Clive Dutton, the city's former Director of Planning and Regeneration, described Madin's Central Library as a “concrete monstrosity”.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bdonline.co.uk/story.asp?sectioncode=426&storycode=3097910|title=Birmingham reveals new library plans|work=Building Design|date=19 October 2007|first=Heidi|last=Ancell}}</ref> There have been campaigns launched to get the building listed status in more recent times.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.c20society.org.uk/docs/casework/birmingham.html |title=One step closer to save Birmingham Central Library? |publisher=Twentieth Century Society |date=2006-10-28 |access-date=2007-09-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927193455/http://www.c20society.org.uk/docs/casework/birmingham.html |archive-date=27 September 2007 |url-status=dead }}</ref> However these have been unsuccessful and the building is being demolished.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.expressandstar.com/news/2011/02/26/birmingham-central-library-to-be-demolished/|newspaper=Express and Star|title=Birmingham Central Library to be demolished}}</ref> The [[Post and Mail building, Birmingham|Post and Mail building]] was completed in the late 1960s and upon its completion, the tower was hailed as a great achievement by the likes of Douglas Hickman, who worked with John Madin.<ref>{{Harvnb|Hickman|1970|pages=81–2}}</ref> A lesser known building in the city by John Madin, [[Metropolitan House]], shows the variety of architecture he brought to the city. Metropolitan House exhibited the use of exterior materials other than concrete.

However, as Modernist architecture fell out of favour in the 1980s, proposals for the redevelopment of many of the buildings constructed in Birmingham from the 1960s and 1970s were aired including redevelopment proposals for the Post and Mail Tower (most including the total demolition of the tower).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.skyscrapernews.com/buildings.php?id=560 |publisher=SkyscraperNews |title=Post and Mail Scheme (Tower 1 Scheme C) |access-date=2007-09-23| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20071015134915/http://www.skyscrapernews.com/buildings.php?id=560| archive-date= 15 October 2007 | url-status= live}}</ref> In 2005, demolition work began on the tower and a replacement office block has been constructed in its place.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.skyscrapernews.com/buildings.php?id=1788 |publisher=Skyscrapernews |title=Colmore Plaza |access-date=2007-09-23}}</ref> A building of similar architecture, the Birmingham Chamber of Commerce on the Hagley Road, still remains, however is under threat from demolition as the Birmingham Chamber of Commerce look for new premises.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/england/west_midlands/4104476.stm |title=The changing face of Birmingham |work=BBC News |date=2007-07-10 |access-date=2007-09-23}}</ref> Also set to be demolished is [[103 Colmore Row|NatWest House]]. The proposed demolition of the tower was resisted by conservation groups calling for the building to be listed, however, [[English Heritage]] concluded that there was not sufficient evidence for the tower to be listed. Many of Machin's other buildings in Birmingham have been replaced.

==Contemporary architecture==
{{wide image |Birmingham Skyline from Queen Elizabeth Hospital.jpg|905px|The [[skyline]] of Birmingham in June 2012. Birmingham's skyline stretches from [[Five Ways, Birmingham|Five Ways]] to the student towers at [[Aston University]] and is located mainly on the sandstone ridge where the city centre is. The skyline began to take shape in the 1960s and 1970s, when high rise buildings were built. Recent proposals include taller towers that will extend Birmingham's skyline into [[Eastside, Birmingham|Eastside]] and off the sandstone ridge.}}
[[File:Selfridges Birmingham from Park Street car park.jpg|upright|thumb|[[Selfridges Building, Birmingham|Selfridges]], by [[Future Systems]], 2003.]]
Birmingham has witnessed a [[Redevelopment of Birmingham|new period of construction]], prompted by the regeneration of Broad Street through [[Brindleyplace]], which began construction in the early 1990s. It features office and other mixed-use buildings designed by separate architects.<ref>{{cite book |author=Andy Coupland |title=Reclaiming the City: Mixed Use Development |year=1997 |publisher=Taylor & Francis |isbn=0-419-21360-0}}</ref> including the [[National Sea Life Centre (Birmingham)|National Sea Life Centre]], designed by [[Foster and Partners]].<ref name=carmona>{{cite book |author=Matthew Carmona |title=The Value of Urban Design: A Research Project Commissioned by CABE and DETR to Examine the Value Added by Good Urban Design |year=2001 |publisher=Thomas Telford |isbn=0-7277-2981-0}}</ref> Other architects involved in the development of Brindleyplace include [[Terry Farrell (architect)|Terry Farrell]], [[Demetri Porphyrios]], [[Allies and Morrison]] and [[Associated Architects]].<ref name=carmona />

Other large-scale projects include the major [[Bull Ring, Birmingham|Bullring Shopping Centre]] development by The Birmingham Alliance, which replaced the earlier 1960s shopping centre which had fallen out of favour with the public. The new shopping centre was completed in 2004 and was designed by Benoy<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.benoy.com/ |title=Benoy |access-date=2007-09-23| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20070811124442/http://www.benoy.com/| archive-date= 11 August 2007 | url-status= live}}</ref> in partnership with [[Future Systems]] who designed the iconic and award-winning [[Selfridges Building, Birmingham|Selfridges Building]] which is an irregularly-shaped structure, covered in thousands of reflective discs (see picture) and is a form of [[blobitecture]]. In [[Eastside, Birmingham|Eastside]], the Learning and Leisure Zone has seen the construction of the Eastside campus of [[Matthew Boulton College]], [[Millennium Point (Birmingham)|Millennium Point]] and the [[New Technology Institute]]. Future projects will build upon the educational presence that has been established in the area.

One of the most recent high-rise buildings to be constructed and opened within the city centre itself is [[Ian Simpson (architect)|Ian Simpson]]'s [[10 Holloway Circus|Holloway Circus Tower]], which opened in January 2006. When topped out, it became the second tallest building in Birmingham at {{convert|122|m|ft|0}}, only being beaten by the [[British Telecom Tower (Birmingham)|BT Tower]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.skyscrapernews.com/buildings.php?id=153 |publisher=SkyscraperNews |title=Holloway Circus Tower |access-date=2007-09-23| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20070930165408/http://www.skyscrapernews.com/buildings.php?id=153| archive-date= 30 September 2007 | url-status= live}}</ref> This has been prompted by the publication of the city council's "''High Places''" document which outlined locations along the city centre sandstone ridge that were deemed appropriate for the construction of high rise structures.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.birmingham.gov.uk/GenerateContent?CONTENT_ITEM_ID=13971&CONTENT_ITEM_TYPE=0&MENU_ID=1453 |title=High Places |publisher=Birmingham City Council |access-date=2007-10-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071012100523/http://birmingham.gov.uk/GenerateContent?CONTENT_ITEM_ID=13971&CONTENT_ITEM_TYPE=0&MENU_ID=1453 |archive-date=12 October 2007 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Developers [[Urban Splash]] recently completed the refurbishment of [[Fort Dunlop]] and [[Rotunda (Birmingham)|The Rotunda]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.emporis.com/en/bu/nc/ne/?id=101855 |title=Urban makes a splash at Rotunda |publisher=Emporis News |date=2007-07-29 |access-date=2007-09-24 |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071023203621/http://www.emporis.com/en/bu/nc/ne/?id=101855 |archive-date=2007-10-23 }}</ref> and are involved in the redevelopment of the former Cincinnati Lamb factory in Erdington and the future refurbishment of three tower blocks on the Birchfield Road in [[Perry Barr]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.propertyweek.com/story.asp?storyCode=3090255 |title=Urban Splash makes waves in Birmingham |publisher=[[Property Week]] |date=2007-06-27 |access-date=2007-09-24}}</ref>

</gallery>

==Future developments==
{{Main|Big City Plan}}
{{update-section|date=November 2024}}
[[File:Curzon St Illustration.png|thumb|left|CGI of the proposed new [[Birmingham Curzon Street railway station|Curzon Street]] [[High Speed 2]] terminus.]]

New projects and redevelopment schemes are planned for the city as part of Birmingham City Council's '''Big City Plan'''.  The new [[Library of Birmingham]] in [[Centenary Square]], which is seen as a flagship project for the [[Big City Plan]],<ref>{{citation | url=http://www.ibtimes.com/articles/214672/20110915/in-progress-library-of-birmingham-mecanoo-architecten.htm|work=International Business Times|title=Library of Birmingham - Mecanoo architecten|access-date=2011-09-15}}</ref> opened in September 2013. The other major project is the redevelopment of [[Birmingham New Street railway station|New Street station]], the 1960s station is currently being completely refurbished and clad in stainless steel. The [[Grand Central, Birmingham|Grand Central Shopping Centre]] which sits above the station was completely refurbished as part of the works with a new [[John Lewis (department store)|John Lewis]] department store as the anchor tenant.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.newstreetnewstart.co.uk/about-the-development/our-vision.aspx |publisher=Network Rail |title=New Street: Our Vision |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120903082906/http://www.newstreetnewstart.co.uk/about-the-development/our-vision.aspx |archive-date=2012-09-03 }}</ref>

[[Eastside, Birmingham|Eastside]] is a major development area of currently{{when|date=November 2024}} vacant land after demolition of buildings over the previous years. Included is [[Eastside City Park]], a 6.75 acre park, which is the first city park created since the 19th century.<ref>[http://www.birminghammail.net/news/top-stories/2010/09/30/work-to-start-on-13m-green-oasis-in-birmingham-city-centre-97319-27368751/2/ Birmingham Mail report on Stage 2] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120930131734/http://www.birminghammail.net/news/top-stories/2010/09/30/work-to-start-on-13m-green-oasis-in-birmingham-city-centre-97319-27368751/2/ |date=2012-09-30 }}</ref> [[Birmingham City University]] have built a new city centre campus adjacent to [[Millennium Point (Birmingham)|Millennium Point]] with further plans for the vacant adjacent plots.<ref>[http://www.birminghampost.net/news/west-midlands-news/2011/02/04/birmingham-city-university-submits-new-plans-for-eastside-campus-65233-28110590/ Birmingham Post BCU City Centre Campus]</ref> Future developments include a new Museum Quarter named Curzon Square which will use the former [[Birmingham Curzon Street railway station (1838-1966)|Curzon Street station]] as an art gallery. The new Museum Quarter will sit alongside a new railway station which will be the terminus for the [[High Speed 2]] railway line.<ref>{{Citation| url = http://www.ikon-gallery.co.uk/Repository/pages/197/0485f379-66d0-48f3-b585-88cce714e9b1.pdf| title = Curzon Square| access-date = 14 April 2012| publisher = Ikon| url-status = dead| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20130513020407/http://www.ikon-gallery.co.uk/Repository/pages/197/0485f379-66d0-48f3-b585-88cce714e9b1.pdf| archive-date = 13 May 2013}}</ref>

A large project completed in April 2013 is [[Snowhill]], which has seen the construction of two large office blocks alongside Snow Hill station. Developers [[Argent Group]] have put forward proposals for Paradise Circus in the civic centre. This included demolition of [[Birmingham Central Library|Central Library]] and the surrounding buildings and the construction of new hotels, offices, public squares, restaurants and bars.<ref>{{Citation | url = http://www.paradisecircus.co.uk/public-consultation/ParadiseCircus-Boards-2012.pdf | title = Paradise Circus| access-date = 14 April 2012| publisher =Argent}}</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Architecture of Brazil
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}} <!-- "none" is preferred when the title is sufficiently descriptive; see [[WP:SDNONE]] -->
[[File:São Francisco de Assis.jpg|thumb|The [[Church of São Francisco de Assis, Ouro Preto|Church of São Francisco de Assis]] in [[Ouro Preto]], one of the best known architectural icons of Baroque architecture in Brazil]]
[[File:Palacio Alvorada commons.jpg|thumb|The [[Palácio da Alvorada]] in [[Brasília]], listed as a [[List of National Historic Heritage of Brazil|National Historic Heritage Site]]]]

The '''architecture of Brazil''' is influenced by Europe, especially Portugal. It has a history that goes back 500 years to the time when [[Pedro Álvares Cabral|Pedro Cabral]] arrived in Brazil in 1500. [[Portuguese colonial architecture]] was the first wave of architecture to go to Brazil.

In the 18th century, during the time of the [[Empire of Brazil|Empire]], Brazil followed European trends and adopted [[Neoclassical architecture|Neoclassical]], [[Baroque architecture|Baroque]], and [[Gothic Revival architecture]]. Then, in the 20th century especially in [[Brasília]], Brazil experimented with [[Modernist architecture]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Uma visão de arquitetura colonial no Brasil |trans-title=A vision of colonial architecture in Brazil)|last=Hue|first=Jorge de Souza|date=1999|isbn=9788522005185}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite book|title=The Golden Age of Brazil, 1695-1750: Growing Pains of a Colonial Society|last=Boxer|first=Charles Ralph|date=1962|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=9780520015500|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/goldenageofbrazi00boxe}}</ref> The modernist approach was named as minimalism without the need for excessive frills or decoration. Instead, the architecture became more simplistic, with clean lines and a functional form. This style became more popular around the end of World War II, when function was more important than form.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.brazil.org.za/architecture.html |title=Brazil Architecture |last=Meyer |first=Amelia |date=2010 |website=Brazil.org.za|access-date=14 April 2019}}</ref> During this time, [[Oscar Niemeyer]], who became and remains one of the world's greatest modernists, began to present a style that was to become Brazil's very own style.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://www.biography.com/people/oscar-niemeyer-9423385|title=Oscar Niemeyer|website=Biography|access-date=2019-03-25|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170425135626/http://www.biography.com/people/oscar-niemeyer-9423385|archive-date=2017-04-25|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=http://brazil.com/home/culture/architecture-landmarks/architecture-history-timeline/|title=Architecture in Brazil - A Brief History |website=Brazil.com |access-date=14 April 2019}}</ref>

==Indigenous architecture==
[[File:Taba indigena.jpg|thumb|left|An 1854 depiction of an indigenous village (''taba'') showing a group of ocas arranged in a circle surrounded by a wooden [[palisade]]]]

The diverse groups of [[Indigenous Brazilians]] developed architectural styles that varied by region and available materials. An important style of dwelling is the so-called [[Oca (structure)|oca]]. A wooden structure covered with straw or palm leaves, that was for collective use and had no internal divisions. Several ocas could be organized around a circular plaza. They could reach up to 30 m in length and 10 m in height.

Another example is the [[Maloca]], a type of large, communal cabin used by some indigenous people in the Amazon regions of northern Brazil and southern Colombia.

This [[vernacular architecture]] is still common among contemporary indigenous peoples in northern Brazil. Historically this type of architecture did not have widespread use among non-indigenous Brazilians. Recently, however, these architectural models, reinterpreted with current techniques and materials, have received attention from some architects as an ecological alternative to address modern housing problem.{{Citation needed|date=June 2025}}

== Portuguese colonial architecture in the 16th century ==
[[File:Salvador-CCBY-2.jpg|thumb|Portuguese colonial architecture, Salvador.]]
The [[Portuguese colonial architecture|colonial architecture]] of Brazil dates to the early 16th century when Brazil was first explored, created and settled by the Portuguese, who created an architecture familiar to them in Europe. They built sacred and secular buildings, including houses and forts in Brazilian cities and the countryside. They founded [[Recife]], [[São Paulo]], [[Rio de Janeiro]], [[Salvador, Bahia|Salvador]] in the colonial period; these cities saw the best expression of Brazilian architecture.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" />

Buildings of this period were distinct because they followed similar rules such as:
* symmetry
* box-like structure
* alcoves and recessed windows
* constructed from stone and mortar
* covered with plaster for a smooth finish

The best examples are in the city of Salvador, with its multi-colored colonial buildings that outline the streets and depict Salvador's history.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4">{{Citation|last=Monetti|first=Eliane|chapter=Brazil|date=2002|doi=10.1007/978-1-4615-0869-4_24|pages=333–342|publisher=Springer US|isbn=9781461352792|title=Real Estate Education Throughout the World: Past, Present and Future|volume=7|series=Research Issues in Real Estate}}</ref>

=== Salvador ===
Founded in the 1500s, Salvador is one of the oldest cities in Brazil and home to impressive colonial and baroque architecture. The city was Brazil's first capital until 1763 and is known for its spectacular colonial and baroque styles. After defeating the Dutch in the 17th century, Portuguese settlers built and refurbished several forts along the Bay, including São Marcelo Fort. The port stands perfectly round on a small reef bank about 1,000 feet off the coast. Brazilian writer Jorge Amado described it as the "Belly button of Bahia.".<ref name=":4" />

One of the most well-known pieces of architecture in Salvador is the Lacerda Elevator. Built around 1872, this structure linked both upper and lower cities with four elevators, with air conditioning and offering views of the bay. Furthermore, the city has numerous buildings with meaningful cultural and historical significance.<ref name=":4" />

== 18th-19th century Brazilian architecture ==

[[File:Teatro Municipal de São Paulo 8.jpg|thumb|Municipal Theatre of São Paulo shows Neoclassical architecture in Brazil.]]
Between the 18th and 19th Century Brazilian architecture is a period that saw the introduction of more European styles to Brazil such as Neoclassical and Baroque architecture. This was usually mixed with Brazilian influences from their own heritage which produced a unique form of Brazilian architecture.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

=== Baroque ===
{{Main|Baroque in Brazil}}
The best examples of Baroque architecture in Brazil are found in the city of Ouro Preto where buildings start to take more ornate forms and rounded corners. Certain structures also depict painting which are incorporated into the walls.<ref name=":3" /> In 1980, Unesco declared the city a “world monument” with 13 churches, 11 chapels, major museums, ancient bridges, and well-preserved houses. The best preserved residence is the Casa dos Contos, built in 1780. A beige and white three-story building with a stone watering trough for horses in the back yard as well as dark flagstone cubicles where slaves lived.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last=Ferreira|first=Carla Mercês da Rocha Jatobá|last2=Lopes|first2=Eliane Marta Teixeira|last3=Rahme|first3=Mônica Maria Farid|date=April 2016|title=Professora Dra. Anne-Marie Chartier|journal=Revista Brasileira de Estudos Pedagógicos|volume=97|issue=245|pages=17–29|doi=10.1590/s2176-6681/403314607|issn=2176-6681|doi-access=free}}</ref> Today the structure is served as the office of the city's postal authorities while depicting the city's history and simplistic styles.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nytimes.com/1983/06/12/travel/the-baroque-of-minas-gerais.html.|title=The Baroque of Minas Gerais|last=Hoge|first=Warren|date=June 12, 1983|website=The New York Times}}</ref><ref name=":5" />

=== Neoclassicism ===
Neoclassicism refers back to ancient Rome and Greece by adopting their large multi story columns and grand triangular roofs. The liberal use of white soapstone, limestone, or marble are also indicators of Neoclassical buildings. Great examples lay in the city of Manaus, specifically the Theatro Amazonas .<ref name=":3" /> By the turn of the 20th century, the Amazonian region of Brazil began to prosper. The increasing amounts of money from exports from its rubber plantations region flourished particularly the capital city of Manaus. Wealthy rubber barons tried to recreate lavish lifestyle of European elites. In order to do so, an Opera House, the Teatro Amazonas, was built in the middle of the rainforest. The construction began in 1884 under the supervision of an Italian Architect. The roofing came from Alsace, the furniture from Paris, marble from Italy and the steel from England. The entire dome is wonderfully covered with 36,000 decorated ceramic tiles painted in the colors of the Brazilian national flag: Blue, yellow, and green.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.atlasobscura.com/places/teatro-amazonas-manaus|title=Teatro Amazonas em Manaus|date=April 10, 2010|website=Atlas Obscura|access-date=14 April 2019}}</ref>

== 20th century Brazilian architecture ==
[[File:Brasilia Congresso Nacional 05 2007 221.jpg|thumb|Brasília National Congress, an example of Modernist architecture.]]
In the 1950s Brazil decided to found a new capital city in the interior of Brazil to help develop Brazil's interior. The city was [[Brasília]] and it would see a great experiment in modernist architecture. Government buildings, churches and civic buildings would be constructed in the modernist style.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> Throughout the modern age, Brazil began to define itself as a county in its architecture. This was done so with the help of Brazil's most famous architect and designer, [[Oscar Niemeyer]]. He designed the Edificio Copan in São Paulo, one of Brazil's biggest cities, and the entire city of Brasília. His buildings were characterized by the use of concrete and free-flowing curves.<ref name=":3" />

=== Oscar Niemeyer ===
[[File:Oscar Ribeiro de Almeida Niemeyer Soares Filho..tif|thumb|left|upright|Oscar Niemeyer in 1958]]
As a young man, Niemeyer worked for his father as a typographer before entering the [[Escola Nacional de Belas Artes]]. After his graduation, Niemeyer went off to work for [[Lúcio Costa]], who was an architect from the [[Modern architecture|Modernist school]].<ref name=":2" /> In 1941, Niemeyer launched his solo career by designing multiple buildings called the Pampulha Architectural Complex in the city of [[Belo Horizonte]]. This was when Niemeyer began developing some of his well-known design trademarks such as the heavy uses of solid and an inclination towards curves. Niemeyer stated: "I consciously ignored the highly praised right angle and the rational architecture of T-squares and triangles, in order to wholeheartedly enter the world of curves and new shapes made possible by the introduction of concrete into the building process".<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":6">{{Cite web|url=https://www.pritzkerprize.com/biography-oscar-niemeyer|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190516200247/https://www.pritzkerprize.com/biography-oscar-niemeyer|url-status=live|archive-date=May 16, 2019|title=Biography: Oscar Niemeyer|website=The Pritzker Architecture Prize|access-date=14 April 2019}}</ref>

Interesting enough, Niemeyer was introduced in the [[Brazilian Communist Party]] during his youth years and officially joined in 1945. This became an issue for him in 1964 as the Brazilian military removed the government and viewed Niemeyer as a dangerous individual, thus ransacking his office as well. Shocked, he decided to leave the country for good and move to France, furthering his career and designs there.<ref name=":2" />

Nevertheless, Niemeyer redefined architecture in Brazil by leaning away from old and European-influenced styles and creating new and aesthetic designs instead. Particularly in cities such as Brasília, where he obtained a structural solution that would distinct the city's architecture. In order to do so, he made the structures very different, where the columns became more narrow at a point where the structures would seem to barely touch the ground.<ref name=":6" /> As a result, Niemeyer remains one of the most well-known architects in Brazil as his structures are visited by many worldwide.

=== Presidential Palace (Palácio da Alvorada) ===
One of Niemeyer's greatest successes was the [[Palácio da Alvorada]] in Brasília. A two-story glass and concrete structure with curved supports forming the façade on all of the four walls.<ref name=":3" /> These walls are stretched between the supports are translucent walls of tinted glass. The nave is entered by an impressive subterranean passage rather than a conventional doorway.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.britannica.com/place/Brasilia.|title=Brasilia|date=September 21, 2018|website=Encyclopedia Britannica|access-date=}}</ref> Thus, the Presidential Palace, along with many other of Oscar's designs drew attention to the architecture in Brazil and created a modern style for Brazil as well.
