======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Architecture of Denmark
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}} <!-- "none" is preferred when the title is sufficiently descriptive; see [[WP:SDNONE]] -->
{{Use dmy dates|date=February 2020}}
[[File:Frederiksborg-2.jpg|alt=A palace, with several copper-covered spires, a dome, and tiered wings with dormers, is reflected in a large artificial lake in the foreground.|thumb|300px|Renaissance-styled [[Frederiksborg Palace]] completed by [[Hans van Steenwinckel the Younger]] in 1620]]
The '''architecture of Denmark''' has its origins in the [[Viking Age]], revealed by archaeological finds. It was established in the [[Middle Ages]] when first [[Romanesque architecture|Romanesque]], then [[Gothic architecture|Gothic]] churches and cathedrals, were built throughout the country. During this period, brick became the construction material of choice for churches, fortifications and castles, as the country had little access to stone.

Under the influence of [[Frederick II of Denmark|Frederick II]] and [[Christian IV of Denmark|Christian IV]], both of whom had been inspired by the [[Château|castles of France]], Dutch and Flemish designers were brought to Denmark to improve the country's fortifications. They increasingly transitioned to building magnificent royal castles and palaces in the [[Renaissance architecture|Renaissance]] style. In parallel, the half-timbered style became popular for ordinary dwellings in towns and villages across the country.

Late in his reign, Christian IV also became an early proponent of [[Baroque architecture|Baroque]] which was to continue for a considerable time with many impressive buildings both in the capital and the provinces. [[Neoclassical architecture|Neoclassicism]] came initially from France but was slowly adopted by native Danish architects who increasingly participated in defining architectural style. A productive period of [[Historicism (art)|Historicism]] merged into the 19th century [[National Romantic style]].

In the 1960s, Danish architects entered the world scene with their highly successful [[Functionalism (architecture)#Denmark|Functionalism]]. This evolved into designs such as the [[Sydney Opera House]] and the [[Great Belt Fixed Link|Great Belt Bridge]], allowing Danish designers to be rewarded for excellence both at home and abroad.

==Middle Ages==

=== Viking Age ===
[[File:Fyrkat hus stor.jpg|alt=A primitive one-storey hut made of wooden planks with shingled roof, a single entrance and a few small skylights.|thumb|Reconstructed Viking house, Fyrkat]]
[[Archaeological excavations]] in various parts of [[Denmark]] have revealed much about the way the [[Vikings]] lived. One such site is [[Hedeby]], located {{cvt|45|km}} south of the Danish border near [[Schleswig, Schleswig-Holstein|Schleswig]], it probably dates back to the end of the 8th century. Oak [[Framing (construction)|frames]] were used for the walls, and the roofs were probably [[thatched]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1553/|title=Archaeological Border complex of Hedeby and the Danevirke|publisher=Unesco|accessdate=16 September 2024 |language=}}</ref>

Viking ring houses, such as those at [[Trelleborg (Slagelse)|Trelleborg]], have a ship-like shape with long walls bulging outwards. Each house had a large central hall, {{cvt|18| ×|8|m}}, and two smaller rooms, one at each end. Those at [[Fyrkat]] ({{circa|980}}), in the north of [[Jutland]], were {{convert|28.5|m|ft|abbr=on}} long, {{convert|5|m|ft|abbr=on}} wide at the ends and {{convert|7.5|m|ft|abbr=on}} in the middle, the long walls curving slightly outwards. The walls had double rows of posts with planks wedged horizontally between them. A series of outer posts slanted towards the wall were possibly used to support the building like buttresses.<ref>{{Citation | url = http://www.sydhimmerlandsmuseum.dk/fyrkat/vikingeborgen.htm | title = Vikingeborgen Fyrkat | language = da | access-date = 16 November 2009 | publisher = Sydhimmer landsmuseum | place = DK | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090804110119/http://www.sydhimmerlandsmuseum.dk/fyrkat/vikingeborgen.htm | archive-date = 4 August 2009}}.</ref>

===Romanesque style===
[[File:Ringsted kosciol mpazdziora.JPG|alt=A cruciform, copper-roofed, brick church in Romanesque style with rounded window arches and domed apse. The large tower has pointed Gothic-styled windows.|thumb|left|[[St. Bendt's Church]] in [[Ringsted]], 1170]]
Denmark's first churches from the 9th century were built of timber and have not survived. Hundreds of stone churches in the [[Romanesque style]] were built in the 12th and 13th centuries. They had a flat-ceilinged [[nave]] and [[chancel]] with small rounded windows and round arches. Granite boulders and limestone were initially the preferred building materials, but after brick production reached Denmark in the middle of the 12th century, brick quickly became the material of choice.<ref>{{Citation|url=http://www.natmus.dk/cons/walls/chrchpnt.htm |title=Introduction to the Restoration of Danish Wall Paintings |publisher=The National Museum |place=[[Denmark|DK]] |access-date=11 November 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091124021603/http://www.natmus.dk/cons/walls/chrchpnt.htm |archive-date=24 November 2009 }}.</ref> Notable examples of [[brick Romanesque]] buildings are [[St. Bendt's Church]] in [[Ringsted]] ({{circa|1170}})<ref>{{Citation | place = DK | url = http://www.visitvordingborg.dk/international/en-gb/productpage/produktside.htm?id=2649 | contribution = St Bendt's Ringsted | title = Visit Vordingborg | access-date = 11 November 2009 | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110719133116/http://www.visitvordingborg.dk/international/en-gb/productpage/produktside.htm?id=2649 | archive-date = 19 July 2011}}.</ref> and the unique [[Church of Our Lady, Kalundborg|Church of Our Lady]] in [[Kalundborg]] ({{circa|1200}}) with its five tall towers.<ref>{{Citation|url=http://vorfruesogn.folkekirken.dk/index.php?id=18086 |title=Vor Frue Sogn |contribution=Summary |access-date=15 December 2009 |publisher=Folke Kirken |place=DK |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090804143452/http://www.vorfruesogn.folkekirken.dk/index.php?id=18086 |archive-date=4 August 2009 }}.</ref>

The [[Østerlars Church|church at Østerlars]] on the island of [[Bornholm]] was built around 1150. Like three other churches on the island, it is a [[round church]]. The three-storeyed building is supported by a circular outer wall and an exceptionally wide, hollow central column.<ref>{{Citation | title = Home of our fathers | url = http://www.homeofourfathers.com/lisbeth/oesterlarsoesterherredbornholmdk.htm | contribution = Østerlars Kirke | access-date = 15 November 2009 | archive-url = https://archive.today/20130103024403/http://www.homeofourfathers.com/lisbeth/oesterlarsoesterherredbornholmdk.htm | archive-date = 3 January 2013 | url-status = usurped}}.</ref>

Construction of [[Lund Cathedral]] in [[Scania]] started in about 1103 when the region was part of the Kingdom of Denmark. It was the first of great Danish Romanesque cathedrals in the shape of a three-aisled basilica with transepts. It seems to have been related to earlier German buildings, though there are also traces of [[Norman architecture|Anglo-Norman]] and [[Lombardy|Lombard]] influences.<ref>{{Citation|place=[[United Kingdom|UK]] |url=http://www.viamichelin.co.uk/web/Datasheet/SWE0000057/41104/Cathedral?from=DIRECTORY |contribution=Lund Cathedral |title=The Green Guide |publisher=Via Michelin |access-date=15 January 2009 }}{{dead link|date=October 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}.</ref> [[Ribe Cathedral|Ribe]], which followed with its great cathedral (1150–1250), had close trade contacts with the [[Rhine]] region of Germany. Both the materials, sandstone and [[tufa]], and the models were taken from there.<ref name="um.dk">{{Citation|url=http://www.um.dk/Publikationer/UM/English/Denmark/kap4/4-2.asp#4-2-1 |title=Architecture |place=DK |publisher=Ministry of Foreign Affairs |access-date=11 November 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090513041557/http://www.um.dk/Publikationer/UM/English/Denmark/kap4/4-2.asp |archive-date=13 May 2009 }}</ref>

===Gothic style===
[[File:Skt. Peders Kirke - Næstved.jpg|thumb|[[St. Peter's Church, Næstved]] (1375)]]
Towards the end of the 13th century, and until about 1500, the [[Gothic style]] became the norm. This resulted in rebuilding or adopting older, Romanesque churches to the Gothic style: the flat ceilings were replaced by high cross vaults, windows were enlarged with pointed arches, chapels and towers were added, and the interiors were decorated with murals.<ref>{{Citation | url = http://www.visitdenmark.com/irland/en-ie/menu/turist/inspiration/detkulturelledanmark/kunst/churces-and-cathedrals.htm | title = Culture | contribution = Churches and cathedrals | publisher = Visit Denmark | access-date = 5 December 2009 | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110717215248/http://www.visitdenmark.com/irland/en-ie/menu/turist/inspiration/detkulturelledanmark/kunst/churces-and-cathedrals.htm | archive-date = 17 July 2011}}.</ref> Red brick was the material of choice as seen in [[St. Canute's Cathedral]], [[Odense]] (1300–1499), and [[St. Peter's Church, Næstved]]. St. Canute's presents all the features of Gothic architecture: pointed arch, buttresses, [[rib vault|ribbed vaulting]], increased light and the spatial combination of nave and chancel.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.odensedomkirke.dk/kirker/domkirken-skt-knuds-kirke/domkirkens-arkitektur|title=Domkirkens arkitektur|publisher=Odense Domkirke|accessdate=1 September 2024 |language=da}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://denstoredanske.lex.dk/gotisk_arkitektur|title=Gotisk arkitektur|publisher=lexdk: Den Store Danske|author=Fleischer, Jens|date=12 April 2024|accessdate=1 September 2024 |language=da}}</ref>
 
Most Gothic architecture in Denmark is found in churches and monasteries, though there are also examples in the secular field. [[Glimmingehus]] (1499–1506), a rectangular castle in Scania, was commissioned by the Danish nobleman Jens Holgersen Ulfstand who hired [[Adam van Düren]], a North German master who also worked on [[Lund Cathedral]]. The building contains many defensive features of the times, including parapets, false doors, dead-end corridors, murder-holes for pouring boiling pitch over the attackers, moats, drawbridges and various other death traps to protect the nobles against peasant uprisings.<ref>{{Citation | url = http://www.algonet.se/~sylve_a/glimmhus.htm | contribution = Glimmingehus | title = Skånska slott och herrestäten | language = sv | access-date = 8 December 2009 | publisher = Algo net | place = [[Sweden|SE]]}}.</ref>
[[File:Anne Hvides Gaard Svendborg.jpg|alt=Large three-storied, half-timbered house, with plaster filling.|thumb|[[Anne Hvides Gård]], [[Svendborg]] (1560)]]

===Half-timbered buildings===

During the late Middle Ages, a slow transition began from the traditional wooden houses in towns and villages towards [[half-timbered]] properties. One of the oldest in Denmark is [[Anne Hvides Gård]], a two-storeyed townhouse in [[Svendborg]] on the island of [[Funen]], constructed in 1560.<ref>{{Citation | url = http://fynhistorie.dk/node/26033 | title = Anne Hvides Gård i Fruestræde | publisher = Fynhistorie | place = DK | language = da | access-date = 14 November 2009}}.</ref> The building now forms part of the Svendborg Museum.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://svendborgmuseum.dk/om-museet/anne-hvides-gaard/|title=Anne Hvides Gård|publisher=Svendborg Museum|accessdate=1 September 2024 |language=da}}</ref>

[[Ystad]] in the southern Swedish region of [[Scania]], which was formerly part of Denmark, still has some 300 half-timbered houses, several of them of historic importance.<ref>{{Citation|place=[[Sweden|SE]] |url=http://www.ystad.se/Ystadweb.nsf/AllDocuments/C7605627BFE06797C125730E0023A73E |title=A walk through the centuries |publisher=Ystads kommun |access-date=22 November 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090725063006/http://www.ystad.se/Ystadweb.nsf/AllDocuments/C7605627BFE06797C125730E0023A73E |archive-date=25 July 2009 }}.</ref> The oldest surviving half-timbered house in Denmark, built in 1527, is located in [[Køge]] on the east coast of [[Zealand (Denmark)|Sealand]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://groenomstilling.koege.dk/groen-omstilling/det-groenne-hus-2|title=Det Grønne Hus|publisher=Køge Kommune|accessdate=1 September 2024 |language=da}}</ref>

The Old Town in [[The Old Town, Aarhus|Aarhus]], Jutland, is an open-air village museum consisting of 75 historical buildings collected from all parts of the country. They include a variety of half-timbered houses, some dating back to the middle of the 16th century.<ref>{{Citation|url=http://www.dengamleby.dk/collect.htm |title=Collections |publisher=DenGamleBy |access-date=22 November 2009 |place=DK |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100519121705/http://www.dengamleby.dk/collect.htm |archive-date=19 May 2010 }}</ref>

==Renaissance==
[[File:Egeskov Slot spejling Edit 2.jpg|thumb|[[Egeskov Castle]] on Funen from the 16th century.]]
[[Renaissance architecture]] thrived during the reigns of [[Frederick II of Denmark|Frederick II]] and especially [[Christian IV of Denmark|Christian IV]]. Inspired by the [[Château|French castles]] of the times, Flemish architects designed [[Kronborg Castle]] in [[Helsingør]] and [[Frederiksborg Palace]] in [[Hillerød]]. In Copenhagen, [[Rosenborg Castle]] (1606–24) and [[Børsen]] or the former stock exchange (1640) are recognized as important Renaissance buildings.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://denstoredanske.lex.dk/nederlandsk_ren%C3%A6ssance|title=Nederlandsk renæssance|publisher=lexdk: Den Store Danske|author=Funder, Morten Johan|work=Den Store Danske |date=16 April 2024|accessdate=1 September 2024 |language=da}}</ref>

During the reign of [[Frederick II of Denmark|Frederick II]], Kronborg Castle was designed by two Flemish architects: [[Hans Hendrik van Paesschen]] who started the work in 1574, and [[Anthonis van Obbergen]] who finished it in 1585. Modelled on a three-winged French castle, it was completed as a full four-winged building. The castle burnt down in 1629 but, under orders from Christian IV, was quickly rebuilt under the leadership of [[Hans van Steenwinckel the Younger]], son of the famous Flemish artist. It is recognized as an outstanding Renaissance castle and is a UNESCO [[World Heritage Site]].<ref>{{Citation | url = https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/696 | contribution = Kronborg | publisher = UNESCO | title = World Heritage Site | access-date = 11 November 2009}}.</ref>

[[Frederiksborg Palace]] (1602–20) in Hillerød is the largest Renaissance palace in [[Scandinavia]]. Christian IV had most of Frederick II's original building pulled down to have van Steenwinckel complete a three-winged French-styled castle with a low terrace wing around a courtyard. The architectural expression and the decorative finish reflect [[Dutch Renaissance]] preferences, as evidenced by the ornamental portals and windows and especially in sweeping Italianate gables.<ref name=um.dk />
[[File:Rosenborg-1.jpg|alt=Castle with turrets and spires and walled enclosure, on the tip of a narrow peninsula.|thumb|left|{{Citation | title = [[Rosenborg Castle]] | place = Copenhagen | author1-link = Hans van Steenwinckel the Younger| first1 = Hans | last1 = van Steenwinckel | first2 = Bertel | last2 = Lange | year = 1624}}]]

[[Rosenborg Castle]] in Copenhagen, also built by Christian IV, is another example of the Dutch Renaissance style. In 1606, the king first had a two-storey summerhouse built on a site he used as a park for relaxation. He then decided to start work on the castle, which developed in stages until the [[Dutch Renaissance]] building was completed in 1624. Predating the castle, the Renaissance-style park is Denmark's oldest royal garden.<ref>{{Citation|publisher=Rosenborg slot |url=http://www.rosenborgslot.dk/asp/menu/menuPages/omslottet_2.asp?countryID=2 |title=The History of Rosenborg Castle |place=[[Denmark|DK]] |access-date=7 December 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070318062902/http://www.rosenborgslot.dk/asp/menu/menuPages/omslottet_2.asp?countryID=2 |archive-date=18 March 2007 }}.</ref>

Sponsored by Christian IV, Børsen was built from 1618 to 1624 as one of the first commodity exchanges in Europe. It was designed to emphasize Copenhagen's position as a commercial metropolis. Although inspired by the Dutch Renaissance style, the towers and garrets on the roof reflect the taste of Christian IV. The spire of the building, with four intertwined dragon tails topped by three crowns, symbolises the kingdoms of Denmark, [[Norway]], and [[Sweden]].<ref>{{Citation | url = http://www.visitcopenhagen.com/content/press/press_information/copenhagen_specialities/copenhagen_remembers_the_renaissance | title = Copenhagen specialities | contribution = Copenhagen Remembers the Renaissance | publisher = Visit Copenhagen | access-date = 11 November 2009 | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20081025072842/http://www.visitcopenhagen.com/content/press/press_information/copenhagen_specialities/copenhagen_remembers_the_renaissance | archive-date = 25 October 2008}}.</ref>

In 1614, Christian IV began work on the construction of the then Danish [[Kristianstad]] in Scania, now in the south of Sweden, completing many of its buildings in the Renaissance style. The [[Trinity Church, Kristianstad|Church of the Trinity]] (1618–28) designed by Flemish-Danish architect [[Lorenz van Steenwinckel]] is considered by many to be Scandinavia's most beautiful Renaissance church.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.svenskakyrkan.se/kristianstad/historik|title=Historik|publisher=Svenska kyrkan|date=17 October 2019|accessdate=1 September 2024 |language=sv}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sydsverige.dk/?pageID=153|title=Heliga Trefaldighets kyrkan i Kristianstad|publisher=Sydsveige.dk|accessdate=15 September 2024 |language=da}}</ref>

[[File:Holbæk - Gamle huse.JPG|thumb|Holbæk, Zealand (17th century). Timber-framed houses with bricks and paned glass windows.]]
Christian IV also initiated a number of projects in Norway that were largely based on Renaissance architecture<ref>{{Citation | first = Joakim A | last = Skovgaard | title = A king's architecture: Christian IV and his buildings | place = London | year = 1973 | isbn = 0-238-78979-9}}.</ref>{{Rp | needed = yes | date =February 2013}}  He established mining operations in [[Kongsberg (town)|Kongsberg]] and [[Røros (town)|Røros]], now a World Heritage Site. After a devastating fire in 1624, the town of [[Oslo]] was moved to a new location and rebuilt as a fortified city with an [[Grid plan|orthogonal layout]] surrounded by ramparts, and renamed [[Christiania, Norway|Christiania]]. King Christian also founded the trading city of [[Kristiansand (town)|Kristiansand]], once again naming it after himself.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://snl.no/Christian_4.|title=Christian 4.|publisher=Store Norske Leksikon|accessdate=1 September 2024 |language=no}}</ref>

[[Holbæk]] in northwestern [[Zealand (Denmark)|Sealand]] began to develop towards the end of the Middle Ages. Prosperity peaked in the 17th century as corn grown locally was traded with Germany and the Netherlands. The half-timbered houses which now form the museum date back to that period, providing an insight into how the town functioned at the time.<ref>{{Citation|url=http://bibliotek.holbaek.dk/site.aspx?MenuID=19&Langref=1&Area=&topID=&ArticleID=17357&expandID=7526 |title=Holbæks historie |publisher=Bibliotek Holbæk |place=[[Denmark|DK]] |language=da |access-date=17 November 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719124449/http://bibliotek.holbaek.dk/site.aspx?MenuID=19&Langref=1&Area=&topID=&ArticleID=17357&expandID=7526 |archive-date=19 July 2011}}.</ref>

Danish country [[Rectory|vicarages]] from this period tended to be built in the same style as farmhouses, though usually rather larger. A fine example is Kølstrup Vicarage near [[Kerteminde]] in north-eastern Funen. The house itself is a thatched half-timbered building with a large rectangular courtyard flanked by outhouses.<ref>{{Citation | title = [[:da:Fil:Koelstrup Praestegaard.jpg|Kølstrup Vicarage]] | type = [[JPEG]] | publisher = Wikipædia | place = DK}}.</ref>

==Baroque==
[[File:Schloss Ledreborg 2.JPG|alt=An iron gate opens on to a two-story rectangle palace with large, attached wings. Rounded arch windows and a stone work over the entrance and on the second floor of the wings.|thumb|{{Citation | title = Ledreborg Palace | place = Roskilde | author-link = Lauritz de Thurah | first = Lauritz | last = de Thurah | year = 1745}}]]
As during the Renaissance period, it was again principally Dutch influence which predominated in Baroque architecture, although many of the features originated in Italy and France.  Symmetry and regularity were primary concerns, often enhanced by a projecting central section on the main façade.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.realdaniabyogbyg.org/baroque-and-rococo|title=Baroque and Rococo 1630-1770|publisher= |accessdate=1 September 2024 |language=}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://denstoredanske.lex.dk/barok|title=Barok|publisher=lexdk: Den Store Danske|author=Nykjær, Mogens|date=26 February 2024 |accessdate=1 September 2024 |language=da}}</ref>

Copenhagen's [[Rundetårn|Round Tower]] was also one of Christian IV's projects after he provided funding for an observatory as proposed by the astronomer [[Tycho Brahe]]. Under the initial leadership of [[Hans van Steenwinckel the Younger|Hans van Steenwinckel]] who surprisingly adapted the design to Dutch Baroque, the Tower was completed in 1642 with a height of almost 40 m. The bricks, specially ordered from the Netherlands, were of a hard-burned, slender type, known as ''muffer'' or ''mopper''.<ref>{{cite web| location= [[Denmark|DK]]| url= http://www.kloakviden.dk/peter_privat/Historie/trinitatis_kirke_og_rundetaarn.htm| title= Trinitatis Kirke og Rundetårn| publisher= Kloakviden| access-date= 2 December 2009| url-status= dead| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110109034646/http://www.kloakviden.dk/peter_privat/Historie/trinitatis_kirke_og_rundetaarn.htm| archive-date= 9 January 2011| df= dmy-all}}</ref> A 210-meter-long spiral ramp leads to the top, providing panoramic views over Copenhagen. The Round Tower is the oldest functioning observatory in Europe.  Until 1861 it was used by the University of Copenhagen, but today, anyone can observe the night sky through the tower's astronomical telescope during the winter.<ref>{{Citation | url = http://www.copenhagenet.dk/CPH-RoundTower.htm | title = Round Tower | publisher = Copenhagenet | place = Copenhagen, DK | access-date = 9 December 2009}}.</ref>

[[Nysø Manor]] (1673) near [[Præstø]], Sealand, was built for the local functionary Jens Lauridsen. It was the first Baroque country house in Denmark, replacing the earlier Renaissance style. The inspiration came from Holland and the architect was probably [[Ewert Janssen]].<ref>{{Citation|place=[[United Kingdom|UK]] |url=http://www.astoft2.co.uk/nysoeuk.htm |contribution=Nysø |title=The Astoft Collection of Buildings of Denmark |access-date=22 November 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100820045322/http://www.astoft2.co.uk/nysoeuk.htm |archive-date=20 August 2010 }}.</ref>

One of the foremost designers of the times was the Danish architect [[Lambert van Haven]] whose masterpiece was the [[Church of Our Saviour, Copenhagen]] (1682–96) which relies on the Greek cross for its basic layout. The façade is segmented by Tuscan pilasters extending up to the full height of the building. Other features such as the distinctive corkscrew spire were however not undertaken until the reign of [[Frederick V of Denmark|Frederick V]].  It was [[Lauritz de Thurah]] who finally completed the building in 1752.<ref>{{Citation | url = http://www.vorfrelserskirke.dk/historie | title = Vor Frelsers Kirke | contribution = Historie | place = DK | language = da | access-date = 12 November 2009 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20100826065202/http://www.vorfrelserskirke.dk/historie | archive-date = 26 August 2010 | url-status = dead }}.</ref>

[[File:Charlottenborg, Kopenhagen 2007.JPG|alt=Three story palace with two large wings.  Many decorative elements such as cornices, window pediments, and a stone balcony over the entrance.|thumb|{{Citation | title = [[Charlottenborg Palace]] | place = Copenhagen | author-link = Ewert Janssen | first = Ewert | last = Janssen | year = 1683}}]]
[[Charlottenborg Palace|Charlottenborg]] (1672–83), on [[Kongens Nytorv]] in the centre of Copenhagen, is said to be the most important pure Baroque building remaining in Denmark.  Van Haven may have been involved in its design although [[Ewert Janssen]] is usually credited with the work. Several other mansion houses in Denmark have been based on its design.<ref>{{Citation | last = Renouf | first = Norman | title = Copenhagen & the best of Denmark alive! | place = Edison, NJ | publisher = Hunter | year = 2003 | id = bA3Y5761}}, 257 pp.</ref>

It was [[Henrik Ruse]], a Dutch building engineer, who was charged by [[Frederik III of Denmark|Frederick III]] to develop the area around [[Kongens Nytorv]], especially in connection with the [[Nyhavn|Nyhavn Canal]] which was designed to become Copenhagen's new harbour. It was not, however, until [[Christian V of Denmark|Christian V]] became king in 1670 that Niels Rosenkrantz completed the work.  Over the next few years, numerous town houses were built along the northern or sunny side of the canal. The oldest, Number 9, was completed in 1681, probably by Christen Christensen, the harbour master.<ref>{{Citation | place = DK | url = http://www.rikkitikki.dk/index.php?id=256 | title = Rikkitikki | contribution = Historien om Nyhavn 9 | language = da | access-date = 16 November 2009}}.</ref>

[[Clausholm Castle]] (1693–94) near [[Randers]] was designed by the Danish architect Ernst Brandenburger with assistance of the Swede [[Nicodemus Tessin the Younger|Nicodemus Tessin]] who was invited to decorate the facade.<ref>{{Citation|publisher=Musik historisk museum |place=DK |url=http://www.musikhistoriskmuseum.dk/reg/clausholm_oid_ramme.htm |title=Clausholm Slotskapel |language=da |access-date=12 November 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928002039/http://www.musikhistoriskmuseum.dk/reg/clausholm_oid_ramme.htm |archive-date=28 September 2007 }}.</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://trap.lex.dk/Clausholm|title=Clausholm|publisher=lexdk: TrapDanmark|author=Lund Annemarie; Korsgaard, Peter; Smed, Mette|date=1 November 2019|accessdate=1 September 2024 |language=da}}</ref>
 
The [[Christiansborg Palace#First Christiansborg|first Christiansborg Palace]] in Copenhagen, designed by [[Elias David Häusser]] and completed in the 1740s, was certainly one of the most impressive Baroque buildings of its day. Although the palace itself was destroyed by fire in 1794, the extensive showgrounds and riding arena completed by Niels Eigtved have survived undamaged and can be visited today.<ref>{{Citation|place=DK |url=http://www.dac.dk/visKanonVaerk.asp?artikelID=2523 |title=Christiansborgs Ridebane |publisher=Dansk Arkitektur Center |language=da |access-date=7 January 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719123938/http://www.dac.dk/visKanonVaerk.asp?artikelID=2523 |archive-date=19 July 2011}}.</ref> [[Fredensborg Palace]] (1731), the royal residence on the shore of [[Zealand (Denmark)|Sealand]]'s Lake Esrum, with its exquisite Chancellery House, is the work of Johan Cornelius Krieger who was the court gardener at Rosenborg Castle.<ref>{{Citation|url=http://www.dac.dk/visKanonVaerk.asp?artikelID=2526 |title=Fredensborg Slot |place=DK |publisher=Dansk Arkitektur Center |language=da |access-date=7 January 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719124007/http://www.dac.dk/visKanonVaerk.asp?artikelID=2526 |archive-date=19 July 2011}}.</ref> The park at Fredensborg is one of Denmark's largest and best preserved Baroque gardens.<ref>{{cite web| location = DK | url= http://kpn.dk/article1706195.ece |title=Slotshave restaureres for 44 millioner|publisher=Jyllands Posten|access-date= 29 November 2009}}</ref>

After the turn of the 18th century, architecture developed into the late Baroque style. Among the major proponents were [[Johan Conrad Ernst]] who built the Chancery Building<ref>{{Citation | place = DK | publisher = Københavns historie | url = http://www.kobenhavnshistorie.dk/bog/kko/k/kko_k-3.html | contribution = Kancellibygningen (Den røde bygning), Slotsholmsgade 4 | title = København. Kulturhistorisk opslagsbog | language = da | access-date = 22 November 2009 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110719125616/http://www.kobenhavnshistorie.dk/bog/kko/k/kko_k-3.html | archive-date = 19 July 2011 | url-status = dead}}.</ref> or ''Kancellibygningen'' (1721) on [[Slotsholmen]] and [[Lauritz de Thurah]] who designed the [[Eremitage Palace]] (1734) in Dyrehaven, just north of Copenhagen. Even more ambitious was de Thurah's work at [[Ledreborg]] near [[Roskilde]], where he succeeded in working the components into a well-balanced and cohesive Baroque palace.<ref>{{Citation | place = DK | url = http://www.ledreborg-slot.dk/en/ | title = Ledreborg slot | trans-title = Ledreborg Palace | access-date = 7 December 2009 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110719125604/http://www.ledreborg-slot.dk/en/ | archive-date = 19 July 2011 | url-status = dead }}.</ref>

===Rococo===
[[File:Gammel Strand 48 København.jpg|alt=Five storied attached brick dwelling on the street. Elaborate ornamentation such as a large gable with curved roof, cornices and stone work around the rounded arch entrance.|thumb|{{Citation | title = Gammel Strand 48 | place = Copenhagen | author-link = Philip de Lange | first = Philip | last = de Lange | year = 1750}}]] 
Following on closely from the Baroque period, [[Rococo]] came into fashion in the 1740s under the leadership of [[Nicolai Eigtved]]. Originally a gardener, Eigtved spent many years abroad where he became increasingly interested in architecture, especially the French Rococo style.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://denstoredanske.lex.dk/rokoko|title=Rokoko|publisher=lexdk: Den Store Danske|author=Gelfer-Jørgensen, Miriam; Brix Søndergaard, Peter; Ryom, Peter; Kjær, Ulla|date=29 March 2024|accessdate=1 September 2024 |language=da}}</ref> On his return to Denmark, he built Prinsens Palæ (1743–44) in Copenhagen as a residence for Crown Prince Frederick (later [[Frederik V of Denmark|Frederick V]]). It is now the [[National Museum of Denmark|National Museum]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://denstoredanske.lex.dk/Prinsens_Pal%C3%A6|title=Prinsens, Palæ|publisher=lexdk: Den Store Danske|author=Smed, Mette|work=Den Store Danske |date=16 April 2024|accessdate=1 September 2024 |language=da}}</ref>

Soon afterwards, he was given prestige assignments including the overall architectural design for the [[Frederiksstaden]] district of Copenhagen 1749, planned around the strictly octagonal square containing the four Amalienborg Palaces and considered to be one of Europe's most important Rococo complexes. [[Adam Gottlob Moltke]] who, as Frederick V's ''overhofmarskal'' or lord chamberlain, was in charge of the project gave Eigtved a free hand, not only to design the principal buildings but also to provide the area with straight broad streets and the mansions which lined them.<ref>{{Citation|url=http://www.dac.dk/visKanonVaerk.asp?artikelID=2610 |title=Frederiksstaden |publisher=Dansk Architectur Center |language=da |access-date=13 November 2009 |place=[[Denmark|DK]] |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719121545/http://www.dac.dk/visKanonVaerk.asp?artikelID=2610 |archive-date=19 July 2011 }}.</ref> Frederick V had wanted to emulate the grand building achievements of the French monarchs. Not surprisingly, therefore, the palace square is inspired by the [[Place de la Concorde]] in Paris from the same period.<ref>{{Citation|url=http://www.crownprincecouple.dk/52000c |title=TRH The Crown Prince and Crown Princess |access-date=22 November 2009 |place=DK |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090220235807/http://www.crownprincecouple.dk/52000c |archive-date=20 February 2009 }}</ref> Although Eigtved died before the work was completed, other architects including Lauritz de Thurah faithfully continued to execute his plans. Perhaps the finest outcomes are the [[Amalienborg Palace| Amalienborg Palace complex]], [[Frederik's Church]] in its immediate vicinity and [[Frederiks Hospital]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://denstoredanske.lex.dk/Nicolai_Eigtved|title=Nicolai Eigtved|publisher=lexdk: Den Store Danske|author=Smed, Mette|date=16 April 2024|accessdate=1 September 2024 |language=da}}</ref>

[[Philip de Lange]], although influenced by Eigtved, developed his own rather strict style during this period. His ornamental facade can be seen on the [[Kunstforeningen]] building (1750) on Gammel Strand in Copenhagen. The top storey with a gable was added later.<ref>{{Citation | url = http://www.bymuseum.dk/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=139&Itemid=515 | title = Gammel Strand | place = København, DK | publisher = ByMuseet | language = da | access-date = 14 November 2009}}.</ref> De Lange also designed the small but well proportioned [[Damsholte Church]] on Møn, the only Rococo village church in Denmark.<ref>{{Citation | url = http://www.damsholtekirke.dk/ | title = Damsholte Kirke | language = da | date = 7 December 2009 | place = DK}}.</ref>

</gallery>

==Neoclassical==
[[File:Fredensborg Palace from the garden.jpg|thumb|Fredensborg Palace in Copenhagen (1753)]]
[[Neoclassical architecture|Neoclassicism]] which relied on inspiration from ancient Greece and Rome, was brought to Denmark by the French architect [[Nicolas-Henri Jardin]]. His countryman, the sculptor [[Jacques Saly]], who was already well established in Denmark, persuaded Frederick V that Jardin could complete Frederik's Church after Eigtved's death. Although Jardin did not succeed in this, he was successful in designing several prestige Neoclassical buildings such as [[Bernstorff Palace]] (1759–65) in [[Gentofte]] and [[Marienlyst Castle|Marienlyst Palace]] near Helsingør.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://denstoredanske.lex.dk/nyklassicisme|title=Nyklassicisme|publisher=lexdk: Ben Store Danske|author=Kjær, Ulla; Thygesen, Anne Lise; Gelfer-Jørgensen, Miriam; Munk, Jens Peter|date=21 August 2023|accessdate=2 September 2024|language=da}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://denstoredanske.lex.dk/Nicolas-Henri_Jardin|title=
Nicolas-Henri Jardin
|publisher=lexdk: Den Store Danske|author=Kjær, Ulla|date=24 April 2023|accessdate=2 September 2024 |language=da}}</ref>

One of Jardin's pupils, [[Caspar Frederik Harsdorff]], turned out to be Denmark's most prominent 18th-century architect and is known as the Father of Danish Classicism. He undertook a considerable amount of redesign work, both for interiors and exteriors, including work on the [[Royal Danish Theatre|Royal Theatre]] (1774) where he introduced a classical temple style with a wide entrance and large hall. He also carried out work on the [[Amalienborg Palace|Amalienborg]] complex including the colonnade, with its eight Ionic wooden columns, linking the crown prince's residence (''Schacks Palæ'') with the king's (''Moltkes Palæ'').<ref>{{Citation | url = http://www.dac.dk/visKanonSide.asp?artikelID=2752 | title = Klassicisme | publisher = Dansk Architectur Center | language = da | access-date = 13 November 2009 | place = [[Denmark|DK]] | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110719123718/http://www.dac.dk/visKanonSide.asp?artikelID=2752 | archive-date = 19 July 2011 | url-status = dead}}.</ref><ref>{{Citation|url=http://www.copenhagenet.dk/CPH-Amalienborg.htm |contribution=Amalienborg Palace |title=Copenhagenet |place=DK |access-date=7 December 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091214060135/http://www.copenhagenet.dk/CPH-Amalienborg.htm |archive-date=14 December 2009}}.</ref>

Another remarkable example of neoclassicism is [[Liselund]] on the island of [[Møn]] in south-eastern Denmark. This rather small country home built in the French [[neoclassicism|Neoclassical style]] in the 1790s is exceptional in that it has a thatched roof. Like the surrounding Romantic park, the house was the work of [[Andreas Kirkerup]], one of the foremost landscape architects of the times.  It was designed as a summer retreat for [[Antoine de la Calmette]], the island's governor, and his wife, Lise.<ref>{{Citation | first1 = Ole | last1 = Eskling | first2 = Erik | last2 = Büchert | title = Liselund park and manor house | place = Møns, DK | publisher = Turistbureau}}.</ref> The building is T-shaped with the main rooms on the ground floor, the first floor consisting of nine bedrooms. The interior was probably decorated by the leading decorator of the day, [[Joseph Christian Lillie]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://natmus.dk/museer-og-slotte/liselund/liselunds-historie/lystslottet/|title=Liselund|publisher=Nationalmuseet|accessdate=2 September 2024 |language=da}}</ref>

==19th century==

===Classicism===
[[File:Med lov skal man land bygge 2004 ubt.jpeg|thumb|[[Copenhagen Court House]] (1815), designed by [[Christian Frederik Hansen]]]]
After Hardorff's death, the main proponent of Classicism was [[Christian Frederik Hansen]] who developed a more severe style with clean, simple forms and large, unbroken surfaces. From 1800, he was in charge of all major building projects in Copenhagen where he designed the [[Copenhagen Court House|Copenhagen City Hall & Courthouse]] (1805–15) on [[Nytorv]]. He was also responsible for rebuilding [[Church of Our Lady (Copenhagen)|Church of Our Lady]] (''Vor Frue Kirke'') and designing the surrounding square (1811–29).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://dac.dk/viden/artikler/klassicismen/|title=Klassicismen|publisher=Dansk Arkitektur Center|accessdate=2 September 2024 |language=da}}</ref>

In 1800, Hansen was also charged with rebuilding Christiansborg Palace which had burnt down in 1794. Unfortunately, it burnt down once again in 1884. All that remains is the magnificent chapel which, with its Ionic columns, conveys a sense of antiquity.<ref>{{Citation|publisher=Guld alder |place=DK |url=http://www.guldalder.dk/show.asp?id=262 |contribution=Christiansborg Palace Chapel |title=Guide to the Danish Golden Age |access-date=7 December 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719124427/http://www.guldalder.dk/show.asp?id=262 |archive-date=19 July 2011 }}.</ref>

[[Michael Gottlieb Bindesbøll]] is remembered above all for designing [[Thorvaldsens Museum]]. In 1822, as a young man, he had experienced [[Karl Friedrich Schinkel]]'s classicism in Germany and France and had met the German-born architect and archaeologist Franz Gau who introduced him to the colourful architecture of antiquity. His uncle, Jonas Collin, who was an active art and culture official under [[Frederik VI of Denmark|Frederick VI]], awakened the King's interest in a museum for [[Bertel Thorvaldsen]], the Danish-Icelandic sculptor, and asked Bindesbøll to make some sketches for the building. As Bindensbøll's designs stood out from those of other architects, he was given a commission to transform the Royal Carriage Depot and Theatre Scenery Painting Building into a museum. Emulating the construction of the [[Erechtheion]] and the [[Parthenon]] as freestanding buildings released from the traditional urban plan of closed streets, he completed the work in 1848.<ref>{{Citation | last1 = Lange | first1 = Bente | first2 = Jens | last2 = Lindhe | title = Thorvaldsen's Museum: Architecture, Colours, Light | place = Copenhagen | publisher = Danish Architectural Press | year = 2002}}.</ref> He also incorporated aspects of ancient [[Egyptian Revival|Egyptian]] architecture into his design, though "the plan as a whole... is neither Egyptian nor Greek, but Bindesbøll's own".<ref>{{Citation | last1 = Laurin | first1 = Carl | last2 = Hannover | first2 = Emil | last3 = Thiis | first3 = Jens | title = Scandinavian Art | publisher = Benjamin Blom | place = New York | year = 1968 | page = 425 | type =  hardback}}.</ref>

===Historicism===
[[File:Hotel-d-angleterre-2004.jpg|thumb|{{Citation | title = [[Hotel D'Angleterre]] | place = Copenhagen | author-link = Vilhelm Dahlerup | first = Vilhelm | last = Dahlerup | year = 1875}}]]
With the arrival of [[Historicism (art)|Historicism]] in the second half of the century, special importance was attached to high standards of craftsmanship and proper use of materials.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://dac.dk/viden/artikler/historicismen/|title=Historicisme|publisher=Dansk Arkitektur Center|accessdate=2 September 2024 |language=da}}</ref> This can be seen in Copenhagen's [[Copenhagen University Library|University Library]] (1861) designed by [[Johan Daniel Herholdt]] and inspired by St Fermo's Church in [[Verona]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://denstoredanske.lex.dk/J.D._Herholdt_-_arkitekt|title=
J.D. Herholdt (arkitekt)
|publisher=lexdk: Den Store Danske|author=Thygesen, Anne Lise|date=2 September 2021|accessdate=2 September 2024 |language=da}}</ref>

[[Vilhelm Dahlerup]] was one of the most productive 19th-century architects. Perhaps more than anyone else, he contributed to the way Copenhagen appears today.<ref>{{cite web|work=Det moderne gennembrud |location=[[Denmark|DK]] |url=http://www.detmodernegennembrud.dk/composite-727.htm |title=Vilhelm Dahlerup |publisher=Golden Days in Copenhagen |access-date=26 April 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081206100017/http://www.detmodernegennembrud.dk/composite-727.htm |archive-date=6 December 2008 }}</ref> His most important buildings include Copenhagen's [[Hotel D’Angleterre]] (1875) and the [[Statens Museum for Kunst|Danish National Gallery]] (1891). With the support of the Carlsberg company, he designed the [[Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek|Ny Carlsberg Glyptoteque]] (1897) and a number of lavishly decorated buildings at the [[Carlsberg (district)|Carlsberg Brewery site]], now under redevelopment as a new district in Copenhagen.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.worldarchitecturenews.com/index.php?fuseaction=wanappln.projectview&upload_id=12836 | title= Carlsberg design develops in Copenhagen| publisher= World Architecture News | access-date = 29 November 2009| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20091127045106/http://www.worldarchitecturenews.com/index.php?fuseaction=wanappln.projectview&upload_id=12836 | archive-date= 27 November 2009 | url-status= live}}</ref>

[[File:Marmorkirken Copenhagen front.jpg|thumb|[[Frederik's Church]] in Copenhagen (completed in 1894).]]
[[Ferdinand Meldahl]], also a proponent of Historicism, completed the reconstruction of [[Frederiksborg Palace]] after the fire in 1859 and designed the [[Alþingishúsið|Parliament Building]] in [[Reykjavík]], Iceland, at that time a Danish colony. His greatest achievement was, however, the completion of [[Frederik's Church]] in Copenhagen. The site had become a ruin after work was stopped on Jardin's original design in 1770. Meldahl's plans differed significantly from Jardin's in that the lateral towers were eliminated, the dome was lower and the columns were reduced from six to four before the main entrance. Nevertheless, the overall height almost matched Jardin's, thanks to the lantern and the taller spire.  The building, commonly known as the Marble Church, was completed in 1894, more than 150 years after Eigtved had drawn up his original plans.<ref>{{Citation|url=http://www.copenhagenet.dk/CPH-Map/CPH-Marble.asp |title=Marble Church |publisher=Copenhagenet |place=Copenhagen, DK |access-date=7 December 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090820064612/http://www.copenhagenet.dk/CPH-Map/CPH-Marble.asp |archive-date=20 August 2009}}.</ref>

===National Romanticism===
[[Martin Nyrop]] was one of the main proponents of the [[National Romantic style]]. The main aim was to use distinctive [[Nordic countries|Nordic]] motifs from the distant past, as is clearly demonstrated in [[Copenhagen City Hall]] which was completed in 1905. The City Hall is certainly Copenhagen's most monumental and most original building from the last quarter of the 19th century with its impressive facade, the golden statue of [[Absalon]] just above the balcony and its tall, slim clock tower. It was inspired by the [[Palazzo Pubblico|Siena City Hall]].<ref>{{Citation | publisher = Waymarking | title = Waymarks | url = http://www.waymarking.com/waymarks/WM3N6P_Rdhustrnets_ur_City_Hall_Tower_Clock_Copenhagen_Denmark | contribution = City Hall Tower Clock | access-date = 13 November 2009}}.</ref>

Another participant in the National Romanticism movement was [[Hack Kampmann]] who designed the [[Aarhus Theatre]] in the [[Art Nouveau]] style at the very end of the century.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://denstoredanske.lex.dk/Hack_Kampmann|title=Hack Kampmann|publisher=lexdk: Den Store Danske|author=Zahle, Karen|date=23 April 2023|accessdate=2 September 2024 |language=da}}</ref>

===Urban development===
The harbour town of [[Svendborg]] in the south east of Funen dates back to the 13th century. Real prosperity emerged in the 19th century when shipbuilding and trade became important drivers. The town subsequently underwent a period of renovation with new brick and stone buildings lining its narrow streets. The old town has now become an important tourist attraction.<ref>{{Citation | url = http://fynhistorie.dk/node/390 | contribution = Svendborgs historie | title = Fyn historie | language = da | access-date = 17 November 2009 | place = DK}}.</ref>

The fine architectural style of [[Skagen]] on the northern tip of Jutland is quite distinctive. From the 19th century on, the houses were whitewashed and had red-tiled roofs.  Yellow and red tones dominated, backed by white chimneys and roof decorations. These traditions are not only to be found in the town's old districts but are maintained in the newer residential areas.  Several of the town's more imposing buildings from the beginning of the 20th century were designed by the [[Ulrik Adolph Plesner|Ulrik Plesner]], others were designed by well-known architects such as [[Thorvald Bindesbøll]].<ref>{{Citation | url = http://www.skagen-tourist.dk/international/en-gb/menu/turist/omraade/skagen-aalbaek/skagens-historie.htm | contribution = Skagen's history | publisher = Visit Denmark | access-date = 17 November 2009 | title = Skagen tourist | place = DK | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110719131218/http://www.skagen-tourist.dk/international/en-gb/menu/turist/omraade/skagen-aalbaek/skagens-historie.htm | archive-date = 19 July 2011}}.</ref>
<gallery class="center"  widths=160px heights=130px>
File:Thoraldsens Museum.jpg|{{Citation | title = [[Thorvaldsens Museum]] | author-link = Michael Gottlieb Bindesbøll | first = Michael | last = Gottlieb Bindesbøll | year = 1838–48}}
File:Herholdt lores.jpg|{{Citation | title = [[Copenhagen University Library]] | author-link = Johan Daniel Herholdt | first = Johan Daniel | last = Herholdt | year = 1857–61}}
File:Aarhus Teater (front).jpg|{{Citation | title = [[Aarhus Theatre]] | author-link = Hack Kampmann | first = Hack | last = Kampmann | year = 1898–1900}}

</gallery>

==20th century==

===Nordic Classicism===
[[File:Pv jensen-klint 05 grundtvig memorial church 1913-1940.jpg|thumb|{{Citation | title = [[Grundtvig's Church]] | place = Copenhagen | author1-link = Peder Vilhelm Jensen-Klint | first1 = Peder Vilhelm | last1 = Jensen-Klint | author2-link = Kaare Klint | first2 = Kaare | last2 = Klint | year = 1921–40}}]]
Neoclassicism or increasingly [[Nordic Classicism]] continued to thrive at the beginning of the century until about 1930 as can be seen in [[Kay Fisker]]'s Hornbækhus apartment buildings (1923) and [[Hack Kampmann]]'s police headquarters (1924). Its development was no isolated phenomenon, drawing on existing [[Classical architecture|classical]] traditions in the Nordic countries, and from new ideas being pursued in German-speaking cultures. It can thus be characterised as a combination of direct and indirect influences from [[vernacular]] architecture (Nordic, Italian and German) and [[Neoclassical architecture|Neoclassicism]].<ref>{{Citation | place = [[Denmark|DK]] | url = http://www.denmark.dk/en/menu/About-Denmark/Danish-Design-Architecture/Architecture/FirstHalfOfThe20thCentury/ | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160303232613/http://denmark.dk/en/menu/About-Denmark/Danish-Design-Architecture/Architecture/FirstHalfOfThe20thCentury/ | url-status = dead | archive-date = 3 March 2016 | contribution = First half of 20th century | title = Danish Architecture | publisher = About Denmark | access-date = 28 December 2009}}.</ref>

While the movement had its greatest level of success in Sweden, there were a number of other important Danish proponents including [[Ivar Bentsen]], [[Kaare Klint]], [[Arne Jacobsen]], Carl Petersen and [[Steen Eiler Rasmussen]]. Bentsen, with the assistance of Thorkild Henningsen, designed Denmark's first [[terraced house]]s in the Bellahøj district of Copenhagen. Very appropriately Klint, working with Bentsen, adapted the design of [[Frederiks Hospital]] to serve as the [[Danish Museum of Art & Design]]. Carl Petersen's main achievement was the [[Faaborg]] Museum built for collections of art from Funen. Steen Rasmussen is remembered above all for his town planning activities and for his contributions to the Dansk Byplanlaboratorium (Danish town planning laboratory).<ref>{{cite book| last1 =Angeletti| first1 =Angelo| first2 =Gaia | last2 = Remiddi |title= Alvar Aalto e il Classicismo Nordico|year=1998|location= Rome|publisher= F.lli Palombi| isbn = 88-7621-666-9 | language = it, en}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|publisher=LANL |url=http://www.ees.lanl.gov/staff/steen/0607short-2.pdf |contribution=Steen Rasmussen |type=CV |title=EES |access-date=28 December 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100527141146/http://ees.lanl.gov/staff/steen/0607short-2.pdf |archive-date=27 May 2010}}.</ref>

===Expressionism===
[[Grundtvig's Church]] in [[Bispebjerg]], Copenhagen, is named after the Danish philosopher and pastor [[N. F. S. Grundtvig|Nikolai Grundtvig]], remembered by most Danes for his resounding hymns, now an integral part of the national culture. As a result of its unusual appearance, it is Denmark's most famous [[Expressionist architecture|expressionist]] church. Designed by [[Peder Vilhelm Jensen-Klint]], it relied heavily on Scandinavian brick [[gothic architecture|gothic]] traditions, especially Danish village churches with [[Crow-stepped gable|stepped gable]]s. Jensen-Klint combined the modern geometric forms of [[Brick Expressionism]] with the classical vertical of Gothic architecture.  Construction began in 1921 but was only completed by his son [[Kaare Klint]] in 1940 after Jensen-Klint's death. The most striking feature of the building is its west facade, reminiscent of a [[westwork]] or of the exterior of a church organ.<ref>{{Citation|place=[[Denmark|DK]] |url=http://www.grundtvigskirke.dk/indhold/om-kirken |title=Grundtvigs Kirke |access-date=1 December 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100201210715/http://www.grundtvigskirke.dk/indhold/om-kirken |archive-date=1 February 2010 }}.</ref>

===Functionalism===
[[File:Århus Kommunehospital (bygning 22) 01.jpg|thumb|Danish functionalism. Detail from [[Århus Kommunehospital]] (1935) by [[C.F. Møller]]. Affordable materials, full focus on functionality and a harmonious and simplistic appearance with no decorative structures whatsoever.]]
[[Functionalism (architecture)|Functionalism]], which began in the 1930s, relied on rational architecture making use of bricks, concrete, iron and glass, preferably to meet social needs. Its main proponents in Denmark were [[Frits Schlegel]], [[Mogens Lassen]], [[Vilhelm Lauritzen]] and, especially [[Arne Jacobsen]] with his [[Bellavista housing estate|Bellavista developments]] north of Copenhagen. Another of Jacobsen's masterpieces was the [[Aarhus City Hall]] which he designed together with [[Erik Møller]] in 1937 and completed in 1948. The tower is 60 meters tall and the tower clock face has a diameter of seven meters. The building is made of concrete plated with marble from [[Porsgrunn]] in Norway.<ref>{{Citation | url = http://www.visitdenmark.com/irland/en-ie/menu/turist/inspiration/detkulturelledanmark/arkitektur/danish-architecture-an-overview.htm#SubHeader8 | title = Danish architecture: an overview | contribution = Functionalism and Tradition | publisher = Visit Denmark | access-date = 28 December 2009 | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110719130528/http://www.visitdenmark.com/irland/en-ie/menu/turist/inspiration/detkulturelledanmark/arkitektur/danish-architecture-an-overview.htm#SubHeader8 | archive-date = 19 July 2011}}.</ref><ref>{{Citation |title= The City Council Hall |publisher= Århus Kommune |id=28 December 2009}}.</ref>

A more traditional approach was taken by [[Kay Fisker]] who, together with [[C. F. Møller]], designed buildings for [[Aarhus University]] from 1931 onwards.<ref>{{Citation | publisher = Essential architecture | url = http://www.essential-architecture.com/STYLE/STY-062.htm | title = World Architecture Images | contribution = Danish Functionalism | access-date = 28 December 2009 | archive-date = 4 January 2010 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20100104045632/http://essential-architecture.com/STYLE/STY-062.htm | url-status = usurped }}.</ref>

===Modernism===
[[File:Rødovre town hall, 1952-1956.jpg|thumb|left|{{Citation | author-link = Arne Jacobsen | first = Arne | last = Jacobsen | title = Rødovre Town Hall | year = 1956}}]] 
After [[World War II]], Functionalism drew on trends in [[American modernism|American Modernism]] with its irregular ground plans, flat roofs, [[open plan]] interiors and glass facades.  Good examples are [[Utzon's House in Hellebæk|Jørn Utzon's own family house]] (1952) on the outskirts of Hellebæk near [[Helsingør]] where good use is made of reasonably cheap materials for post-war housing;<ref>{{Citation | url = http://www.visitdenmark.dk/uk/en-gb/menu/turist/inspiration/detkulturelledanmark/arkitektur/danish-architecture-an-overview.htm#SubHeader9/ | contribution = Second half of the 20th Century | title = Danish architecture: an overview | publisher = Visit Denmark | place = DK | access-date = 15 January 2010 | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110719133206/http://www.visitdenmark.dk/uk/en-gb/menu/turist/inspiration/detkulturelledanmark/arkitektur/danish-architecture-an-overview.htm#SubHeader9/ | archive-date = 19 July 2011}}.</ref> and the [[Kingo Houses]] (1956–58) in Helsingør which consist of 63 L-shaped houses based on the design of traditional Danish farmhouses.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://dac.dk/viden/arkitektur/kingohusene/|title=Kingohusene / Romerhusene Bolig|work=Dansk Arkitektur Center - DAC |publisher=Dansk Arkitektur Center|accessdate=2 September 2024 |language=da}}</ref> Another project, noted for the synthesis it creates between architecture and landscape, was the [[Louisiana Museum of Modern Art]] (1958) in [[Humlebæk]], designed by [[Jørgen Bo]] and [[Vilhelm Wohlert]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://louisiana.dk/en/museum/architecture-and-history/|title=Architecture & Histor|publisher=Louisiana|accessdate=2 September 2024 |language=}}</ref>

During this period, Arne Jacobsen became the country's leading [[Modern architecture|Modernist]] with the design of the [[Radisson SAS Royal Hotel, Copenhagen|SAS Hotel]] in Copenhagen (1960). Rødovre Town Hall, completed in 1956, shows how well Jacobsen combined the use of different materials: sandstone, two types of glass, painted metalwork and stainless steel.<ref>{{Citation|place=DK |url=http://www.rk.dk/kultur-fritid-idraet/kulturarv-og-kulturfremme/kulturarv-og-kulturfremme/arne-jacobsen-om-roedovre-raadhus/ |publisher=RK |title=Kulturarv og kulturfremme |contribution=Rødovre Kommune – Arne Jacobsen |access-date=15 December 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091130142813/http://www.rk.dk/kultur-fritid-idraet/kulturarv-og-kulturfremme/kulturarv-og-kulturfremme/arne-jacobsen-om-roedovre-raadhus/ |archive-date=30 November 2009}}.</ref>

Following in Jacobsen's footsteps, Danish artictects had some outstanding successes in 20th-century architecture. Most notably, [[Jørn Utzon]]'s iconic [[Sydney Opera House]] earned him the distinction of becoming only the second person to have his work recognized as a [[World Heritage Site]] while still alive.<ref>{{cite news | author = Kathy Marks | title = World Heritage honour for 'daring' Sydney Opera House | url = https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/australasia/world-heritage-honour-for-daring-sydney-opera-house-455193.html | work = [[The Independent]] | publisher = [[Independent News & Media]] | date = 27 June 2007 | access-date = 14 September 2009 | location = London | archive-date = 8 January 2010 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20100108032541/http://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/australasia/world-heritage-honour-for-daring-sydney-opera-house-455193.html | url-status = dead }}</ref> His [[Bagsværd Church]] (1968–76) in Copenhagen has been considered an outstanding example of [[critical regionalism]], for the synthesis created between universal civilisation and regional culture.<ref>{{Citation | url = http://home.earthlink.net/~aisgp/texts/regionalism/regionalism.html | title = Scott Paterson: Critical Analysis of "Towards a Critical Regionalism" | publisher = Earthlink | first = Kenneth | last = Frampton | access-date = 13 December 2009}}.</ref>

[[File:Sydneyoperahouse.JPG|thumb|[[Jørn Utzon]]: [[Sydney Opera House]] (1973)]]
Winning the [[Architectural design competition|international competition]] for the [[Grande Arche]] at [[La Défense]] in [[Puteaux]], near [[Paris]], with a design based on simple geometrical forms brought [[Johann Otto von Spreckelsen]] international fame.  Prolific [[Henning Larsen]] designed the Foreign Ministry building in [[Riyadh]], as well as a variety of prestige buildings throughout [[Scandinavia]], including the [[Copenhagen Opera House]].<ref>{{Citation | url = http://www.denstoredanske.dk/Kunst_og_kultur/Arkitektur/Danmark/Henning_Larsen | place = DK | contribution = Henning Larsen | title = Kunst og kultur: Arkitektur Danmark | publisher = Den Store Danske | language = da | access-date = 5 November 2009}}.</ref>

From the success of the [[Strøget]]'s transformation into a [[pedestrian zone]] in Copenhagen in the 1960s and his influential book ''Life Between Buildings'', [[Jan Gehl]] earned an international reputation in [[urban design]]. He has advised on numerous city planning developments including those for [[Melbourne]], [[London]] and [[New York City|New York]].<ref>{{cite web| type = biography | url= http://www.arc.govt.nz/albany/fms/main/Documents/Auckland/Aucklands%20growth/Jan%20Gehl%20Biography.pdf |title=Jan Gehl|publisher = JGA | access-date= 29 November 2009}}</ref> His work has often drawn on Copenhagen and its [[Cycling in Copenhagen|bicycle culture]], to improve the quality of [[public space]] in city centres.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://nymag.com/news/intelligencer/40345/ |title=Gehl on Wheels|date=21 September 2007 |publisher= New York News & Features | access-date = 23 June 2009}}</ref>
<gallery class="center"  widths=160px heights=130px>
File:Arne Jacobsen Bellavista 2005-02.jpg|{{Citation | title = Bellavista | type = apartments | author-link = Arne Jacobsen | first = Arne | last = Jacobsen | year = 1933–34}}
File:Aarhus university - fisker, møller, stegmann, sørensen 1931.jpg|{{Citation | title = Århus University | author-link = Kay Fisker | first = Kay | last = Fisker | year = 1931}}
File:Århus Rådhus 01.jpg|{{Citation | title = Århus Rådhus ([[Aarhus City Hall]]) | author1-link = Arne Jacobsen | first1 = Arne | last1 = Jacobsen | author2-link = Erik Møller | first2 = Erik | last2 = Møller | year = 1939–42}}
</gallery>

=== Postmodernism ===
[[Postmodernism]] and [[postmodern architecture]] have also had its imprint on Danish architecture, with large and notable projects such as [[Høje-Taastrup]] train station from 1986 by [[Jacob Blegvad]], the multi-purpose venue of Scala in central Copenhagen, just across from [[Tivoli Gardens]], redeveloped in 1989 from a design by architect and professor [[Mogens Breyen]], but torn down in 2012, or [[Scandinavian Center]] in Aarhus by [[Friis & Moltke]] from 1995.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.arkitekturbilleder.dk/bygning/hoeje-taastrup-station/ |title=Høje taastrup Station |access-date=9 November 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171110114628/http://www.arkitekturbilleder.dk/bygning/hoeje-taastrup-station/ |archive-date=10 November 2017 |url-status=dead  }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.information.dk/moti/2012/02/farvel-festhus|title=Farvel til et festhus|publisher=Information|author=Haahr Rasmussen, Anders|date=18 February 2022|accessdate=2 September 2024 |language=da}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.arkitekturbilleder.dk/bygning/scandinavian-center/ |title=Scandinavian Center |access-date=9 November 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171110114712/http://www.arkitekturbilleder.dk/bygning/scandinavian-center/ |archive-date=10 November 2017 |url-status=dead  }}</ref> Several housing projects in Denmark, especially larger social housing projects, from the 80s and early 90s were also inspired by the postmodern movement of the time. Notable examples include the relatively small apartment complex ''Det Blå Hjørne'' (The Blue Corner) in [[Christianshavn]], by [[Tegnestuen Vandkunsten]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://dac.dk/viden/arkitektur/broestes-grund-en-lille-boligrevolution-paa-christianshavn/|title=Brøstes Grund: En lille boligrevolution på Christianshavn|work=Dansk Arkitektur Center - DAC |publisher=Dansk Arkitektur Center|accessdate=2 September 2024 |language=da}}</ref> or the larger and much more recent [[Bispebjerg Bakke (building)|Bispebjerg Bakke]], in [[Bispebjerg]] from 2006, designed in collaboration with artist [[Bjørn Nørgaard]].<ref>[https://realdania.dk/projekter/bispebjerg-bakke Bispebjerg Bakke]</ref>
