There are also larger detached Georgian mansions and villas, such as [[Allerton Hall]] built c.1736 for slave traders John Hardman and his brother James, is a rare example in Liverpool of [[Palladian architecture]]. A rare example of an 18th-century merchant's villa is May Place, Broad Green Road, Old Swan, know to be in existence by 1768.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p483">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p483</ref> The former Rectory of St Mary's Walton (c.1800), built in a Gothic style, the [[porte-cochère]] was added in 1830.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p491">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p491</ref> A fine detached late eighteenth-century house is Olive Mount, Wavertree, built for James Swan grocer and tea dealer.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p498">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p498</ref> [[Sudley House]] built 1824 for corn merchant [[Nicholas Robinson (mayor)|Nicholas Robinson]] and extended in the 1880s that is run as an [[Historic house museum]], although the architect is not known for certain John Whiteside has been suggested as the designer.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p444">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p444</ref> The burnt out ground floor of Allerton House (1815) by [[Thomas Harrison (architect)|Thomas Harrison]], for Jacob Fletcher whose father made a fortune [[privateer]]ing, survives on Allerton Golf Course, the Lodge also survives and is probably Harrison's work.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p390">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p390</ref> A large mansion of 1828 is [[Calderstones House]], built for Joseph Need Walker, a [[Shot (pellet)|lead shot]] manufacturer.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p389">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p389</ref> Bark Hill, Mossley Hill, is an 1830s villa with a Doric porch, close by is Holmefield, also 1830s with an Ionic Porch.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p442">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p442</ref> Beaconsfield House, Beaconsfield (1830s) was built for solicitor Ambrose Lace, but only the Coachman's House and Stables survive as 84 Beaconsfield Road in a Jacobethan style.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p514">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p514</ref> Childwall hall (1806) a castellated Gothic mansion by [[John Nash (architect)|John Nash]], built for [[Bamber Gascoyne (the younger)|Bamber Gascoyne]] and was demolished in 1949, but the gate lodge survives and maybe the work of Nash.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p399">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p399</ref> Leyfield House, Honeys Green Lane, West Derby is a fine stuccoed villa with a Doric porch.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p507">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p507</ref> Another fine stuccoed villa is Beechley, Harthill Road Allerton.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p388">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p388</ref>

===Georgian public buildings and memorials===
[[Liverpool Town Hall]] was built in the [[Palladian architecture|Palladian style]] between 1749 and 1754 to a design by [[John Wood, the Elder|John Wood the Elder]] replacing an earlier town hall nearby. It was significantly extended and altered by [[James Wyatt]] from 1785. Its sumptuous interiors also by Wyatt, are highly regarded examples of late [[Georgian architecture]], in refined [[Neoclassical architecture|neoclassical style]], the actual building work was overseen by [[John Foster Sr. (engineer)|John Foster Sr.]] who was the Surveyor to the Corporation of Liverpool from 1790 to 1824. The city's stock exchange and financial district are set immediately behind this building, showing the close ties between local government and commerce. Other public buildings in the city of this era are the [[Liverpool Royal Institution]] that was constructed in c.1799 as a house and business premises for a merchant called Thomas Parr and was adapted by [[Edmund Aikin]] in 1815, who added the [[Doric order]] porch<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p316">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p316</ref> and [[Edge Hill railway station]] is a rare pre-Victorian (1836) railway station, it was between 1830–1836 the original terminus of the [[Liverpool and Manchester Railway]].<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), pp413-414">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), pp413-414</ref> 

The [[Wapping Tunnel]] by [[George Stephenson]] was created (1826–29) to link Edge Hill and the new railway to the southern docks, it initially operated with a static steam engine hauling wagons through it. [[John Foster (architect, born 1786)|John Foster Jr]], succeeded his father as Surveyor to the Corporation of Liverpool 1824–35 and was responsible for the design of [[St James Cemetery]] laid out (1827–29), he designed several buildings for the cemetery including the Lodge, entrance arch, the Oratory and Huskisson Monument (see the neo-classical section below for these last two) and is a Grade I Historic Park. [[Wavertree Botanic Gardens]], originally started in the 1830s and a Grade II*, the park has a late Georgian entrance lodge. The facade of the former Grecian (1829) survives in Dale street.<ref name="Sharples & Stonard 2008), p71">Sharples & Stonard (2008), p71</ref> An unusual relic is the Hearse House (1811) in the churchyard of All Saints' Childwall.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p399"/> Another unusual building is the [[Village lock-up|lockup]] (1787), Shaw Street, Everton,<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p424">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p424</ref> used to imprison drunks overnight to sober up or someone awaiting magistrates, there is a second such building in the city [[Wavertree Lock-up]] (1796).

Behind the Town Hall is the [[Nelson Monument, Liverpool|Nelson Monument]], it was designed by [[Matthew Cotes Wyatt]] and sculpted by [[Richard Westmacott]] as a memorial to [[Horatio Nelson, 1st Viscount Nelson|Horation Nelson]] and unveiled in 1813.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p4323">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p323</ref> Westmacott also sculpted the bronze equestrian statue of [[George III of the United Kingdom|George III]] on London Road.<ref name="Sharples & Stonard 2008), p259">Sharples & Stonard (2008), p259</ref> In the grounds of Allerton Manor, a now ruinous house in Allerton Road, lies an 18th-century [[obelisk]].<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p390"/>

===Georgian commercial buildings===

In 1786 the Liverpool Improvement Act was passed stipulating that £175,000 would be available over three years. One of the consequences was the widening of Castle Street overseen by John Foster Sr., which meant the west side of the street had to be completely rebuilt. only Nos 46, 52 & 54 survive from this period.<ref name="Hollinghurst 2009), p11">Hollinghurst (2009), p11</ref> The Thomas Parr House in Colquitt Street with warehouse behind, is a rare surviving 18th-century warehouse.<ref name="Giles & Hawkins 2006), p24">Giles & Hawkins (2006), p24</ref> In Brunswick Street is the former Bank of Arthur Heywood and Sons (1798–1800), possibly the design of John Foster Sr.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p309">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p309</ref> There is an interesting example of a late Georgian Gothic inn building in the Childwall Abbey Hotel.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p399"/> The Union News Room (1800) in Duke Street was designed by John Foster Sr.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p206">Sharples (2004) p206</ref> The facade of the former Grecian Hotel, 51–55 Dale Street survives as part of a modern office block. Harrington Chambers (c.1830) is a rare survival of Georgian shops with office floors above.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p328">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p328</ref> No 75-79 Bold Street (c.1833), by Joseph Franklin, is an example of [[Greek Revival architecture]].<ref name="Sharples 2004), p196">Sharples (2004) p196</ref>

Some of Liverpool's landmarks are mainly known for their oddness, such as the [[Williamson Tunnels]] which are architecturally unique as the largest underground folly in the world.

===Georgian churches===
Liverpool has several churches built in the Georgian era, these are: The Church of England [[Church of St James, Liverpool|Church of St James]], built-in 1774–75 by Cuthbert Bisbrown, it has a later chancel and other alterations have been made. The oldest surviving Roman Catholic church in the city (now a restaurant) is [[St. Peter's Roman Catholic Church, Liverpool]] (1788) built three years before the [[Roman Catholic Relief Act 1791]].<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p284">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p284</ref> [[Holy Trinity Church, Wavertree]] (1794) was designed by John Hope, as an Anglican chapel and a new chancel was added (1911) by [[Charles Herbert Reilly|Charles Reilly]]. The Anglican [[Church of Our Lady and Saint Nicholas, Liverpool|Church of Our Lady and St Nicholas]] is Liverpool's parish church. Colloquially known as "the sailors' church", it has existed near the waterfront since 1257. The current building, designed by [[Thomas Harrison (architect)|Thomas Harrison]], was begun in 1811 following the catastrophic collapse of the old tower. While Harrison's tower is still original, the main body of the church has been rebuilt following [[Second World War]] damage. Another example of Georgian Gothic architecture is the [[Church of St Luke, Liverpool]] designed in 1802 by [[John Foster Sr. (engineer)|John Foster Sr.]] & [[John Foster (architect, born 1786)|John Foster Jr.]] (both men were born in Liverpool), it was built in 1811–32. St Mary's [[Edge Hill, Liverpool|Edge Hill]] was built (1812–13) and extended (1825–25) architect unknown.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p411">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p411</ref> [[Thomas Rickman]] who began his career as an architect in Liverpool designed two churches in the city, both for the Church of England [[St George's Church, Everton]] in 1813–1815 with its unusual [[cast iron]] interior and [[St Michael's Church, Aigburth]] in 1814–1815 altered in 1900 by [[W. & G. Audsley]], both are examples of late Georgian [[Gothic Revival architecture]]. John Slater designed the Roman Catholic [[St Patrick's Church, Liverpool]] in 1821–27 in a simple classical style, also for the same denomination is the gothic [[St Anthony's Church, Scotland Road]] 1832–33 by John Broadbent a pupil of Rickman's. Built for the [[Presbyterianism|Presbyterian's]], [[St Andrew's Church, Liverpool]] by Daniel Stewart with the facade by John Foster Jr. was long derelict,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.liverpoolviews.co.uk/danger/andrews.html |title=St. Andrew's Church |publisher=Liverpoolviews.co.uk |access-date=12 January 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ancient-egypt.co.uk/liverpool/pyramid/pages/2005-mar-11%20629.htm |title=Report on the Pyramid in St Andrew's Scotch Church Liverpool |publisher=Ancient-egypt.co.uk |date=31 August 2008 |access-date=13 December 2011}}</ref> but was restored in 2015 as student accommodation. The tower of [[St Mary's Church, Walton-on-the-Hill]] dates from 1828 to 1832 and was designed by John Broadbent. [[St John the Evangelist, Knotty Ash]] (1834–36) is an example of Georgian Gothic. Several Georgian parish churches and chapels have been demolished in the centre of Liverpool, see the demolished Georgian buildings section below for details.

==19th century neo-classical buildings==
{{Main|St. George’s Hall, Liverpool}}
Liverpool has a rich tradition of [[neo-classical architecture]] running through the late Georgian right to the end of the Victorian period. Some prime early examples are [[The Lyceum, Liverpool|the Lyceum]] by [[Thomas Harrison (architect)|Thomas Harrison]] (1802), the [[Wellington Rooms, Liverpool|Wellington Rooms]] by [[Edmund Aikin]] (1815–16; a grade II* listed building, now at risk in a "very bad" condition<ref>[http://www.english-heritage.org.uk/content/publications/publicationsNew/heritage-at-risk/har-2011-registers/acc-nw-HAR-register-2011.pdf Heritage at Risk register 2011 North West, pp. 66].</ref>). [[The Oratory]] using a [[Doric order|Greek Doric style]], by [[John Foster (architect, born 1786)|John Foster Jr.]] (1829) who based the building on the [[Temple of Hephaestus]] in [[Athens]], also by Foster is the Huskisson Monument (1834) in St. James Cemetery based on the [[Choragic Monument of Lysicrates]], these are pure examples of [[Greek Revival architecture]].<ref name="Hollinghurst 2004), p92">Hollinghurst (2004), p92</ref> Also impressive is the grade I listed [[Bank of England Building, Liverpool|Bank of England Building]] built by [[Charles Robert Cockerell]] between 1845 and 1848<ref>{{cite book |last=Hughes |first=Quentin |title=Liverpool: City of Architecture |publisher=[[Bluecoat Press]] |year=1999 }}</ref>(Cockerell spent the years 1810–1815 studying [[Ancient Greek architecture|ancient buildings]] in Greece with John Foster Jr.<ref>page 8, The Life and Work of C.R. Cockerell, David Watkin, 1974, Zwemmer Ltd, {{ISBN|0-302-02571-5}}</ref>) and the North and South Wales Bank in [[Derby Square]] by Edward Corbett and is now known as Castle Moat House.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p321">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p321</ref> [[Liverpool Institute High School for Boys]] (1835–37) was designed by [[Arthur Hill Holme]].<ref name="Sharples 2004), p238">Sharples (2004), p238</ref> [[Liverpool Medical Institution]] (1836–37) was designed by [[Clark Rampling]].<ref name="Sharples 2004), p213">Sharples (2004), p213</ref>

The unique ensemble of High Victorian neo-classical buildings around [[William Brown Street]] has been labelled the city's "Cultural Quarter". Located here are the [[William Brown Library and Museum]] (1857–60), paid for by [[Sir William Brown, 1st Baronet, of Richmond Hill|William Brown]], based on a design by [[Thomas Allom]] the building was modified in execution by John Weightman the corporation surveyor to save money; it now houses the [[World Museum Liverpool]] and [[Liverpool Central Library]], the [[Picton Library]] by [[Cornelius Sherlock]] (1875–79), and the [[Walker Art Gallery]], paid for by [[Andrew Barclay Walker]], designed by Sherlock and [[Henry Hill Vale (architect)|H. H. Vale]] (1874–77) and was extended by Sherlock (1882–84) with additional galleries at the back. Not strictly a neo-classical design and much closer to [[Beaux-Arts architecture]], the [[County Sessions House, Liverpool|County Sessions House]] (1882–84) by Liverpool architects [[F & G Holme]].<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p300">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p300</ref> next to the Walker fits in with its more playful [[Classical order|classical]] vocabulary.
Dominating the area, the magnificent St George's Hall was built 1841–54 to a design by [[Harvey Lonsdale Elmes]] and after Elmes's early death [[Charles Robert Cockerell|C.R. Cockerell]] designed the interiors, most notably the great hall and small concert room, this last was entirely Cockerell's design. It served a variety of civic functions, including that of a concert hall and as the city's law courts. Alluding to the ancient Roman ''[[SPQR]]'', its doors are inscribed with the letters ''S.P.Q.L.'' (initials for the Latin phrase ''Senatus PopulusQue Liverpudliensis''—"the senate and people of Liverpool"). Together with its grand architecture, this proclaims the municipal pride and ambition of the city in the mid-19th century. Also nearby are [[Wellington's Column]] designed by Andrew Lawson with a sculpture by [[George Anderson Lawson]] and the [[Steble Fountain]].

:"''St George's Hall is much more prominent than the [[Royal Exchange, London|Royal Exchange]]. From its high position in Lime Street, opposite Liverpool's main railway station, the enormous edifice dominated the city from the first. Later the clearing of the area behind it and the erection of a range of more or less harmonious public structures to the north made it the center of one of the most impressive open spaces created in Victorian England''" [[Henry-Russell Hitchcock]]<ref name="Hitchcock 1954), p309">Hitchcock (1954)p309</ref>

There are a few places of worship in the neo-classical style in Liverpool, [[St Bride's Church, Liverpool]] (1829–30) by Samuel Rowland<ref name="Sharples 2004), p207">Sharples (2004), p207</ref> and [[Great George Street Congregational Church]] (1840–41) by Joseph Franklin surveyor to Liverpool Corporation.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p207"/>

The Dock Office at the [[Royal Albert Dock, Liverpool|Albert Dock]] was constructed in (1848) to a design by [[Philip Hardwick]], the portico and its [[Tuscan order|Tuscan]] columns are of [[cast iron]].<ref name="Sharples 2004), p111">Sharples (2004)p111</ref>

==Victorian (1837–1901)==
[[File:Liverpool and Birkenhead 1866 by J Bartholomew edited.jpg|thumb|right|Map of Liverpool in 1866]]

Liverpool continued to grow throughout the Victorian period from a population of 165,000 in 1831 to 685,000 by 1901.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p10"/> This meant a growing demand for housing and other buildings. After the opening of the Liverpool to Manchester Railway, other railway links to Liverpool were made, the [[Grand Junction Railway]] gave access to Birmingham and London in 1837; [[Chester and Birkenhead Railway]] (1840) then to Liverpool via Steam Ferry operational since 1815; [[Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway]] (1847) and [[Cheshire Lines Committee]] (1873).<ref name="Ritchie-Noakes 1984), p7"/> In 1880 Liverpool was granted [[City status in the United Kingdom|city status]].

"''Among the great cities of the world.... there is no other so exclusively devoted to commerce. Every house in Liverpool is either a counting-house, a warehouse, a shop, or a house that in one way or another is either an instrument or the result of trade.....and the inhabitants are nearly all to a man traders or the servants of traders''" [[Johann Georg Kohl]] 1844, in ''The British Isles and Their Inhabitants''<ref name="Sharples & Stonard 2008), p1"/>

=== Victorian docks and warehouses ===
{{Main|Port of Liverpool|Royal Albert Dock, Liverpool{{!}}Albert Dock}}
[[File:Albert Dock Panorama2.jpg|upright=1.35|thumb|Industrial Dock Architecture at the Albert Dock<br />(1841–47; Grade I)]]
The docks are central to Liverpool's history, eventually, they would stretch seven miles along the Mersey and at their widest be 0.5 miles deep.<ref name="Ritchie-Noakes 1984), p9">Ritchie Noakes (1984), p9</ref> Traffic into the docks went from 4.7&nbsp;million tons in 1865 to 12.4&nbsp;million by 1900.<ref name="Ritchie-Noakes 1980), p7">Ritchie Noakes (1980), p7</ref> The docks created during this period are: under [[Jesse Hartley]] Dock Engineer (1824–60): [[Coburg Dock]], completed 1840; [[Toxteth Dock]], opened 1841, extensively extended and reopened 1888; [[Canning Half Tide Dock]], opened 1844; [[Harrington Dock]], opened 1844; The [[Royal Albert Dock, Liverpool|Albert Dock]], completed 1847; [[Collingwood Dock]], opened 1848; [[Salisbury Dock]], opened 1848; [[Stanley Dock]] opened 1848; [[Nelson Dock, Liverpool|Nelson Dock]], opened 1848; [[Bramley-Moore Dock]], opened 1848 linked to the [[Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway]] and used for [[coal]] export;<ref name="Ritchie-Noakes 1984), p12"/> [[Wellington Dock]], opened 1851; [[Sandon Half Tide Dock]], opened 1851; [[Sandon Dock]], opened 1851; [[Wapping Dock]], completed 1852; [[Huskisson Dock]], opened 1852; [[Canada Dock]], opened 1859; under [[George Fosbery Lyster]] Dock Engineer (1861–97): [[Carriers' Dock]], opened 1862; [[Brocklebank Dock]], opened 1862; [[Herculaneum Dock]], opened 1866; [[Langton Dock]], opened 1881; [[Alexandra Dock, Liverpool|Alexandra Dock]], opened 1881; [[Hornby Dock]], opened 1884.

[[William Allingham]] writing in 1870 described Liverpool's trade:<ref name="Sharples & Stonard 2008), p2">Sharples & Stonard (2008), p2</ref>

:"''Hither converge in ceaseless streams the cotton of America, India, Egypt, the wool of Australian plains, the elephants' tusks and palm oil of African forests, the spermaceti of Arctic seas, the grain from the shores of the Mississippi, St Lawrence, Elbe, Loire, Danube, Vistula and many another stream, the hides of South America, the sugar, copper, tobacco, rice, timber, guano & c., of every land the sun's eye look upon. Hence radiate to all quarters of the globe, bales of cotton goods, linen, wollen, bulks of machinery. inexhaustible leather and hardware, salt and soap, coals and iron, copper and tin''"

[[File:Liverpool from Wapping 1875 John A Grimshaw.jpg|thumb|''Quay at Wapping Dock looking north'', 1875, by [[John Atkinson Grimshaw]], none of the buildings depicted survive, visible centre right is one of the porticoes of the Custom House]]
Despite being the main target of the [[Liverpool Blitz]] several Victorian dock buildings survived. With the best-known being the [[Royal Albert Dock, Liverpool|Albert Dock]] (1841–47). Designed by [[Jesse Hartley]]<ref name="Ritchie-Noakes 1980), p23">Ritchie Noakes (1980), p23</ref> and constructed in cast iron, brick and stone, it provides the first enclosed, non-combustible dock warehouse system in the world. Restored in the 1980s, the Albert Dock has the largest collection of Grade I listed buildings in Britain. Part of the old dock complex is now the home to the [[Merseyside Maritime Museum]] (an Anchor Point of ERIH, The [[European Route of Industrial Heritage]]), the [[International Slavery Museum]] and the [[Tate Liverpool]]. Other relics of the dock system include [[Victoria Tower, Liverpool|Victoria Tower]] and the warehouse at the north side of [[Stanley Dock]], and the warehouse at [[Wapping Dock]] all three by Hartley. The Waterloo Grain Warehouse (1867) by [[George Fosbery Lyster]] at [[Waterloo Dock (Liverpool)|Waterloo Dock]], who also designed the casemates (1881–82) at [[Herculaneum Dock]], used to store [[Petroleum]]<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p272">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p272</ref> and the [[Stanley Dock Tobacco Warehouse]] designed by [[Anthony George Lyster]], which at the time of its construction in 1901, was the world's largest building in terms of floor area, and is still the world's largest brickwork building. Other remains of the Victorian dock system are the tower (1889–90) that worked hydraulic machinery for [[Toxteth Dock]] survives, now known as Bradbury House, The Pilotage Building (1883) next to [[Canning Half Tide Dock]] was probably designed by John Arthur Berrington.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p112">Sharples (2004), p112</ref> The Warehouse at 45–51 Greenland Street (late 19th century) is a survivor of a warehouse not part of the docks,<ref name="Giles & Hawkins 2004), p30">Giles & Hawkins (2004), p30</ref> another warehouse just outside the docks is the large Clarence Warehouse probably designed by A.H. Holme.<ref name="Giles & Hawkins 2004), p39">Giles & Hawkins (2004), p39</ref>

===Victorian bank & office buildings===
At the heart of 19th century, Liverpool was [[Commerce]], the docks being second only to the [[Port of London]], and provision was needed for housing [[Bank]]s to finance enterprises, [[Insurance]] companies and businesses involved in trade and [[Maritime transport|shipping]], these activities were based in the centre of the city and were housed in grand buildings.<ref name="Sharples & Stonard 2008), pvii">Sharples & Stonard (2008), pvii</ref> Victorian banks and office buildings are particularly concentrated in [[Dale Street]] and Castle Street. Lawyers and accountants favoured Cook Street, Harrington Street, North and South John Street for their offices.<ref name="Sharples & Stonard 2008), p23">Sharples & Stonard (2008), p23</ref> An improvement [[Act of Parliament (UK)|act]] in 1826 by the Corporation of Liverpool,<ref name="Sharples & Stonard 2008), p33">Sharples & Stonard (2008), p33</ref> oversaw the creation of a new street, St George's Crescent in central Liverpool and the widening Lord Street and North and South John Streets. [[Victoria Street, Liverpool|Victoria Street]] was created in 1868, and most of its fine Victorian buildings survive.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p164">Sharples (2004), p164</ref> [[Exchange Flags]] behind the Town Hall was the centre of the cotton trade, cotton traders were based in the surrounding streets, surviving offices used by cotton traders include the Albany Building in Old Hall Street, Berey's Buildings, Bixteth Street and Mason's Building in Exchange Street East, in 1896 cotton trading moved indoors to Brown's Buildings were the former Martin Bank Headquarters is now.<ref name="Sharples & Stonard 2008), p19">Sharples & Stonard (2008), p19</ref> Liverpool's first [[Corn exchange]] opened in 1808 in Brunswick Street, designed by John Foster Sr., it was rebuilt on the same site in 1853–64 to designs by J.A. Picton but was destroyed in World War II bombing, Corn Merchants' offices were in the immediate area, but have largely been demolished.<ref name="Sharples & Stonard 2008), p19"/> Shipping companies were generally located near the waterfront and the docks,<ref name="Sharples & Stonard 2008), p28">Sharples & Stonard (2008), p28</ref> the major surviving shipping company buildings are Mersey House and Albion House. Starting in the 1840s [[Palazzo style architecture]] became popular for Banking and Office Buildings. The trading cities of [[Italian Renaissance|Renaissance Italy]] having appeal to Liverpool's merchants, especially [[Venice]] the once-great maritime trading city.<ref name="Sharples & Stonard 2008), p37">Sharples & Stonard (2008), p37</ref>

====Victorian banks====

The bank buildings of most architectural interest are: The Royal Bank, 18 Queen Avenue, off Dale Street, by Samuel Rowland;<ref name="Sharples & Stonard 2008), p27">Sharples & Stonard (2008), p27</ref> North & South Wales Bank (1838–40) (Now Castle Moat House), Derby Square, by Edward Corbett (See Neoclassical above for Illustration); [[Bank of England Building, Liverpool|Bank of England]] (1846–48), Castle Street, by [[Charles Robert Cockerell]];<ref name="Sharples 2004), p139">Sharples (2004), p139</ref> The former headquarters of the Liverpool Savings Bank (1861) by William Culshaw;<ref name="Sharples 2004), p197"/> [[62 Castle St|The Alliance Bank]] (1868), 62 Castle Street, by Lucy & Littler;<ref name="Sharples 2004), p138">Sharples (2004), p138</ref> Liverpool Union Bank (c.1870), now Halifax House, Brunswick Street, probably by [[John Cunningham (architect)|John Cunningham]], extended by [[George Enoch Grayson]];<ref name="Sharples 2004), p135">Sharples (2004), p135</ref> Former Bank of Liverpool (1882), Victoria Street by George Enoch Grayson;<ref name="Sharples 2004), p167">Sharples (2004), p167</ref> Former Union Bank of Liverpool (1885), 43 to 47 Bold Street, by George Enoch Grayson; Adelphi Bank (c.1891–92), Castle Street, by [[W. D. Caröe]];<ref name="Sharples 2004), p139"/> Leyland & Bullin's Bank; 36 Castle Street, former Leyland and Bullens Bank (1895), by [[Grayson and Ould]];<ref name="Sharples 2004), p139"/> Parr's Bank (Now Nat West Bank) (1898–1901), Castle Street, by [[Richard Norman Shaw]], execution overseen by Willink & Thicknesse.<ref name="Sharples & Stonard 2008), p64">Sharples & Stonard (2008), p64</ref>

For both the Prudential Assurance Building and Pearl Assurance Building see the section on Alfred Waterhouse. Mersey Chambers (c.1878) was designed by G.E. ====Victorian speculative office buildings====
Office buildings erected speculatively include: The Royal Bank Building (c.1837–38), Dale Street, by Samuel Rowland, the bank (see above) occupied the building in the court to the rear and let the building; The Temple (1864–65), Dale Street by James Picton;<ref name="Sharples 2004), p146"/> [[Albany (Liverpool)|The Albany]] (1856–58) by [[James Kellaway Colling]] and let to cotton traders;<ref name="Sharples & Stonard 2008), p36">Sharples & Stonard (2008), p36</ref> Hargreaves Building (1859), 5 Chapel Street by James Picton;<ref name="Sharples & Stonard 2008), p37"/> Berey's Buildings (1864), Bixteth Street, designed by William Culshaw and let to cotton traders; Rigby's Buildings (1865) Dale Street, stuccoed office building with older warehouse behind;<ref name="Sharples 2004), p146"/> Mason's Building (c.1866), Exchange Street East, by John Cunningham, let to cotton traders;<ref name="Sharples & Stonard 2008), p20">Sharples & Stonard (2008), p20</ref> Imperial Chambers (c.1870), Dale Street, architect unknown, in a Gothic style and with a glazed roof courtyard;<ref name="Sharples 2004), p147">Sharples (2004), p147</ref> Built as an office with warehouse behind, for the brewer Peter Walker, 64 to 66 Duke Street, designed by John Elliot Reeve;<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p321"/> Central Buildings, North John Street, large office building for the period, by Thomas C. Clarke;<ref name="Sharples 2004), p156">Sharples (2004), p156</ref> Princes Buildings (1882), Dale Street, by Henry Shelmerdine;<ref name="Sharples & Stonard 2008), p13">Sharples & Stonard (2008), p13</ref> [[12 Hanover Street]] (1889–90), office building with adjoining warehouse, by [[Edmund Kirby]];<ref name="Sharples 2004), p150"/> Victoria Chambers (1893); 40–42 Castle Street, by Grayson & Ould.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p138"/> Century Buildings (1901), Victoria Street is by Henry Hartley.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p165"/> Boldly Gothic is Musker's Buildings (1881–82) in Dale Street by Thomas E. Murray.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p147"/> 25 & 27 Victoria Street (1881), by W.H. Picton.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p165"/> New Zealand House (1893), 18 Water Street is by Walter Aubrey Thomas. Imperial Buildings (1879), Victoria Street are by E. & H. Shelmerdine.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p168">Sharples (2004), p168</ref>

====Office buildings by Peter Ellis====
[[Peter Ellis (architect)|Peter Ellis]] was an obscure architect and [[civil engineer]] who, nevertheless, designed the pioneering [[Oriel Chambers]] (1864)<ref name="Ainsworth & Jones 2013), p169">Ainswoth & Jones (2013), p169</ref> in Water Street as  "one of the first office buildings to be clad in glazed [[Curtain wall (architecture)|curtain-walling]]"<ref name=nomination /> in its rear courtyard. Well ahead of its time, the building was severely criticised in ''The Builder'' of 16 June 1866 as a "large agglomeration of protruding plate-glass bubbles", a "vast abortion" without any aesthetic qualities.<ref>Q. Hughes, ''Seaport'', Bluecoat Press, 1993, p.62.</ref> In all likelihood, however, it was studied by young [[John Wellborn Root]] who spent some time in Liverpool to escape the [[American Civil War]] just when Ellis' building had been finished. Root took some of Ellis' ideas back to America where he later became an important architect of the [[Chicago school (architecture)|Chicago School of Architecture]]. Oriel Chambers, therefore, played an important role in the development of the [[skyscraper]]. Ellis' only other known building, [[16 Cook Street]], Liverpool, dates from 1866<ref name="Ainsworth & Jones 2013), p127">Ainswoth & Jones (2013), p127</ref> and also features a curtain wall in its rear courtyard.

===Victorian retail and wholesale buildings===
As Liverpool expanded so [[retail]] buildings grew in grandeur to meet the rising demand in an increasingly prosperous city. Victorian retail buildings are found amongst others on Church Street, Victoria Street, Lord Street & Bold Street and include: 14–16 Bold Street, built (1848) for John Cripps, Shawl Merchant and manufacturer;<ref name="Sharples 2004), p194">Sharples (2004) p194</ref> 25 Church Street (1858) was built for Elkington's art metalworkers and [[Electroplating]] business by [[Lewis Hornblower]];<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p314">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p314</ref> [[Compton House, Liverpool|Compton House]] (1866–67), Church Street, built for J.R. Jeffrey by Thomas Haigh & Company, it one of the first purpose-built [[Department store]]s in the world;<ref name="Sharples 2004), p150">Sharples (2004), p150</ref> Former Agnew's art dealers (1877), 1 Castle Street;<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p310">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p310</ref> Former Robert & Jones jewellery shop at 2 Castle Street (1882), in an early 16th-century French style;<ref name="Sharples 2004), p139"/> The Fruit Exchange (c.1888), Victoria Street, built as a goods depot, converted to exchange in 1923;<ref name="Sharples 2004), p166">Sharples (2004), p166</ref> 92 Bold Street (1890s), is a late example of [[Greek Revival architecture]], attributed to [[W. & G. Audsley]];<ref name="Sharples 2004), p197">Sharples (2004), p197</ref> 58 Bold Street (c.1900), is an unusual example of an [[Arts and Crafts movement]] shop, ascribed to T. Myddleton Shallcross.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p195"/> Wholesale is represented by the Commercial Saleroom Buildings (1879), Victoria Street, by James F. Doyle, used for wholesale auctions of imported fruit.<ref name="Sharples & Stonard 2008), p23"/> The bold arches, the Italian Gothic 81–89 Lord Street by [[Walter Aubrey Thomas]] is a grand building, also in Lord Street is Venice Chambers, by Edmund Kirkby.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p154">Sharples (2004), p154</ref>

===Victorian buildings for health, education & social care===
In an age before [[social security]] or the [[National Health Service]], any provision of medical or social care depended on [[Charity (practice)|charity]] or had to be privately paid for, even education prior to the [[Elementary Education Act 1870]] was so dependent. Liverpool's wealthy elite and the comfortable class below them created institutions and supported them through donations. For example, [[Andrew Barclay Walker]] not only paid for the Walker Art Gallery with a £50,000 (over £5,000,000 in 2019) donation but gave towards the founding of the university, as did [[Henry Tate]] and [[George Holt (merchant)|George Holt]]. Both [[William Pickles Hartley]] and [[William Rathbone VI|William Rathbone]] gave away a third of their income to charity.<ref name="Giles 2008), p15">Giles (2008), p15</ref>
See the Alfred Waterhouse section below for buildings designed by him, including Royal Infirmary, University of Liverpool, the Turner Memorial Home and the Seaman's Orphanage. Liverpool had many examples of Victorian buildings created to provide health, social care and education.

====Victorian schools, colleges and libraries====
Notable educational buildings of the era are [[Liverpool Collegiate School]], (1840–43) in a Tudor Gothic style by [[Harvey Lonsdale Elmes]]. Other institutional buildings include [[Blackburne House]] built 1788 and extensively remodelled (1874–76) by W.I. Mason in [[Second Empire architecture|French Second Empire style]], became the Blackburne House Girls' School (1844). The former [[Royal School for the Blind, Liverpool|Royal School for the Blind]], Hardman Street, (1849–51) in classical style by A.H. Holme (Now a Trades Union Building), a new building for the school opened in 1899 in Wavertree. An example of a [[School boards in England and Wales|board school]], formerly Arnot Street School, Walton, is a post-1870 education school and was designed by [[Edmund Kirby]] (1884 extended 1894), other surviving board schools are, Chatsworth School (1874), Edge Hill, designed by [[Thomas Mellard Reade]],<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p413">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p413</ref> who also designed Granby Street School (1880), Toxteth.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p475">Sharples (2004), p475</ref> [[Liverpool College of Art]] designed by Thomas Cook and opened in 1883 in the [[Queen Anne style architecture]].<ref name="Sharples 2004), p236">Sharples (2004), p236</ref> At the end of the period the [[College of Technology and Museum Extension]] was built to the designs of [[Edward William Mountford]], completed (1901). The first branch library in the city was Kensington Library 1890 extended 1897, Edge Hill by the City of Liverpool Surveyor [[Thomas Shelmerdine]],<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p412">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p412</ref> who also designed [[Everton Library]], built in 1896, also the designed by Shelmerdine is the Technical Institute, Picton Road, Wavertree.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p494">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p494</ref> The former St Austin's school (1860), Aigburth Road provided elementary education for the local Roman Catholic population of Aigburth.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p383">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p383</ref> [[Henry Clutton]] designed a major extension (1877) to [[St Francis Xavier's College, Liverpool]] for the Roman Catholic Church to provide education for adherents of the Church. The former Gordon Working Lads' Institute (1886) by David Walker, in a northern Renaissance style, it provided technical education for the working class and contained classrooms, gymnasium and concert hall, it was paid for by merchant and ship owner William Cliff.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p435">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p435</ref> The equivalent for girls was the Bankhall Girls' Institute (1889), Stanley Road, Kirkdale, this was funded by Thomas Worthington Cookson, merchant and shipowner.<ref name="Giles 2008), p41">Giles (2008), p41</ref> The Catholic church built St Vincent's School for the Blind (1899), Yew Tree Lane, West Derby.<ref name="Giles 2008), p73">Giles (2008), p73</ref>

====Victorian hospitals and buildings for social care====
Buildings for health care and social provisions include the Adult Deaf and Dumb Institute now, [[Merseyside Centre for the Deaf]] by E.H. Banner in a red brick gothic; the now-demolished [[Liverpool Sailors' Home]] provide hospitality and a bed for the night for sailors visiting the city. Hospitals founded in the period include [[Liverpool Maternity Hospital]]; founded in 1741 the [[Liverpool Royal Infirmary]] underwent vast expansion in the late 1880s. Lunatics were catered for at the now-demolished [[Lunatic asylum]], [[Rainhill Hospital]] (1846–51) designed by Harvey Lonsdale Elmes, just outside the city. Workshop for the Outdoor Blind (1870), Cornwallis Street, designed by G.T. Redmayne, provided employment for the blind, who made baskets, matting and brushes.<ref name="Giles 2008), p71">Giles (2008), p71</ref> The [[YMCA]] building, Mount Pleasant was built (1874–77), l designed in a gothic style by H.H. Vale, it contained a gymnasium, reading room, library, lecture hall and classrooms. Church House (1885), Hanover Street by [[Walter Aubrey Thomas]] built to house the Central Institute of the Mersey Mission to Seaman and a [[Temperance movement|temperance]] public house;<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p324">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p324</ref> The former Eye and Ear Hospital (1878–80), Myrtle Street by C.O. Ellison, in an old English style,<ref name="Sharples 2004), p236"/> also in Myrtle Street and by C.O. Ellison is the former Sheltering Home for Destitute Children (1888–89).<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p378">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p378</ref> The former [[Liverpool Homeopathic Hospital]] (1887) was designed by [[F & G Holme]] in the [[French Renaissance architecture]] style.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p237">Sharples (2004), p237</ref> The [[Florence Institute]] (1889) is the oldest surviving purpose-built boys' club in Britain, probably designed by H.W. Keef, paid for by merchant Bernard Hall.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p273">Sharples (2004), p273</ref> The Gordon Smith Institute for Seaman (1899) by James Strong of Walker & Strong, in Paradise Street, was created to provide seamen with a library, reading room and assembly hall.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p208">Sharples (2004), p208</ref> Former Eye and Ear Hospital, 3–5 Myrtle Street, was designed by C.O. Ellsion. The former Walton [[Workhouse]] (1864–68) was designed by William Culshaw.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p491"/> The New Hall complex (1887–89), Longmoor Lane, Fazakerley, designed by Charles H. Lancaster, was built as cottages to house deprived children, the group of cottages is terminated by a monumental hall with a clock tower.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p428">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p428</ref>

===Victorian public buildings===
Many public buildings of the era survive in central Liverpool. The major public building of the mid-Victorian age was [[Municipal Buildings, Liverpool|Municipal Buildings]] (now a hotel) started in 1860 by Liverpool Corporation surveyor John Weightman (not to be confused with his near-contemporary [[John Grey Weightman]]), and finished in 1866 by his successor as surveyor E.R. Robson, who amended the design. The style is a mixture of [[Italianate architecture]] and [[French Renaissance]], the latter style is evident in the elaborate roofs of the building. The building function as municipal offices to house the growing council workforce. Most of the grand public buildings in the centre of Liverpool were in the [[Neoclassical architecture|Neoclassical style]], so are dealt with in the dedicated section above. Weightman also designed the Main Bridewell and the Magistrates' Courts. The partially surviving old General Post Office (1894–97), in Victoria Street, was designed by [[Henry Tanner (architect)|Henry Tanner]].<ref name="Sharples 2004), p167"/> The former offices for the city's Education Department (1897–98), Sir Thomas Street by Charles E. Deacon survives. The Old Bridewell police station, Campbell Square, was built (1861).<ref name="Sharples 2004), p204">Sharples (2004), p204</ref> Thomas Shelmerdine designed the Central Fire Station that was opened in 1897, also at the end of the 19th century he remodelled the council chamber in the Town Hall.

Several Victorian public buildings survive in the suburbs. John Weightman designed [[HM Prison Liverpool|Walton Gaol]] that was constructed between 1848 and 1855, the gatehouse and chapel are in [[Romanesque Revival architecture|Neo-Norman style]]. Also in Walton are the former School Board Offices (c.1890) by Edmund Kirkby. The [[Toxteth Town Hall|Public Offices]] in Toxteth (1865–66) are in Italianate style by Thomas Layland.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p474">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p474</ref> The Cross, West Derby Village, was designed by [[William Eden Nesfield]] and carved by [[James Forsyth (sculptor)|James Forsyth]].<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p503">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p503</ref> The [[Picton Clock Tower]] of 1884 was designed and paid for by James Picton as a memorial to his wife.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p497">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p497</ref> There are several former Victorian Police Stations around the city, including the one in Lark Lane (1885) by F.U. Holme;<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p455">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p455</ref> Rice Lane, Walton; Old Swan, Derby Road, Tue Brook now flats; in Durning Road, Edge Hill is a combined police and fire station, mid-19th century, in a Tudor Gothic style;<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p413"/> The former Police and Fire Station, Westminster Road, Kirkdale, by city surveyor Thomas Shelmerdine.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p435"/> The Gregson Memorial Institute, Garmoyle Road, Wavertree, was a privately funded library and museum designed by A.P. Fry, the collections have been dispersed.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p494"/>

===Alfred Waterhouse===
{{Main|Alfred Waterhouse}}
Born Stone Hill, Liverpool 19 July 1830, but grew up in [[Aigburth]], architect Alfred Waterhouse established his architectural practice first in [[Manchester]] in 1854 and from 1865 in London. He achieved national fame for a large number of mostly institutional, commercial and educational buildings throughout England, his best-known buildings being [[Manchester Town Hall]] and the [[Natural History Museum, London]]. He also designed several structures for his home city.<ref name="Cunningham Waterhouse & 1992), p84">Cunningham & Waterhouse (1992), p84</ref> Including the [[University of Liverpool]]'s [[Victoria Building, University of Liverpool|Victoria Building]], completed in (1889–92). Waterhouse's use of striking red brick and [[Burmantofts Pottery|Burmantofts terracotta]] as building materials for its exterior and tiles inside inspired [[Edgar Allison Peers]], a Spanish professor at Liverpool, to coin the term "[[Red Brick University]]" and to then apply it collectively to six recently founded institutions of higher education in some of the major industrial cities of England.<ref>{{cite book | last = Peers | first = Edgar Allison | title = Redbrick University | year = 1943 }}</ref> Waterhouse designed other buildings for the university including the Chemical Laboratories (1884–87); the Walker Engineering Block (1887–91), the Gossage Chemical Laboratories (1895–97), the Medical School (1895–97), the Thompson Yates Laboratories (1895–98) and one final work for the university was a joint work with his son [[Paul Waterhouse]] for the Medical School, the Whelan Building (1899–1904) that housed the Anatomy Department. Other important Waterhouse complexes are the [[Liverpool Royal Infirmary]] (1886–92) and [[Newsham Park Hospital]] (1870–75) built as The Liverpool Seamen's Orphan Institution. Waterhouse also designed the [[Great North Western Hotel]] (1871) in [[French Renaissance architecture|French renaissance style]], that served Liverpool Lime Street railway station. He also designed [[Prudential Assurance Building, Liverpool]] (1885–86), he designed several office buildings for The Prudential Assurance company throughout Britain in the same style. He also designed the Pearl Assurance building, now known as St John's House. A smaller commission was the [[Turner Home, Liverpool]]. Waterhouse also designed three large Gothic houses in the city: the first is New Heys (1861–65) for lawyer W.G. Bateson, Allerton Road; then [[Allerton Priory]] (1866–75) and its entrance Lodge for [[Coal mining|colliery]] owner John Grant Morris and Mossley Hill House (1869–72), Park Avenue, for general [[broker]] Lloyd Rayner, it is now part of Mossley Hill Hospital.

===Victorian places of worship===

As Liverpool grew so the need grew for new places of worship, the Georgian churches were largely concentrated in the centre of the city. The new suburbs spreading further from that centre, this resulted in a major building programme of places of worship.<ref name="Brown & de Figueiredo 2008), p13">Brown & de Figueiredo (2008), p13</ref> Princes Park & Sefton Park areas saw the construction of some of the finest places of worship in Liverpool. In Prince's Road at the north end: [[Greek Orthodox Church|Greek Orthodox]] Church of St Nicholas built for the city's small but wealthy Greek community whose wealth largely derived from shipping;<ref name="Brown & de Figueiredo 2008), p77">Brown & de Figueiredo (2008), p77</ref> Welsh [[Presbyterianism|Presbyterian]] Church (1865–67), the Welsh born population of the city was 20,000 in 1870 rising to 80,000 in 1891, much of their wealth came from property speculation;<ref name="Brown & de Figueiredo 2008), p25">Brown & de Figueiredo (2008), p25</ref> the Princes Road Synagogue was built for [[Orthodox Judaism|Orthodox Jewish]] community; and the Church of St Margaret of Antioch has one of the most elaborate interiors of any of the city's churches.<ref name="Brown & de Figueiredo 2008), p21">Brown & de Figueiredo (2008), p21</ref> Near Sefton Park the [[Church of England|Anglican]] church of Saint Agnes and Saint Pancras, Ullet Road; the [[Catholic Church|Roman Catholic]] St Clare's Church, Arundel Avenue;<ref name="Brown & de Figueiredo 2008), p24">Brown & de Figueiredo (2008), p24</ref> Ullet Road [[Unitarianism|Unitarian]] Church; the Anglican Christ Church, Linnet Lane.

Certain churches were built to cater for the poorest areas of the city, St Clement, Beaumont Street, Toxteth, that was [[Low church]] Anglican;<ref name="Brown & de Figueiredo 2008), p36">Brown & de Figueiredo (2008), p36</ref> and for Roman Catholic congregations St Alban's, Athol Street, Vauxhall (1849), now used as a climbing centre, Our Lady of Reconciliation (1859–60), Eldon Street, Vauxhall; St Sylvester's (1889), Silvester Street, Vauxhall; All Souls' (1870 demolished 1967), Collingwood Street, Kirkdale, St Briget's Bevington Hill, Vauxhall (1870 demolished 1967). These catered to a largely Irish Catholic working-class population, who had migrated to the city and congregated in the northern suburb of Vauxhall in the wake of the [[Great Famine (Ireland)|Great Famine]].<ref name="Brown & de Figueiredo 2008), p40">Brown & de Figueiredo (2008), p40</ref>

By the late 19th century Liverpool was a cosmopolitan city, there were many immigrant communities, many seamen passing through the port including natives of West Africa and the Far East, [[Chinatown, Liverpool|Chinatown]] dates from the 1860s, not many have left traces of their often temporary places of worship.<ref name="Brown & de Figueiredo 2008), p67">Brown & de Figueiredo (2008), p67</ref> A notable exception is Gustav Adolf Church (1883), Park Lane, by the mid-1850s over 50,000 Swedish seamen were visiting the city annually, the church was built for them.<ref name="Brown & de Figueiredo 2008), p68">Brown & de Figueiredo (2008), p68</ref> This era saw the establishment in 1889 of what is believed to be Britain's first Mosque, the [[Liverpool Muslim Institute]] in No. 8 Brougham Terrace, West Derby Road.<ref name="Brown & de Figueiredo 2008), p77"/>

====Victorian non-conformists churches, chapels, synagogues and Greek Orthodox church====

Victorian Liverpool's notable places of worship include the [[Greek Orthodox Church of St Nicholas]] built in the [[Neo-Byzantine architecture]] style 1864–1870 original design William Hardie Hay (1813–1901) & James Murdoch Hay (1823–1915), built by Henry Sumners of [[Culshaw and Sumners]]; Former Victoria Chapel (1878–80), for the Welsh Calvinists, Crosshall Street by W.H. Picton, now used as the Juvenile Court;<ref name="Sharples 2004), p144">Sharples (2004), p144</ref> [[W. D. Caröe]]'s [[Gustav Adolf Church, Liverpool|Gustav Adolf Church]] (the Swedish Seamen's Church, reminiscent of Nordic styles). Fine examples of [[Nonconformist (Protestantism)|nonconformist]] churches in a Gothic style are the [[Welsh Presbyterian Church (Liverpool)|Welsh Presbyterian Church]] by Liverpool-based architects [[W. & G. Audsley]]; [[Ullet Road Unitarian Church]] and library of (1896–99) and the cloister and Church Hall (c.1901), both by [[Thomas Worthington (architect)|Thomas Worthington]] & [[Percy Worthington]], the stained glass is mostly by [[William Morris]] and [[Edward Burne-Jones]], the mural paintings in the vestry and adjacent library are by [[Gerald Moira]], in the cloister, there are memorials from an older church including a bust of [[William Roscoe]] by [[John Gibson (sculptor)|John Gibson]],<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p450">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p450</ref> many of Liverpool's richest families were members of the congregation and included the Holts, the Tates, the Roscoes, the Rathbones and the Brunners.<ref name="Brown & de Figueiredo 2008), p31">Brown & de Figueiredo (2008), p31</ref> Having a Jewish community since the mid-18th century, Liverpool has several synagogues. The grade I listed [[Princes Road Synagogue]], by W. & G. Audsley in the [[Moorish Revival]] style is architecturally the most important.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p249">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p249</ref> and cost nearly £15,000<ref name="Brown & de Figueiredo 2008), p25"/> Two further orthodox synagogues are in the [[Allerton, Liverpool|Allerton]] and the [[Childwall]] district, where a significant Jewish community resides.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.liverpoolheritageforum.org.uk/articles.php?id=36 |title=Liverpool's Jewish heritage |access-date=13 May 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070206010004/http://www.liverpoolheritageforum.org.uk/articles.php?id=36 |archive-date=6 February 2007 |url-status=dead}}</ref> There are several classical style chapels in Liverpool including the small Particular Baptist Chapel, Everton (1847) architect unknown, converted to flats 2005<ref name="Sharples 2004), p261">Sharples (2004), p261</ref> and the Old Welsh Chapel, by Oliver and Lamb of Newcastle, now the Chatham Building University of Liverpool.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p219">Sharples (2004), p219</ref>

====Anglican parish churches====

During the 19th century, three generations of the Horsfall family had a major influence on Anglican church building in Liverpool. [[Charles Horsfall]] a merchant and stockbroker was a founder of St George's Everton, his sons built Christ Church (1848) (destroyed by bombing 1941), Great Homer Street, Everton, in his memory. His son Robert and grandson Douglas became strong advocates of the [[Oxford Movement]].<ref name="Brown & de Figueiredo 2008), p20">Brown & de Figueiredo (2008), p20</ref> Robert Horsfall paid for St Margaret's of Antioch,<ref name="Brown & de Figueiredo 2008), p21"/> [[Douglas Horsfall]] paid for Church of St Agnes and St Pancras, cost £28,000.<ref name="Brown & de Figueiredo 2008), p22">Brown & de Figueiredo (2008), p22</ref>

Many Liverpool suburbs have [[Gothic Revival architecture|Gothic Revival]] churches, those belonging to the [[Church of England]] include: [[Church of St Clement, Liverpool]] by Arthur and George Yates Williams;<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p469">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p469</ref> Holy Trinity, Walton Breck, Anfiled by John Hay;<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p393">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p393</ref> [[St Mary's Church, West Derby, Liverpool|St Mary's Church, West Derby]] by [[George Gilbert Scott]]; [[Church of Saint John the Baptist, Liverpool|Church of Saint John the Baptist]] by [[George Frederick Bodley]]; [[Christ Church, Toxteth Park]] by [[Culshaw and Sumners]]; [[Church of St Margaret of Antioch, Liverpool|Church of St Margaret of Antioch]] by [[George Edmund Street]]; [[Church of St Matthew and St James, Mossley Hill]] by [[Sharpe, Paley and Austin|Paley and Austin]]; [[All Saints Church, Speke]] by [[John Loughborough Pearson]]; [[Church of All Hallows, Allerton]] by [[George Enoch Grayson]], most of the stained glass is by [[William Morris]]'s firm some to the designs of [[Edward Burne-Jones]];<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p386">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p386</ref> St Michael's Church, Garston by Thomas D. Barry & Son;<ref name="PPp429"/> [[Church of St Agnes and St Pancras, Toxteth Park]] by John Loughborough Pearson; St Cyprian's Durning Road, Edge Hill is by Henry Sumners;<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p410">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p410</ref> [[St Peter's Church, Woolton, Liverpool]] by [[Grayson and Ould]]; [[Church of St Dunstan, Liverpool|Church of St. Dunstan's]] by Charles Aldridge and Charles Deacon.

An example of [[Romanesque Revival architecture]] is the parish church of [[Church of St Anne, Aigburth|St Anne, Aigburth]] architects Cunningham and Holme. The now redundant Christ Church (1870), Kensington, Edge Hill by W & G Audsley is red brick in an Italian Romanesque style.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p410"/>

====Roman Catholic churches====

Gothic style parish churches that are [[Catholic Church|Roman Catholic]] include: [[St Oswald's Church, Old Swan, Liverpool|St Oswald's Church, Old Swan]] (1840–42) by [[Augustus Pugin]], the interior rebuilt (1951–57) by [[Adrian Gilbert Scott]] in a modern idiom, the tower and spire by Pugin survive, the associated Convent of Mercy is almost certainly also by Pugin;<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), pp480-481">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), pp480-481</ref> [[St Francis Xavier Church, Liverpool|St Francis Xavier Church]], Everton, by [[Joseph John Scoles]] is one of the grandest Catholic churches in the city; [[St Anne's Church, Edge Hill]] by Charles Francis Hansom later altered by Pugin & Pugin; [[Church of St Vincent de Paul, Liverpool]], by [[E. W. Pugin]]; [[Church of Our Lady of Reconciliation, Liverpool|Our Lady of Reconciliation]] by E. W. Pugin; [[St Sylvester's Church, Vauxhall]] by [[Pugin & Pugin]]; [[Our Lady of Mount Carmel RC Church]] (1876–78), Toxteth was designed by Liverpool architect James O'Byrne;<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p471">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p471</ref> [[Sacred Heart Church, Liverpool|Sacred Heart Church]] (1885–86), Hall Lane, Everton, by [[George Goldie (architect)|George Goldie]], Charles Edwin Child  & [[Edward Goldie]], with a high altar by Pugin & Pugin;<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p420">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p420</ref> [[Church of St Clare, Liverpool]] (1888–90) by [[Leonard Stokes]], cost £7,834 paid for by brothers and cotton brokers Francis & James Reynolds, the high altar [[Triptych]] was painted by [[Robert Anning Bell]] and relief sculpture by [[George Frampton]].<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p448">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p448</ref> An example of a church in [[Italianate architecture|Italianate]] style is the [[Church of Saint Bridget, Liverpool|Church of Saint Bridget]], Wavertree by E.A. Heffer. [[Our Lady of the Annunciation Church, Liverpool|Bishop Eton Monastery]], Chapel begun 1851, Augustus Welby Northmore Pugin, and Edward Welby Pugin completed 1858, the high altar of 1866 was designed by [[John Francis Bentley]].<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p400">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p400</ref>

===Victorian infrastructure and transport===
[[Liverpool Corporation Waterworks]] founded in (1847), oversaw the supply of drinking water and disposal of sewerage for the city. [[James Newlands]] was appointed in 1847 as borough engineer and designed the city's integrated sewer network, believed to be the first in the world. The [[Everton water tower]] and works completed 1857 to a design by Thomas Duncan, appointed in 1846 as the city's water engineer working for Newlands, is a notable example of Victorian infrastructure, and was connected to the then-new [[Rivington Reservoirs]].<ref name="Sharples 2004), p25">Sharples (2004), p25</ref> The ever-growing city resulted in a greater demand for water and between 1881 and 1888 the Corporation went on to created [[Lake Vyrnwy]] in Wales, the cost was over £2&nbsp;million, (nearly a £ quarter of a billion in 2019), the engineers responsible for the project were [[George Deacon (civil engineer)|George Deacon]] borough engineer and [[Thomas Hawksley]]. In an era when [[gas lighting]] was used both for street lighting and increasingly throughout the period to light homes and from the 1880s [[gas stove]]s started to become common. [[Gasworks]] became essential to everyday life, Liverpool Gas Company 1845–1956 operated the now-demolished gasworks at [[Garston, Liverpool|Garston]].

<gallery>
File:Everton Water Works (5).JPG|Everton Water Tower, Everton Waterworks, Margaret Street<br />(1857; Grade II)
File:Everton Water Works (8).JPG|South Building, Everton Waterworks, Margaret Street<br />(1857; Grade II)
File:Gas holder, Banks Road, Garston.jpg|Gas holder, Garston Gasworks<br />(1891; demolished 2015)
File:Water tower, Reservoir Road, Woolton.jpg|Water Tower, Reservoir Road, Woolton<br />(c.1900; Grade II)
</gallery>

[[Liverpool Lime Street railway station]] opened in 1836 as the terminus of the [[Liverpool and Manchester Railway]], initially with a wooden roof by [[John Cunningham (architect)|John Cunningham]] and [[Arthur Hill Holme]] the classical facade was by John Foster Jr.; in 1846–50 it was rebuilt by [[William Tite]] with an iron roofed train shed of 153 feet span by [[Richard Turner (iron-founder)|Richard Turner]]. This in turn was replaced by the current roof (1867) by [[William Baker (engineer)|William Baker]] and F. Stevenson, at 200 feet span this was briefly the widest roof in the world, In 1878–79 the train shed was doubled with the new span to the south of the existing one by E.W. Ives, being a copy of the earlier one.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p304">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p304</ref>

The Midland Railway Warehouse now the [[National Conservation Centre]] was built in 1872 to designs of Henry Sumners of [[Culshaw and Sumners]]. The Engine house, 1849, at Edge Hill Station was Built for Liverpool and Manchester Railway<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p414">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p414</ref> Another survivor of the Victorian railway age is [[Liverpool Exchange railway station|Exchange railway station]], designed by [[John Hawkshaw]], originally opened in 1850 as the terminus of the [[Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway]], the current building was built between 1886 and 1888 by Henry Shelmerdine.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p164"/>
[[St Michaels railway station]] to serve northern Aigburth, and [[Aigburth railway station]] to serve central Aigburth both opened 1864, were both originally part of the [[Garston and Liverpool Railway]] and later became part of the [[Cheshire Lines Committee]]. [[Cressington railway station]] that serves southern Aigburth and [[Hunts Cross railway station]], are representative of the fine suburban railway stations built in 1873 for the Cheshire Lines Committee. 1886 would see the creation of Liverpool's first underground railway stations [[List of underground stations of the Merseyrail network]], as part of what is now [[Mersey Railway]], there was a necessity for a pumping station to keep the rail tunnel (opened 1886) under the [[River Mersey]] free of water, the one at the Liverpool end of the tunnel is located on [[Mann Island]], it is now redundant. An unusual piece of infrastructure is the [[Wapping Tunnel]] by George Stephenson with construction between 1826 and 1829, when this was converted to use by steam trains several ventilation towers were built in the 1890s. The [[Liverpool Overhead Railway]] opened (1893) designed by [[Charles Douglas Fox]] and [[James Henry Greathead]], demolished (1957–58), this early electric railway, at its greatest extent, stretched along the Docks from [[Seaforth & Litherland railway station]] to [[Dingle railway station]].

In an age when transport was dominated by the railways, a rare example of a canal warehouse (1874) is found at 41 Bankhall Street, Kirkdale, used to transship goods for the Leeds and Liverpool canal.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p436">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p436</ref>

===Victorian cemeteries and parks===
{{Main|Parks and open spaces in Liverpool}}
English Heritage National Register of Historic Parks describes Merseyside's [[:Category:Parks and commons in Liverpool|Victorian Parks]] as collectively the "most important in the country".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.liv.ac.uk/mcs/lfs/consultations/blandfordlet0205.pdf|title=Dr. Peter Brown, chair, Merseyside Civic Society|access-date=12 January 2012|archive-date=20 September 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130920155812/http://www.liv.ac.uk/mcs/lfs/consultations/blandfordlet0205.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> The city of Liverpool has ten listed parks and cemeteries, including two Grade I and five Grade II*, more than any other English city apart from London.

The Victorian era saw the creation of many of the city's best parks. [[Prince's Park, Liverpool|Prince's Park]] (1842–43; Grade II*), planned by [[Joseph Paxton]] and [[James Pennethorne]] covering 110 acres (45 hectares), was a private development by local industrialist Richard Vaughan Yates, and included the development of [[middle class]] housing surrounding the park;<ref name="Sharples 2004), p276">Sharples (2004), p 276</ref> eighty years after its opening the City Council acquired it. There developed in the late 1860s the concept of a 'ribbon of parks'<ref name="Layton-Jones & Lee 2008), p26">Layton-Jones & Lee (2008), p 26</ref> surrounding the centre of Liverpool; these were all paid for by the City Council: [[Newsham Park]] (1864–68; Grade II) by [[Edward Kemp (landscape architect)|Edward Kemp]];<ref name="Layton-Jones & Lee 2008), p29">Layton-Jones & Lee (2008), p29</ref> [[Stanley Park, Liverpool|Stanley Park]] (1870; Grade II) by Edward Kemp, buildings for the park were designed by the corporation surveyor E.R. Robson;<ref name="Layton-Jones & Lee 2008), pp33-34">Layton-Jones & Lee (2008), pp.&nbsp;33–34</ref> [[Sefton Park]] (1867–1872; Grade I) by [[Édouard André]] & [[Lewis Hornblower]], covers 269 acres (109 hectares)<ref name="Layton-Jones & Lee 2008), p37">Layton-Jones & Lee (2008), p37</ref> the main building in Sefton Park is the Palm House (1896) by Mackenzie & Moncur paid for by [[Henry Yates Thompson]],<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p454">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p454</ref> many of the buildings in Sefton Park are by the corporation surveyor Thomas Shelmerdine, for example the Ullet Road gates.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p282">Sharples (2004), p282</ref> Also by Mackenzie & Moncur is the Isla Gladstone Conservatory, Stanley Park.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p396">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p396</ref>

The best cemeteries for Victorian architecture are [[Toxteth Park Cemetery]] established 1855–56, the architect was Thomas D Barry, landscaping by [[William Gay (landscape gardener and surveyor)|William Gay]],<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p474"/> listed Grade II and [[Anfield Cemetery]] that was laid out 1856–63, covering 140 acres (57 hectares) the cemetery landscape is listed Grade II* and was the work of [[Edward Kemp (landscape architect)|Edward Kemp]], many of the buildings, including entrance lodges, Lansdowne House used as the registrar's offices, chapels only the non-conformist chapel survives (the Anglican chapel has been demolished) and the catacombs are by architects Lucy & Littler<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p394">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p394</ref> and monuments have individual listings. For example, the McLennan monument is in the [[Egyptian Revival architecture|Egyptian revival style]] and is listed grade II. [[Everton Cemetery]] was the layout and buildings designed by Thomas D. Barry and Sons.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p427">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p427</ref> [[West Derby Cemetery]] opened (1884) has a fine entrance lodge, the landscape is Grade II by William Wortley and the architect was F. Bartram Payton.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p405">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p405</ref> One of the first Crematoria (1894–96) in the country is in Anfield Cemetery, designed by James Rhind.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p395">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p395</ref>

===Victorian buildings for entertainment, sport & leisure===
In Lord Nelson Street is the former Socialist Hall of Science, part of an [[Owenism|Owenite]] group, later used as a concert hall.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p186">Sharples (2004), p186</ref> The Lamb Hotel, High Street, Wavertree, looks Georgian but was built in the 1850s.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p497"/> Marlborough House (1852–53), #52, Bold Street, on the corner of Bold Street and Concert Street, the ground floor was shops the upper floors functioned as a [[Music hall]], by [[Arthur Hill Holme]].<ref name="Sharples 2004), p195">Sharples (2004), p195</ref> The oldest extant theatre in the city is the [[Liverpool Playhouse]], originally built 1866, remodelled 1895 and a new auditorium built-in 1911 by [[Stanley Davenport Adshead]].<ref name="Sharples 2004), p189">Sharples (2004), p189</ref> [[The Philharmonic Dining Rooms]] on [[Hope Street, Liverpool|Hope Street]] built (c. 1898 – 1900) designed by [[Walter W. Thomas]],<ref name="Sharples 2004), p234">Sharples (2004), p234</ref> not only have a flamboyant exterior with [[Art Nouveau]] style ironwork and intricate internal decor but are also noteworthy for their ornate Victorian toilets, which have become a tourist attraction in their own right. The former Reform Club (1879) home to the [[Liberal Party (UK)|Liberal Party]] in Liverpool, by Edmund Kirkby, is a red brick palazzo,<ref name="Sharples 2004), p146"/> also in Dale Street the former [[Municipal Annexe|Conservative Club]] (1880–83), centre of the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]] in Liverpool, was designed by [[F & G Holme]] in the French Second Empire style.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p147"/> The Masonic Hall (1872) on Hope Street by Danson & Davies, in the style of an Italian palazzo.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p235">Sharples (2004), p235</ref> [[Swimming pool|Swimming baths]] of this era that survive in the city are Steble Street Baths (1874), Toxteth and Woolton Baths (1893), Quarry Street South, designed by Horton & Bridgford of Manchester. The pavilion of [[Aigburth Cricket Ground, Liverpool|Aigburth Cricket Ground]] (c.1880–82) was designed by Thomas Harnett Harrison.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p283">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p283</ref>

===Victorian industrial buildings===
Liverpool's industries largely depended on goods imports through the docks, for example, sugar for Hartley's Jam Factory. Partially surviving Victorian industrial buildings include: Heap's Rice Mill was a rice processing mill and warehouse complex, early-mid-19th century, with late-19th and early 20th century additions and alterations, using rice from [[Burma]] and south-east Asia. The former Gateacre Brewery was constructed c.1867.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p432">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p432</ref> The former [[Higsons Brewery]] on Stanhope Street dates from 1887 by James Redford, it was extended in 1902, in bold red brick and terracotta decoration in a Renaissance style, it was built for Robert Cain who also commissioned the Philharmonic Dining Rooms and The Vines Pub.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p271">Sharples (2004), p271</ref> The former Hartley's Jam Factory, built 1886 to designs by James F. Doyle for [[William Pickles Hartley]]<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p428"/> The former Ogden's Tobacco Factory (1900), in Boundary Lane, Everton was designed by Henry Hartley. The surviving former office block with its clock tower is now apartments, the rest of the factory has been demolished and replaced by housing.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p424"/>

===Victorian domestic buildings===
The suburbs of Liverpool that attracted the wealthy were Allerton, Aigburth, Mossley Hill, West Derby and Woolton. Several park estates with gates and lodges were developed, including Fulwood Park, Grassendale Park, Cressington Park, Sandown Park and Sandfield Park. The streets around the city's parks, especially Princes and Sefton, attracted the wealthy.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p250">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p250</ref> Wavertree developed housing for the lower middle class. Areas such as Kirkdale, Vauxhall, Everton and the areas of Toxteth next to the docks were where working-class housing was built.

====Victorian housing in Canning====
The area around St James Cemetery known as [[Canning, Liverpool|Canning]] developed during the Georgian period and continued to expand in the late 1830s and 1840s, although the style of the buildings is a continuation of the Georgian style. The Victorian buildings in this area are Gambier Terrace, Mornington Terrace<ref name="Sharples 2004), p242">Sharples (2004), p242</ref> and Falkner Square – conceived in 1831 and built in the 1840s. William Culshaw of [[Culshaw and Sumners]] is known to have designed no. 29 Falkner Square and may have designed the whole square. Canning Street, first developed in the 1820s, saw more construction in the 1850s with numbers 45–55 being built, in a bold Italianate style, a departure from the [[Regency architecture|Regency style]] used elsewhere in the area.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p374">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p374</ref> Gambier Terrace was extended in the 1870s in a different style.<ref name="Sharples 2004), p242"/>

====Victorian Classical, Italianate and Jacobethan houses and terraces====
St Michael's Manor (also known as Springwood Manor) (1839) and its associated lodge on Woolton Road is a classical style mansion by John Cunningham.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p391">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p391</ref> [[Thingwall Hall]] is an 18th-century building that was remodelled c.1846–47 by [[Harvey Lonsdale Elmes]].<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p438">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p438</ref> Also by Elmes are the classical Lodge on Woolton Road, the Orangery to the now demolished Allerton Tower, and the Lodge to his demolished house of Druid's Cross, Allerton.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p391"/> An Italianate stuccoed house of the 1840s is Hartfield.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p389"/> Lowlands in West Derby is an Italianate house built by Thomas Haigh, architect, for himself.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p504">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p504</ref> The Gateacre Grange, Rose Brow, Gateacre, is a large gabled [[Jacobethan]] house built in 1866 by Cornelius Sherlock for the brewer Sir [[Andrew Barclay Walker]], extended in 1883 to the designs of Sir [[Ernest George]] and [[Harold Peto]], and converted to apartments in 2005.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p433">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p433</ref> The Jacobethan style Camp Hill Lodge (1868) served as an entrance to Camp Hill, once part of the Woolton Hall estate; it was remodelled in 1885, leaving the early elements of the earlier structure to create a Jacobethan look, probably by the architect James Rhind who extended the main house at this time.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p444"/>

====Victorian Gothic houses====
There are several impressive Gothic houses around the city; the Church of England [[Clergy house|vicarages]] and Roman Catholic equivalent [[Presbytery (residence)|presbyteries]] were often Gothic to match their churches. The style was also used to design mansions for the wealthy.

The vicarage for St Margaret's Church (c.1869), Princes Road, is by [[George Edmund Street]].<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p471"/> The vicarage of St Matthew & St James (1873), Rose Lane, Mossley Hill, is almost certainly by the architects of the church [[Paley and Austin]]; the vicarage of St Agnes & St Pancras (1887) is by [[Richard Norman Shaw]]. The vicarage of St John the Baptist (1890), Tuebrook, which has some Jacobethan features, was designed by the architect of the church, [[George Frederick Bodley]].<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p478">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p478</ref>

St. Joseph's Home, Childwall, originally a residential home for Roman Catholics and now a single-family residence, is by [[Augustus Pugin]] (1845–47); it was altered in 1866 by his son [[E. W. Pugin]] who remodelled the garden front.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), pp400-401">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), pp400-401</ref> Also by E.W. Pugin is the presbytery (1856–57) of St Vincent de Paul,<ref name="Sharples 2004), p208"/> and he designed the Presbytery of St Oswald's, Old Swan.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p480">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p480</ref> The presbytery (1893) of [[St Anne's Church, Edge Hill]] is by [[Pugin & Pugin]].<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p412"/> The presbytery of St Clare's Arundel Avenue (1890) was designed by [[Leonard Stokes]].<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p449">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p449</ref> The Lodge to Crosteth Park in West Derby is probably designed by [[William Eden Nesfield]].<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p503"/>

Harthill Lodge, with its decorative [[bargeboards]], was an entrance to the demolished Hart Hill; now it leads to [[Calderstones Park]].<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p389"/> The Dell (1850), Beechwood Road South, Aigburth, is a stucco Tudor Gothic villa. For the three surviving Gothic-style houses by Alfred Waterhouse, see the section above. [[Broughton Hall, Merseyside|Broughton Hall]] (1858–59), by Walter Scott, designed for merchant Gustavus C. Schaube of [[Hamburg]], has notable interiors.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p506">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p506</ref> Holmestead, Mossley Hill was originally built c. 1845 by A.H. Holme but extensively remodelled and extended in 1869–70, probably by Culshaw & Sumners who added the tower; there is a fine Lodge to the house of c. 1845.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p443">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p443</ref> Cleveley Cottage (1865), on Allerton Road, was designed by Sir [[George Gilbert Scott]] for cotton merchant Joseph Leather.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p389"/> Quarrybank House and its Lodge (1866–67), designed by Culshaw and Sumners, was built for James Bland, a timber merchant, and is now a school.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p389"/> Greenbank Lodge (c. 1870), on Greenbank Drive, was designed by André and Hornblower. Streatlam Tower (1871), 5 Princes Road, was designed by W & G Audsley for wool merchant [[James Lord Bowes]], to house his collection of Japanese art.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p476">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p476</ref> An oddity is The Octagon (1867), Grove Street, built by Dr J.W. Hayward; vaguely Gothic, it was built to demonstrate the designer's theories on heating and ventilation.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p374"/>

====Victorian workers' housing====
Workers' housing includes Stanley Terrace and Gordon Place, in Mossley Hill just off Bridge Road, early surviving terraces of workingmen's houses from the 1840s. Orford Street in Wavertree is lined by workers' terraced housing. In Gateacre are Church Cottages (1872), 5–8 Belle Vale Road, built in a [[Tudor Revival architecture|Tudor revival style]].<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p432"/> [[William Pickles Hartley]] created the Hartley's Village for workers at his factory in nearby Long Lane, started in 1888 and designed by William Sugden & Son.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p428"/>

====Victorian housing in Sandfield Park, West Derby====
Sandfield Park, West Derby, one and a half miles south of St Mary's church was one of the most prestigious Victorian housing developments in Liverpool. Developed by T.C. Molyneux from c.1845, several of the mansions have been demolished. Sandfield Tower, now ruinous, is a stone-built Italianate mansion of c.1845, Basil Grange (1880) is a [[Jacobethan]] mansion.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p505">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p505</ref>

====Victorian housing in Sandown Park, Victoria Park, and other areas of Wavertree====
Sandown Park is a residential estate laid out in the late 1840s designed by [[Cornelius Sherlock]] in a [[picturesque]] manner. Only a few of the original early Victorian villas survive; the development was aimed at the lower-middle-class.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p499">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p499</ref> Another housing development just to the south-east of Sandown Park, not a gated community, is Victoria Park, again a lower-middle-class community started in the 1840s but halted after five houses were built, revived under a plan by William Webb that was laid out in 1862. Many of the original houses have been demolished. Also in Mill Lane are four semi-detached villas from the 1840s and 1850s.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p500">Pevsner & Pollard (2006), p500</ref> Sir [[James Picton]] designed Sandy Knowe (1847), Mill Lane, in a Jacobethan style as his home, it was converted to flats in 1975. There are several pairs of 1850s semi-detached houses in Olive Lane.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p499"/> Thornhill and Mossfield, on Childwall Road date from the 1850s and are both Italianate villas.<ref name="Pevsner & Pollard 2006), p500"/>
