======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Architecture of Melbourne
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=March 2015}}
{{Use Australian English|date=March 2015}}
[[File:Rialto architecture Melbourne.jpg|thumb|Victorian era [[Rialto building group, Melbourne|Rialto group of buildings]] contrasted with the 20th Century late modernist [[Rialto Tower|Rialto]].]]
The '''architecture of Melbourne''', [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]], [[Australia]], is characterised by a wide variety of styles. The [[Melbourne|city]] is particularly noted for its mix of [[Victorian architecture|Victorian-era architecture]] and contemporary buildings, with 79 [[skyscrapers]] (buildings {{convert|150|m}} or taller) completed or topped-out, the most of any city in Australia.{{when?|date=October 2026|reason=Use of As of template would be better, here.}}

== Overview ==
{{also|Australian residential architectural styles|Australian non-residential architectural styles}}
In the wake of the 1850s [[Victoria gold rush]], Melbourne entered a lengthy [[Melbourne land boom (1880s)|boom period]] that culminated in the [[real-estate bubble]] of the 1880s and early 1890s. This saw the construction of a large amount of ornate, High Victorian [[Boom style architecture|Boom style]] buildings in the city centre. Melbourne's skyline subsequently transformed, becoming the first [[early skyscraper]] city outside the United States; architectural historian [[Miles Lewis]] described Melbourne of the period as a "[[New World Queen Anne Revival architecture|Queen Anne]] [[Chicago]]".<ref>{{cite news |title=New Buildings in Melbourne: The Loftiest Structures in the City |url=http://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/6132483?searchTerm=new%20building%20loftiest&searchLimits=l-decade=188 |access-date=29 May 2017 |newspaper=[[The Argus (Melbourne)|The Argus]] |location=Melbourne |date=14 June 1888 |via=Trove. [[National Library of Australia]] }}</ref> Melbourne at this time was also second only to [[London]] as the largest and wealthiest city in the [[British Empire]],<ref>{{cite book |first=Henry J. |last=Cowan |title=From Wattle & Daub to Concrete & Steel: The Engineering Heritage of Australia's Buildings |pages=160<!-- Is there an exact page where this "wealthiest city" statement can be cited? --> |isbn=9-780-52284730-7 |year=1998 |publisher=Melbourne University Press }}</ref> and earned the still-quoted moniker "Marvellous Melbourne", coined by English journalist [[George Augustus Sala]] while visiting in 1885.<ref>{{cite web |title=Cultural Cringe and 'The Lost City of Melbourne' |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=16 September 2022 |access-date=16 September 2022 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/09/16/world/australia/cultural-cringe-and-the-lost-city-of-melbourne.html |url-access= }}</ref> The affluence of the period is reflected in many surviving buildings, including the [[Royal Exhibition Building]], Australia's first [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage]]-listed building. Beyond the city centre, suburbs arose and became peppered with mansions, villas and terraces with iron lace verandahs, and many suburbs developed bustling main streets, leaving a substantial architectural legacy.

Following a financial collapse in the early 1890s, Melbourne's growth returned by the early 20th century, and continued at a more modest pace in the following decades. The Federation period of 1900–1915 saw a new crop of commercial buildings in the city centre; concerns about the likely congestion caused by skyscraper development and the influence of the City Beautiful movement saw a {{convert|132|ft|m|adj=on|order=flip}} height limit introduced in 1916 (which still allowed for ornamental towers).<ref>{{Cite web |work={{!}} eMelbourne {{!}} The Encyclopedia of Melbourne Online |publisher=Department of History, School of Historical Studies, [[The University of Melbourne]] |title=Skyscrapers  |url=https://www.emelbourne.net.au/biogs/EM01383b.htm |access-date=2024-03-19 |lang=en-AU }}</ref> Suburban development of detached houses continued, in the new red brick [[Federation architecture|Federation]] style. After the restrictions of World War I, development again resumed, with American influences now evident, such as Stripped Classical office buildings, and [[California Bungalow|Californian Bungalow]] houses. After the interruption of the Great Depression, development again resumed about 1933, with central city commercial buildings now in the Art Deco style, and suburban development in a range of revivals, such as Spanish Mission or Old English. The development of low-rise flats in inner and middle suburban areas, which began just before World War I, continued in the 1920s in various revival styles, and increased markedly in the 1930s, usually in Art Deco style, a small boom which was abruptly terminated by World War II in 1940.

The post-[[World War II]] period ushered in a new boom, and the city hosted the [[1956 Summer Olympics|Summer Olympics in 1956]], and the lifting of height limits at the same time led to a boom in high-rise office building, beginning with [[Orica House|ICI House]], completed in 1958. This boom resulted in the loss of [[List of demolished buildings and structures in Melbourne|many of the city's Victorian-era buildings]], which were replaced by modernist structures. Concern at the losses led to the passage of the {{Cite Legislation AU|VIC|hist_act|hba1974|Historic Buildings Act, 1974}} and the establishment of the Historic Buildings Register, known as the [[Victorian Heritage Register]] following the passage of the {{Cite Legislation AU|VIC|hist_act|ha1995|Heritage Act, 1995}} and later the {{Cite Legislation AU|VIC|act|ha2017|Heritage Act, 2017}}, and the [[List of heritage-listed buildings in Melbourne|heritage list]] now includes many notable landmarks.

Since the 2000s, the central city and neighbouring [[Southbank, Victoria|Southbank]] and [[Melbourne Docklands]] urban renewal areas have been the subject of a residential revival which has seen a new boom in high rise construction. Some blocks of the city are now developed to very high densities, and include the tallest buildings in Australia, including the 297m (92 floors) [[Eureka Tower]], which was the tallest residential tower in the world when completed in 2006, and its spiritual successor [[Australia 108]].<ref name="TallestRes">{{cite web|title=100 Tallest Residential Buildings in the World|url=http://www.skyscrapercenter.com/List/tallest-residential-100-buildings|access-date=3 May 2012|work=Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat|archive-date=7 July 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140707141124/http://www.skyscrapercenter.com/List/tallest-residential-100-buildings|url-status=dead}}</ref> The city has also added some notable architectural landmarks including [[Southern Cross Station]] and [[Federation Square]].

Distinctively Melbourne styles include the many [[bluestone]] (basalt) constructions of the early colonial and gold rush era,<ref name="molten lava">[https://theconversation.com/from-molten-lava-to-cobbled-laneways-how-bluestone-shaped-melbournes-identity-118755 From molten lava to cobbled laneways: how bluestone shaped Melbourne's identity] from The Conversation 27 June 2019</ref> extensive use of [[polychrome brickwork]]<ref>[https://www.melbourne.vic.gov.au/sitecollectiondocuments/history-city-of-melbourne-urban-environment.pdf Thematic history: A history of the City of Melbourne's urban environment ATTACHMENT 3 AGENDA ITEM 5.1 FUTURE MELBOURNE COMMITTEE] 12 June 2012</ref> and a regional variation of the boom-style [[Filigree architecture#Victorian Filigree|Victorian Italianate Filigree]] (decorative cast iron) terrace houses featuring excessively high and ornamented parapets<ref>[https://heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/what-house-is-that/late_victorian.html Late Victorian [1875 > 1901] house styles Heritage Council of Victoria]</ref> from the [[High Victorian]] period and a residential style pioneered by [[Robin Boyd (architect)|Robin Boyd]] and [[Roy Grounds]] known as the post-war Melbourne regional style.<ref>[https://www.nationaltrust.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/HinT-November-Final-1.pdf NATIONAL TRUST OF AUSTRALIA  Heritage in Trust (ACT) November 2022 pg. 2 ISSN 2206-4958]</ref> These attributes are rare elsewhere.

==History==
{{Main|History of Melbourne}}
{{Further|Victorian gold rush}}
[[Cooks' Cottage]], built in 1755, is the former home of British explorer [[James Cook]]. The house was transplanted in 1934 from the English village of [[Great Ayton]], [[North Yorkshire]]<ref name="Cooks Log">[http://www.captaincooksociety.com/ccsu4110.htm The Captain Cook Society: Cook's Log, page 212, volume 6, number 3 (1983).]</ref> by the Australian philanthropist Sir [[Russell Grimwade]] to Melbourne,<ref name="CityMelb">{{cite web|url=https://whatson.melbourne.vic.gov.au/PlacesToGo/CooksCottage/Pages/CooksCottage.aspx|title=Cooks' Cottage|publisher=[[City of Melbourne]]|accessdate=6 August 2017|archive-date=31 January 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200131055807/https://whatson.melbourne.vic.gov.au/PlacesToGo/CooksCottage/Pages/CooksCottage.aspx|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article4746055 |title=CAPTAIN COOK'S COTTAGE. :ANOTHER CENTENARY GIFT.:Mr. Russell Grimwade's Generosity.|newspaper=[[The Argus (Melbourne)|The Argus]] |issue=((27,105)) |location=Melbourne|date=1 July 1933 |accessdate=6 September 2017 |page=21 |via=National Library of Australia}}</ref> making it the oldest extant building in Australia.<ref>{{cite news |author=Walker, Penny |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/travel/destinations/oceania/australia/victoria/melbourne/articles/australias-oldest-building/ |title=How an English cottage became Australia's oldest building |work=[[The Daily Telegraph]] |location=United Kingdom |date=10 January 2019 |access-date= }}</ref>

=== 1835–1850: Earliest buildings ===
[[File:Melbourne_1839.JPG|thumb|Illustration of [[Collins Street, Melbourne|Collins Street]] in 1839 overlooked by [[Wurundjeri]] from the hill on the approximate site of the [[Old Treasury Building, Melbourne|Old Treasury]].]]

The original inhabitants, the [[Wurundjeri]] were known to have created temporary structures called [[Mia-mia]] out of bark, saplings and timber and were observed by [[Protector of Aborigines]] [[William Thomas (Australian settler)|William Thomas]] to be comfortably housed.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.oldtreasurybuilding.org.au/yarra/first-peoples-and-the-yarra/ |title={{Title case|FIRST PEOPLES AND THE YARRA}} |work=Old Treasury Building |date= |access-date= }}</ref>

Melbourne was settled by Europeans in 1835, when rival entrepreneurs from Tasmania, [[John Batman]] and [[John Pascoe Fawkner]], sent expeditions looking for sheep pasture. Batman famously stated that “This is the place for a village”, generally believed to refer to the point on the [[Yarra River]] where freshwater was found (near today's [[Queens Bridge (Melbourne)|Queensbridge]]).<ref>{{cite web |title=The Founding of Melbourne, 1835 |work=[[Museum of Victoria]] |date= |access-date=12 December 2017 |url=https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/articles/6775 }}</ref> However [[Batman's Treaty]] was declared void by the government of the time<ref name="foundingdocs.gov.au">{{cite web |title=Governor Bourke's Proclamation 1835 (UK) |website=Documenting Democracy |url=https://www.foundingdocs.gov.au/item-did-42.html |date= |access-date=20 July 2020 |publisher=Museum of Australian Democracy}}</ref> so what was later known as the [[Port Phillip District]] was established as a [[Squatting|squatter's encampment]].{{clarify|date=October 2025|reason=[[Squatting]] or [[Squatting (Australian history)]]?}} The land to the north of the Yarra was a gentle valley between hills to the east and west, and riding ground to the north. Nevertheless, in 1837, government surveyor Robert Hoddle laid out a [[Hoddle Grid|grid of streets]], approximately {{convert|30|m|ft|0|spell=on}} wide (considerably wider than [[Sydney]] streets) between the two hills and aligned with the river.<ref name="COM2">{{cite web |url=http://www.melbourne.vic.gov.au/info.cfm?top=53 |title=City of Melbourne&nbsp;— Roads&nbsp;— Introduction |work=[[City of Melbourne]] |date= |access-date=29 September 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110220130459/http://www.melbourne.vic.gov.au/info.cfm?top=53 |archive-date=20 February 2011 |df=dmy-all}}</ref>

Early buildings were modest and typical of a [[frontier town]], and there were few landmarks of note. From early accounts{{whose?|date=October 2026}} and sketches{{whose?|date=October 2026}} there were few if any buildings taller than two storeys. Many were of timber construction and those of brick and stone. Almost all were built in the prominent colonial architectural style of the time, the [[Georgian revival]]. Most were detached or semi-detached buildings with gable or hip rooves and simple undecorated walls.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.melbourne.vic.gov.au/sitecollectiondocuments/history-city-of-melbourne-urban-environment.doc |title=A history of the City of Melbourne's urban environment |work=[[City of Melbourne]] |date= |access-date= }}</ref> Melbourne was early to expand and spread from the Hoddle grid along the Yarra and [[Maribyrnong River]] and [[Port Phillip Bay]]. Early buildings that survived later development are located in suburbs such as [[East Melbourne, Victoria|East Melbourne]], [[Fitzroy, Victoria|Fitzroy]], [[Hawthorn, Victoria|Hawthorn]], [[Williamstown, Victoria|Williamstown]], [[St Kilda, Victoria|St Kilda]] and [[Heidelberg, Victoria|Heidelberg]] among others.
 
[[File:St_James’_Old_Cathedral-King_Street_view.jpg|thumb|left|[[St James Old Cathedral|St James' Old Cathedral]] (1839-1847) (relocated 1914), the most prominent of the few remaining buildings from the colonial era.]]
A well-known surviving building from this period is the [[St James Old Cathedral|St James' Old Cathedral]] (1839–1847), which originally stood at the corner of William and Little Collins streets in what was then the centre of town but was later relocated.<ref name="VHD 767">{{Cite VHD|767|St James Old Cathedral|hr=0011|ho=478}}</ref>

Another of Melbourne's oldest buildings [[La Trobe's Cottage]] (1839) was a prefabricated home constructed in England and transported to Melbourne. Like St James', it was relocated, though several times prior to its current site in the [[Kings Domain]].<ref>{{cite news |title=La Trobe Cottage Opened |date=1964-12-03 |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=5xkTAAAAIBAJ&sjid=rZYDAAAAIBAJ&dq=la%20trobe%20cottage&pg=6718%2C499963 |work=[[The Age]] |access-date=2013-08-30 |via=Google Newspapers }}</ref>

Other English styles, including [[English Gothic]], [[Jacobean Revival]] and [[Tudor Revival]] were also evident in some early buildings. Part of [[St Francis' Church, Melbourne|St Francis' Church]] on the corner of Lonsdale and Elizabeth streets dates from 1842, the simple construction is Melbourne's oldest [[Gothic Revival architecture|Gothic Revival]] building, though its original form was later significantly augmented and altered.<ref name=sfcm>{{cite web |url=http://www.stfrancismelbourne.com/early-history/ |title=Early history |work=St Francis’ Church, Melbourne |date= |access-date= }}</ref> The Hawthorns, Hawthorn (1845),<ref>{{cite VHD|575|The Hawthorns|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> [[St Peter's Church, Eastern Hill]] (1846),<ref>{{cite VHD|368|St Peter's Eastern Hill Precinct|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Invergowie in Hawthorn (1846),<ref>{{cite VHD|574|Invergowrie|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Wattle House in St Kilda (1846),<ref>{{cite web |url=https://stkildahistory.org.au/our-collection/houses/jackson-street/item/365-wattlehouse |title=Wattle House |work=St Kilda Historical Society |date= |access-date=}}</ref> as well as [[Banyule Homestead|Banyule]] (1846)<ref name="Banyule">{{cite VHD|589|Banyule|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=2 July 2004|access-date=2020-05-19}}</ref> and St John's Anglican Church (1849)<ref>{{cite VHD|590|St Johns Anglican Church|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> in Heidelberg, Overnewton in [[Keilor, Victoria|Keilor]] (1849–1859)<ref>{{cite AV media |author= |url=http://www.slv.vic.gov.au/pictures/0/0/2/doc/pi002641.shtml |via=[[State Library of Victoria]] |format=photograph |title=Toorak House |date= |access-date= |archive-url=https://archive.today/20070929090234/http://www.slv.vic.gov.au/pictures/0/0/2/doc/pi002641.shtml |archive-date=2007-09-29 }}</ref> and Whitbyfield in [[Brunswick, Victoria|Brunswick]] ({{circa|1850}})<ref>{{cite VHD|174|Whitby House|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> are other examples of early Tudor revival.

[[File:(1)Como_in_Melbourne_Australia.jpg|thumb|right|[[Como House]] in South Yarra (built 1847 and extended in 1853), operated as a museum by the National Trust of Victoria, is the city's best preserved example of residential colonial architecture.]]
Early suburban architecture exhibited a variety of different styles. For example, Charterisville in [[Ivanhoe, Victoria|Ivanhoe]] (1840)<ref>{{cite VHD|4390|Charterisville|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> is a sandstone residence with a strong association with the artists colony at Heidelberg; Wentworth House in [[Pascoe Vale, Victoria|Pascoe Vale]] (1842–1852)<ref>{{cite VHD|919|Wentworth House|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> is one of Melbourne's earliest bluestone houses; [[Como House]] in [[South Yarra, Victoria|South Yarra]] (1847)<ref name="Coventry">{{cite journal |journal=Before/Now |volume=1 |issue=1 |doi=10.17613/d8ht-p058 |year=2019 |last1=Coventry |first1=C.J. |title=Links in the Chain: British slavery, Victoria and South Australia}}</ref> is considered one of the finest colonial era regency style homes in Victoria; [[Toorak House]] (1849) after which [[Toorak, Victoria|Toorak]] was named is a significant pre-gold rush Italianate mansion considered the finest in the colony;<ref>{{cite VHD|1166|Toorak House|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> and, Manor House in [[Broadmeadows, Victoria|Broadmeadows]] (1850) is a combination of Scottish residential style in bluestone.<ref>{{cite VHD|3094|Manor House|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref>

[[File:Duke_of_Wellington_Hotel,_Melbourne.jpeg|thumb|left|Duke of Wellington Hotel on Flinders Street. Dating to 1850 it is one of the city's oldest surviving commercial buildings.]]
[[Devonshire Arms Hotel, Fitzroy|Devonshire Arms Hotel]] in [[Fitzroy, Victoria|Fitzroy]] (1843) a modest Georgian style building is the oldest extant hotel in the city.<ref>{{cite VHD|453|Devonshire Arms Hotel|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Job Warehouse (54-62 Bourke Street) (1848–1849), a double storey building in the Georgian style is the oldest surviving row and typical of the era, though slightly modified.<ref>{{cite VHD|700|Job Warehouse|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Oddfellows Hotel (1848–1850) is another early example.<ref>{{cite VHD|154899|Former Oddfellows Hotel|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> The John Smith Residence (1848–1852) is the oldest surviving residence built in the Hoddle Grid, though the Georgian style home later had an additional storey added.<ref>{{cite VHD|793|Former John Smith House|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> A two-storey colonial regency style shop on the corner of King and Latrobe Street (1850) is recognised as the oldest known building in the Hoddle Grid with an unmodified original appearance.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.3aw.com.au/melbournes-oldest-building-is-set-to-sell-for-the-first-time-in-more-than-100-years/ |title=Melbourne's oldest building is set to sell for the first time in more than 100 years |author=Moclai, Tony Moclai |work=3AW.com.au |date=12 April 2021 |access-date= }}</ref> The [[Duke of Wellington Hotel, Melbourne|Duke of Wellington Hotel]] on Flinders Street (1850), another modest two-storey Georgian style building, is also believed to date to this era and is cited as the oldest public bar in the Hoddle Grid.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.goodfood.com.au/good-food/food-news/new-life-for-the-old-duke-20130416-2hwtd.html |title=New life for the old Duke |work=GoodFood.com.ai |date=16 April 2013 |access-date=20 July 2015}}</ref> Another building known as the Black Eagle Hotel was built in 1850 as two-storey Georgian terraces in Little Lonsdale street may have operated as a hotel from the outset.<ref>{{cite VHD|154900|Black Eagle Hotel|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> By the 1850s the city centre's early subdivisions began to fill in and consisted of fragmented rows of attached buildings, most a couple of storeys high serviced by rear laneways, a plan which helped dictate the form of many buildings in the subsequent decades.<ref name="Bate 1994 p. ">{{cite book |last=Bate |first=Weston |title=Essential But Unplanned |publisher=[[State Library of Victoria]] |publication-place=Melbourne |date=1994 |isbn=0-7306-3598-8 |page=10}}</ref>

Named the capital of the new [[Colony of Victoria]] on 1 July 1851 Melbourne even prior to the discovery of gold it was a successful settlement. Having grown mostly due to rich Victorian pastures it had operated as a busy port since 1841 and had a population of approximately 23,000. Despite being the youngest of the colonial capitals, it had overtaken all but Sydney.<ref>{{cite web |author= |url=https://www.egold.net.au/biogs/EG00013b.htm#:~:text=The%20population%20of%20Melbourne%20grew,city%20of%20'magnificent%20intentions'. |title=The Golden Metropolis: Overview |work=egold.net.au |date= |access-date= }}</ref>

=== 1851–1880: Gold Rush era ===
Following this early settlement period, just after the [[Colony of Victoria]] was separated from the [[Colony of New South Wales]] in 1851, [[gold]] was discovered, and thousands of people flocked to the city from the United Kingdom, as well as Europe and the United States, to seek their fortune on the Victorian [[Gold mining|goldfields]]. Within a year Melbourne had overtaken Sydney as Australia's most populous settlement. As a result of the [[Gold Rush]], Melbourne's population grew from 4,000 in 1837 to 300,000 in 1854. Approximately £100 million worth of gold was discovered in the Victorian fields in the 1850s.{{sfn|Chapman|Stillman|2014|pp=7}} The gold rush was followed by a growth in pastoral wealth, the development of local industries, railways, suburbs, shops, and ports. The immense wealth generated during this period helped fund the construction of many large public buildings during this period including the [[State Library of Victoria|State Library]], [[Parliament House, Melbourne|Parliament House]], the [[Melbourne Town Hall|Town Hall]], [[Old Treasury Building, Melbourne|Old Treasury]],  [[Supreme Court of Victoria (building)|Law courts]],  [[Melbourne GPO|General Post Office]] and [[Royal Exhibition Building]]. They also include two of celebrated Victorian architect [[William Wardell]]'s works: [[St Patrick's Cathedral, Melbourne|St Patrick's Cathedral]] and [[Government House, Melbourne|Government House]].

[[File:Pentridge_Prison_Front_Gate_2020.jpg|thumb|[[HM Prison Pentridge]] built in 1851 to address the explosion of crime from the early gold rush, is one of the most distinctive and intact of Melbourne's large bluestone buildings.]]
Locally quarried [[bluestone#Victoria|bluestone]] (basalt) was a distinctive construction material used from Melbourne's earliest days however it became increasingly popular during the gold rush for institutional buildings due to its heavy [[Rustication (architecture)|rusticated]] effect and its stern, foreboding appearance. As such it was used extensively in buildings for enforcement, the military and warehousing most commonly in combination with Renaissance Italianate or ecclesiastical and educational institution buildings where it was often combined with a gothic revival style. [[HM Prison Pentridge]] (1851) is particularly notable as one of the largest gold rush era bluestone buildings as well as for its distinctive castellated Tudor appearance incorporating medieval style watch towers, arrow slits and [[panopticon]]s.<ref>{{cite VHD|306|Pentridge Prison|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Other primarily bluestone buildings include the remaining wings of the [[Old Melbourne Gaol]] (1852–1854), [[Williamstown Timeball Tower]] (1852), Mac's Hotel (1853),<ref>{{cite VHD|759|Mac's Hotel|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> [[St Peter's Church, Eastern Hill]] transepts (1846–1876), [[Victoria Barracks, Melbourne|Victoria Barracks]] (1856–1872), [[Melbourne Grammar School|Melbourne Church Of England Grammar]] (1856),<ref>{{cite VHD|65621|Melbourne Grammar School|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> [[St Andrew's Church, Brighton]] (1857),<ref>{{cite VHD|160|St Andrew's Church Brighton|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Wesleyan Methodist Church St Kilda (1857–1858)<ref>{{cite VHD|1110|Former Wesleyan Methodist Church St Kilda|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> [[Wesley Church, Melbourne|Wesley Church]] complex (1858–1859)<ref>{{cite VHD|773|Wesley Church|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> All Saints St Kilda (1858–1882),<ref>{{cite VHD|4543|All Saints St Kilda East|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> St Patrick's Cathedral (1858–1939),<ref>{{cite VHD|355|St Patrick's Cathedral|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Seabrook House (1858),<ref>{{cite VHD|65262|Seabrook Building|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> St Mary's Church of England in North Melbourne (1858–1860),<ref>{{cite VHD|886|St Mary's Church of England|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> St Mary's Dandenong Road (1859–1871),<ref>{{cite VHD|1107|St Mary's|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> St John's Toorak (1860–1873)<ref>{{cite VHD|1170|St John's Toorak|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Goldsborough Mort & Co Ltd warehouse (1861–1862),<ref>{{cite VHD|704|Goldsborough Mort & Co Ltd|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> [[Victorian College for the Deaf]] (1866),<ref>{{cite VHD|4438|Victorian College for the Deaf|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Victorian College for the Blind (1868),<ref>{{cite VHD|11939|Victorian College for the Blind|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> St Ignatius Richmond (1867–1870),<ref>{{cite VHD|2085|St Ignatius|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> [[Cathedral College, East Melbourne]] (1869–1870),<ref>{{cite VHD|408|Cathedral College|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> St Augustine's Church and School (1869–1929),<ref>{{cite VHD|707|St Augustine's Catholic Church and former school|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> and Williamstown Primary School (1878).<ref>{{cite VHD|1218|Williamstown Primary School|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Bluestone continued to be used in Melbourne with prominent later examples including the facade of the Carlton & United Brewery (1858–1883).<ref>{{cite VHD|208|Carlton & United Brewery|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Residential examples while rare, are notable, particularly [[Bishopscourt, East Melbourne|Bishopscourt]] (1852); Royal Terrace [[Fitzroy, Victoria|Fitzroy]] (1853–1858);<ref>{{cite VHD|103636|Royal Terrace|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> 115–117 Grey Street, East Melbourne (1854);<ref>{{cite VHD|369|115-117 Grey Street, East Melbourne|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> 35 Hanover Street, Fitzroy (1855);<ref>{{cite VHD|469|35 Hanover Street, Fitzroy|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Gowrie, [[Glenroy, Victoria|Glenroy]];<ref>{{cite VHD|554|Gowrie|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> [[D'Estaville]] [[Kew, Victoria|Kew]] (1859);<ref>{{cite VHD|616|D'Estaville|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Joseph Reed's design of 157 Hotham Street East Melbourne (1861);<ref>{{cite VHD|375|157 Hotham Street|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Crouch and Wilson's design for 12 Jolimont Terrace East Melbourne (1868);<ref>{{cite VHD|604|12 Jolimont Terrace East Melbourne|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> G A Badger's design for 'The Opera House' at 138 Powlett Street East Melbourne;<ref>{{cite VHD|397|The Opera House|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> and Eynesbury Homestead at [[Eynesbury, Victoria|Eynesbury]] (1872–75).<ref>{{cite VHD||Eynesbury|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> The material however proved difficult to shape to finer classical details so in many other city buildings it was instead used as foundation material due to its robust and porous property.<ref name="molten lava" />

[[File:Royal terrace carlton.jpg|thumb|left|The bluestone Royal Terrace (1853–1854) was the first large example of newly popularised terraced housing.]]
[[Terrace house]] developments also grew in importance, especially to house the new middle class and attached housing, including [[shop house]]s, became the dominant form. Early modes were inspired by the colonial Georgian, regency and Renaissance Revival. The most notable early example is Royal Terrace (1853–1854), a large triple storey bluestone row on Nicholson Street in the early residential suburb of Fitzroy, designed to face the reserve that would become [[Carlton Gardens]].<ref>{{cite VHD|481|Royal Terrace|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Royal Terrace differs from Melbourne's later terraces in its ornamental restraint and long horizontal string courses give the impression of a single continuous row with [[party wall]]s expressed only at ground level. The demand for more distinguished homes led to the popularity of stucco rendering to simulate stone details. Examples of this new form are evident in Glass Terrace in Fitzroy (1854–1856),<ref>{{cite VHD|457|Glass Terrace|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> along with Clarendon Terrace (1857),<ref>{{cite VHD|360|Clarendon Terrace|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Nepean Terrace (1864),<ref>{{cite VHD|363|Nepean Terrace|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> and Cyprus Terrace (1867) in East Melbourne.<ref>{{cite VHD|378|Cyprus Terrace|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> The terrace begin to evolve into the distinctive Melbourne style consisting of high Italianate parapets to hide the roofline and rich cast iron ornament. Early predecessors include Cobden Terrace  in Fitzroy (1869–1875),<ref>{{cite VHD|463|Cobden Terrace|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Rochester Terrace in [[Albert Park, Victoria|Albert Park]] (1869–1879) part of the English style square design of [[St Vincent Place]], and Tasma Terrace in East Melbourne (1878) by [[Charles Webb (architect)|Charles Webb]] considered one of the finest three storey terraces in Australia.<ref>[https://www.nationaltrust.org.au/places/tasma-terrace/ Tasma Terrace - National Trust of Victoria]</ref>

[[File:State Library of Victoria - right side.jpg|thumb|right|Joseph Reed's 1854 competition winning entry for the [[State Library of Victoria]]  contributed to the strong academic classical theme in the city's early public buildings.]]
[[Neoclassical architecture|Academic classicism]] was favoured for large institutions and its execution required more versatile materials with the popularity of stone and stucco features producing more elaborate but stately designs. Prolific Melbourne architect [[Joseph Reed (architect)|Joseph Reed]]'s contributions include the [[State Library of Victoria|State Library]] (1854-1870),<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/812 State Library of Victoria - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> [[Collins Street Baptist Church]] (1854),<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/725 Baptist Church - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> facade of the [[Bank of New South Wales building, Melbourne|Bank of New South Wales]] (1856–1857),<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/65761 Former Bank of New South Wales - National Trust of Victoria]</ref> [[Royal Society of Victoria]] building (1859)<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/823 Royal Society of Victoria - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> and [[Melbourne Town Hall]] (1869).<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/813 Melbourne Town Hall - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> Other significant examples include: [[Parliament House, Melbourne|Parliament House]] (1855–),<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/802 Parliament House - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> [[Victorian Trades Hall]] (1859)<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/224 Trades Hall - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> and [[Supreme Court of Victoria (building)|Supreme Court Library]] (1874–1884).<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/825 Library of the Supreme Court - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> Giant order columns or pilasters along with other classical details including pediments, porticos, vaulted ceilings and entry stairs were common elements of their design. Design of large public buildings was ambitious due to the speculative nature of the gold rush. Many of the larger designs featured prominent domes, though their construction relied on future funds which would not be forthcoming. The Supreme Court Library dome, modeled on the [[Four Courts]] in Dublin is one of few original designs which was completed. Joseph Reed's original design for the State Library called for a Museum and Gallery topped by a massive neoclassical dome. Only sections of both buildings were completed and the current building features a different design completed in later decades. [[Peter Kerr (architect)|Peter Kerr]]'s 78 metre high dome design for the Parliament houses were also never constructed.<ref>[https://www.parliament.vic.gov.au/about/history-and-heritage/building/vestibule/ The dome that isn't there] from Parliament Victoria</ref> These features were often still illustrated in depictions of the city from the period due to the confidence that they would eventually be completed. Despite its many missing features Parliament remains one of the most impressive neoclassical structures in the city.

[[File:Melbourne_University_grand_building.jpg|thumb|left|The 1854 Old Quad at the [[University of Melbourne]], designed by English architect Francis Maloney White helped establish Melbourne's Gothic Revival beyond religious buildings.]]
[[File:St_Patrick's_Cathedral_(Gothic_Revival_Style).jpg|thumb|[[William Wardell]]'s design for the massive bluestone Gothic Revival [[St Patrick's Cathedral, Melbourne|St Patrick's Cathedral]], which would become Australia's tallest and largest, began to take shape in 1858]]
Melbourne's Gothic Revival was strong, particularly in early church design, but late to gain traction for other buildings, though the seeds were sown for its extraordinary later popularity. Among the first secular buildings to incorporate the style was the Old Law School Building and Old Quadrangle at the University of Melbourne (1854–1857),<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/912 Old Law School Building and Old Quadrangle at the University of Melbourne - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> which set an academic theme for the entire campus that is still evident despite the later demolitions of the National Museum (1863) and Wilson Hall (1878). The Charles Webb designed Church Of England Grammar School (1856) helped establish gothic revival's popularity with the private schools and combined bluestone with impressive effect. Architects [[Crouch and Wilson]] would further promote this style in their designs for the College for the Deaf (1866) and College for the Blind (1868). Crouch and Wilson would go on to be one of the winners of a competition in 1873 for designs for primary schools (built in 1874  as Primary School No.1467 at South Yarra).<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/569 Primary School No.1467 - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> Architect [[Henry R. Bastow]], head of the building department of the Department of Education used this and the other winning designs, all in Gothic Revival schools, to create a distinctive style, and in some cases simply repeated designs. An example of Bastow's prominent early work is Primary School No.1479 in St Kilda (1874).<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/1095 Primary School No.1479 - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> Bastow established a preference for polychrome brickwork which would contribute to its growing popularity but also designed in other materials including bluestone at Williamstown Primary School (1878). Bishop's Building (1877–1878) by Frederick Wyatt part of the first residential college at Melbourne University's, [[Trinity College, Melbourne|Trinity College]], is another significant gothic revival design in polychrome brick.<ref>[https://trinity-college.shorthandstories.com/150th-anniversary-illustration/index.html Bishop's Building, Trinity College]</ref> Faraday Street State School Number 112 (1876–1877) is one of Reed and Barnes notable early works in education but [[Ormond College]] (1879–1881) is considered their largest and finest. Despite some pre-gold rush examples, gothic was still rare as a residential style. As the popularity of Italianate styles dominated, Tudor revival had fallen out of favour. Notable exceptions include Glenfern at St Kilda East (1857),<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/57/download-report Glenfern - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> a row of houses at 39–41 Nicholson Street, Abbotsford (1858–1869)<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/5 39-41 Nicholson Street, Abbotsford - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> and the Joseph Reed designed 157 Hotham Street East Melbourne (1861). Gothic revival purists sought a major religious landmark for the early city, however despite the numerous spires which dotted the early skyline including those of the bluestone Wesley, but with St Patrick's Cathedral remaining incomplete, would not find a true icon until the construction of the Joseph Reed designed [[Scots' Church, Melbourne|Scots Church]] (1871–1874). Built upon Collins Street hill it was considered to be one of the finest church designs in Australia. Leonard Terry's landmark two storey building in Hawthorn for the ES&A Bank (1873) is an early example of gothic applied to secular buildings and also an early commercial use of Hawthorn brick<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/571 ES&A Bank Hawthorn - Victorian Heritage Register],</ref> a mode of building which would become highly popular with architects over the subsequent decades.

[[File:OTBfrontCOLOUR2.jpg|thumb|right|Old Treasury, designed by John James Clark in 1857 to hold the enormous amount of gold coming from regional Victoria, is considered to be Australia's finest Renaissance Revival building.]]
[[John James Clark]]'s Old Treasury (1858–62) is considered Australia's finest Renaissance Revival building. It features bluestone vaults intended for storing gold mined from the central Victorian goldfields. The Old Treasury, along with his [[Melbourne Mint]] (1872), Government House (1874), Victorian Titles Office (1874–1877)<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/2975 Victorian Titles Office - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> and [[Immigration Museum, Melbourne|Customs House]] (1876) inspired a brief trend of [[Palazzo style architecture]] for public buildings which was also used at 2 Treasury Place (1876).<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/801/download-report Treasury Reserve Precinct Victorian Heritage Council]</ref> While [[Italianate architecture]] styles were outnumbered by academic classical for public buildings they would become extremely fashionable for commercial, institutional and residential architecture across the city. Institutional buildings included Victoria Barracks (1856–1872), Leonard Terry's designs for the [[Melbourne Club]] (1859) the first stage 2 storey Melbourne GPO (1861 – prior to extensions), the [[Royal Arcade, Melbourne|Royal Arcade]] (1870), [[Kew Asylum]] (1871),<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/622 |title=VHD<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=8 April 2016 |archive-date=17 April 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160417092635/http://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/622 |url-status=live }}</ref> Peter Kerr designed Customs House in Williamstown (1873–1875),<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/1228 Former Customs House - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> Leonard Terry's former Campbell Residence (1877)<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/2833 Former Campbell Residence - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> and [[Lloyd Tayler]]'s design for the [[Australian Club (Melbourne)|Australian Club]] (1879).<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/828 The Australian Club - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> Among the commercial buildings were the Former Commercial Bank of Australia (1867),<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/717 Former Commercial Bank of Australia - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> London and Chartered Bank (1870–1871),<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/698 Former London and Chartered Bank - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> [[Lloyd Tayler]]'s Portland House (1872)<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/713 Portland House - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> and the Bank of Australasia (1876).<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/734 Former Bank of Australasia - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> Numerous public hotels across the city employed the style, including [[Young and Jacksons]] (1853–1861),<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/810 Young and Jacksons - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> Former Eastern Hill Hotel (1854–1856),<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/489 Former Eastern Hill Hotel - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> and the [[Esplanade Hotel, Melbourne|Esplanade Hotel]] St Kilda (1878).<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/66696/download-report Esplanade Hotel - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> Italianate became the favoured residential style and despite later widespread demolition the city retains a plethora of palatial examples. Viewing towers, in particular became a signal of wealth, popularised by the earlier landmarks Bishopscourt and Toorak House, others followed notably Rostella (1867 demolished 1970),<ref>[https://www.cbdnews.com.au/where-chloe-once-hung/ Where Chloe Once Hung] By David Thompson for CBD News 18 May 2018</ref> [[Raheen, Kew|Raheen]] (1870–1884), Government House (1871–1876), [[Eildon Mansion|Eildon]] (1872) and [[Werribee Park]] (1874–1877).

[[File:Num_Pon_Soon_Melbourne.jpg|thumb|upright|left|Num Pon Soon built in [[Chinatown, Melbourne|Chinatown]] in 1860 exemplifies the gold rush influence of the Chinese community]]
Melbourne's [[Chinatown, Melbourne|Chinatown]] and nearby [[Little Lon district]] emerged during the gold rush and illustrated a significant contrast in style to the stately institutional buildings with their chaotic development among Melbourne's laneways. Portable prefabricated iron buildings were common in early Melbourne's gold rush slums and some remain especially in Fitzroy, [[Collingwood, Victoria|Collingwood]] and [[South Melbourne, Victoria|Emerald Hill (South Melbourne)]].<ref>[https://www.nationaltrust.org.au/places/portable-iron-houses/ Portable Iron Houses - National Trust of Victoria]</ref> Melbourne's large Chinese community originated through the gold rush. Num Pon Soon (1860–1861) in Chinatown, by Melbourne architects [[Knight & Kerr]], is a rare Australian example of Victorian architecture incorporating Chinese motifs.<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/780 Num Pon Soon - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> Another important building was the Chinese Mission for Victoria society building (1872) by architects Crouch and Wilson was constructed at 196 Little Bourke Street, its visually striking polychrome brick patterning making it a landmark of Chinatown.<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/65208/download-report Chinese Mission Church - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> Further out of the city, the See Yup Society Temple (1856–1866) by architect George Wharton was another landmark to Melbourne's large Chinese community which had strong oriental influences in its design.<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/1063/download-report See Yup Society Temple - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref>

[[Image: St Michael's Church Collins Street Melbourne doorway.jpg|thumb|upright|right|Details of [[St Michael's Uniting Church, Melbourne|St Michaels Church]], Collins Street, 1866, the first example of elaborate polychrome brickwork in Australia, a design feature which proved immensely popular in Victorian era Melbourne]]
Joseph Reed's design for [[St Michael's Uniting Church, Melbourne|Collins Street Independent Church]] (1866) (now St Michael's) is notable not only as the earliest examples of elaborate polychrome brickwork in Australia (a style that became highly popular by the 1880s) but also for its unusual floorplan and tower.<ref name="St Michael's">{{Cite web |title=St Michael's Uniting Church |url=https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/721 |access-date=2020-06-08 |website=Heritage Council of Victoria}}</ref> It was one of the few major church buildings not designed in the popular gothic revival of the time, and its elevated position on the Collins Street hill made it a major landmark of the early city until the construction of nearby Scots Church (1871–1874). Described as [[First Romanesque|Lombardic Romanesque]] in style,<ref name="St Michael's" /> it features a tall square [[bell tower]] marking an important street corner, and round [[Romanesque architecture|Romanesque arches]] around doors and windows and the open cloisters in each side. The interior was designed in the form of a theatre auditorium, in accordance with the principles of the Congregationalist Church, as a place where all members of the congregation could both hear and see the preacher. It features a sloping floor with tiered seating, and a steep gallery behind a ring of high aches on slender cast iron columns, ensuring good sight lines.<ref name="St Michael's" /> The polychromatic style would influence Reed & Barnes' design for [[St Jude's Church, Carlton]] later that year but applied in the gothic style with Florentine arches.<ref>[https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/places/226/download-report St Jude's Anglican Church - Victorian Heritage Register]</ref> Many later religious buildings across Melbourne would be influenced by these designs in the following decades.

[[File:Royal exhibition building tulips straight.jpg|thumb|left|The [[Royal Exhibition Building]] (1879), a UNESCO [[World Heritage Site]].<ref>[http://www.theage.com.au/articles/2002/10/20/1034561388451.html "Global status for our greatest building"], 21 October 2002. URL accessed on 5 September 2006.</ref>]] 
The Royal Exhibition Building, with its UNESCO World Heritage status is Melbourne's most important building internationally. Built to host the [[Melbourne International Exhibition (1880)|Melbourne International Exhibition]] in 1880–81 it went on to play an enormous part in the cultural identity of the city and resisted many attempts at its demolition. Designed by the [[architect]] [[Joseph Reed (architect)|Joseph Reed]] it is an eclectic representative of the Byzantine, Romanesque, Lombardic and Italian Renaissance styles.<ref name="UNESCO World Heritage">{{cite web
 | url =https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1131 
 | title = Royal Exhibition Building and Carlton Gardens 
 | date = 2004
 | website = United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization 
 | access-date = 14 November 2018 }}</ref> The dome was modeled on the [[Florence Cathedral]], while the main pavilions were influenced by the style of [[Rundbogenstil]] and several buildings from Normandy, Caen and Paris.<ref>{{cite book |last=Willis |first=Elizabeth |title=The Royal Exhibition Building, Melbourne. A Guide |publisher=Museum Victoria |year=2004 |location=Melbourne, Victoria |pages=2 |isbn=0-9577471-4-4}}</ref> The building has the scale of the French [[Beaux Arts architecture|Beaux Arts]], with a [[cruciform]] plan in the shape of a Latin cross, with long nave-like wings symmetrically placed east–west about the central dome, and a shorter wing to the north.<ref name="REB">{{cite web
 | title = Royal Exhibition building and Carlton Gardens 
 | url = https://whc.unesco.org/uploads/nominations/1131bis.pdf
 | access-date = 14 November 2018
 }}</ref> The Great Hall is still in beautiful condition, crowned by an octagonal drum and dome rising 68 metres, and 18.3 metres across. The dome was formed using cast iron and timber frame and has a double shell. At the crossing, windows in the drum of the dome bring in sunlight for a bright open space.

=== 1880–1893: "Marvellous Melbourne" Land Boom era ===
{{also|Melbourne land boom (1880s)}}
The 1880s saw the price of land start to boom, and London banks were eager to extend loans to men of vision who capitalised on this by speculation, and grand, elaborate offices, hotel and department stores in the city, and endless suburban subdivisions. This was the growth that so astonished visiting journalist [[George Augustus Sala]] in 1885, that he dubbed the city "Marvellous Melbourne".{{sfn|Davison|1978}}<ref>{{cite web|title=A History of the City of Melbourne's Urban Environment|url=https://www.melbourne.vic.gov.au/SiteCollectionDocuments/history-city-of-melbourne-urban-environment.pdf|date=12 June 2012|access-date=12 December 2017|work=[[Government of Victoria]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Marvellous Melbourne {{!}} State Library Victoria|url=https://www.slv.vic.gov.au/search-discover/galleries/marvellous-melbourne|access-date=2020-06-26|website=www.slv.vic.gov.au}}</ref>

[[File:Spires of St Paul's.jpg|thumb|upright|St Paul's Cathedral designed by [[William Butterfield]] emerged as a major landmark of the city from 1880 even without its later redesigned spires]]
Most of the city's religious buildings were erected during the gold rush era and many were already quite elaborate edifices even before the rising price of land. While many churches had progressed from classical to gothic forms, High Victorian architects now had a wider range of styles from which to draw upon. However the original St Paul's church, occupying a prominent entrance to the city at the intersection of Flinders and Swanston Streets had been planned to be replaced with a large English gothic style cathedral which would become [[St Paul's Cathedral, Melbourne|St Paul's Anglican Cathedral]] (1880–1891).<ref>{{cite VHD|815|St Paul's Cathedral|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Designed by English architect [[William Butterfield]], it occupied a prominent site in the heart of the city on Flinders Street at the entrance of Princes Bridge making it a highly visible landmark even without its later completed spires. The interior features rich colours and strident colour contrasts, characteristic of Butterfield's work, compared to the exterior, with contrasting stripes of the very dark-coloured local bluestone. An unusual design for the period is the [[Sacred Heart Church, St Kilda|Sacred Heart Church]] (1884) in St Kilda designed by Reed, Henderson and Smart in a Baroque Italianate style.<ref>[{{cite VHD|3465|Sacred Heart Church|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> The Former Church of Christ Abbotsford (1888–1889) designed by Jonathan Rankine was modelled on [[Temple Church]] in London and presents a relatively modest Renaissance Revival frontage to the street.<ref>{{cite VHD|8|Former Church of Christ|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> The Former Union Church Elsternwick (1888–1890) is another unusual boom style church in the Scottish Baronial style.<ref>{{cite VHD|428|Former Union Church|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Another large religious building from the land boom period which didn't have its spires completed is [[St Mary Star of the Sea, West Melbourne|St Mary Star of the Sea]] in West Melbourne (1891–1900).<ref>{{cite VHD|1276|St Mary Star of the Sea|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> The Auburn Uniting Church Complex (1890) in Hawthorn is a stunning polychromatic brick building in the Lombardic Romanesque popularised by the Uniting Church in the city.<ref>{{cite VHD|3354|Auburn Uniting Church Complex|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref>

[[File:Parkville_-_University_of_Melbourne_(Ormond_College).jpg|thumb|left|upright|[[Ormond College]] by Joseph Reed completed 1881 was a major education landmark of the land boom era]]
Construction of primary schools continued across the city in a wider variety of styles, designed by the Public Works Department now headed by Bastow. Some of this notable work included St Kilda Park Primary (1882),<ref>{{cite VHD|1109|St Kilda Park Primary|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> North Melbourne (1882),<ref>{{cite VHD|888|Melbourne College of Printing and Graphic Arts|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Carlton Gardens Primary School (1884),<ref>{{cite VHD|242|Carlton Gardens Primary School|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Malvern Primary School (1884),<ref>{{cite VHD|683|Malvern Primary School|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> City Road, South Melbourne (1884–1885),<ref>{{cite VHD|1036|J H Boyd Girls High School|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Middle Park Primary (1887),<ref>{{cite VHD|842|Middle Park Primary|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Yarra Primary School in Richmond (1888),<ref>{{cite VHD|977|Yarra Primary School|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> and Auburn Primary School (1890).<ref>{{cite VHD|31|Auburn Primary School|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Significant education buildings by other architects included the Old Pathology Building University of Melbourne (1885),<ref>{{cite VHD|914|Old Pathology Building|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Francis Ormond Building (1885–1887),<ref>{{cite VHD|3011|Francis Ormond Building|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Former Melbourne Veterinary College (1886),<ref>{{cite VHD|4585|Former Melbourne Veterinary College|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Armadale Primary School (1886),<ref>{{cite VHD|29|Armadale Primary School|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Baldwin Spencer Building Melbourne University (1888),<ref>{{cite VHD|913|Baldwin Spencer Building|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Former Melbourne Teachers College (1888),<ref>{{cite VHD|918|Former Melbourne Teacher's College|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> the University Old Physics Conference Room and Gallery (1888–1889),<ref>{{cite VHD|915|Old Physics Conference Room and Gallery|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Lowther Hall Anglican Grammar (1890),<ref>{{cite VHD|439|Lowther Hall Anglican Grammar|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Working Men's College – RMIT Building No. 4 (1890),<ref>{{cite VHD|64486|RMIT Building No.4|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> and the [[Genazzano FCJ College]] (1890–1891).<ref>{{cite VHD|5415|Genazzano FCJ College|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> The former [[Priory Ladies' School Boarding House]] (1890) in Alma Road, St Kilda, demonstrated a rare shift away from the gothic idiom to the American Romanesque, following a visit by Edward George Kilburn to the United States and Europe.<ref>{{cite VHD|1091|Former Priory Ladies School|hr=0726|ho=20|hi=|date=22 February 1989|access-date=2026-10-04}}</ref>

[[File:Windsor_hotel_in_2010.jpg|thumb|right|The grand luxury 1884 [[Hotel Windsor, Melbourne|Windsor Hotel]] on Spring Street is the most significant surviving example from Melbourne's popular temperance movement]]
Many palatial hotels emerged during the period including a strong temperance movement and many coffee palaces constructed. These almost always featured heavy ornament and prominent towers, often in the Second Empire or Italianate styles. The largest of these, the Federal Coffee Palace, was demolished in 1973. Melbourne's other Victorian luxury hotel, The Menzies, which peaked in 1896, was also demolished in 1969. The best known survivor is the [[Hotel Windsor (Melbourne)|Hotel Windsor]] (1884) designed by Charles Webb and extended in 1888 as the Grand Coffee Palace.<ref>{{cite VHD|804|Windsor Hotel|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Other suburban examples include the Biltmore (former Albert Park Coffee Palace) (1887–1889),<ref>{{cite VHD|11|Biltmore|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Hotel Victoria (1888) in Albert Park designed by Richard Speight,<ref>{{cite VHD|9|Hotel Victoria|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> [[Canterbury Mansions]] (1889)<ref>{{cite VHD|197|Canterbury Mansions|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> and the George Hotel St Kilda (1880–1890).<ref>{{cite VHD|1108|George Hotel St Kilda|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref>

[[File:Melbourne (AU), Princess Theatre -- 2019 -- 1558.jpg|thumb|left|upright|[[Princess Theatre (Melbourne)|Princess Theatre]], the William Pitt 1886 designed theatre is the most significant of Melbourne's once thriving Victorian era scene]]
Theatres became fashionable entertainment for the wealthy. While many of the city's earlier grand theatres are now demolished including the [[Theatre Royal, Melbourne|Royal]] and [[Bijou Theatre, Melbourne|Bijou]], some of the grandest from the boom era remain. William Pitt was a prominent theatre architect of the time. He designed one of Melbourne's best known theatre buildings, [[Princess Theatre (Melbourne)|Princess Theatre]] (1886) in the Second Empire French style. The theatre is full of ornamental flourishes including domed mansard roof detailed cast iron work and gold-plated statuary.<ref>[{{cite VHD|805|Princess Theatre|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Other prominent theatres to survive include Nahum Barnet's Her Majesty's Theatre (1886) in a similar style though now missing its mansard roof.<ref>{{cite VHD|746|Her Majesty's Theatre|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref>

[[File:Melbourne Stock Exchange Collins Street.jpg|thumb|upright|Melbourne Stock Exchange (1887), one of a number of tall elaborate commercial gothic revival buildings surviving near the intersection of Collins and Queen Street]]
The land boom changed Melbourne's skyline, becoming an [[early skyscraper]] city and the first in the southern hemisphere to be home to several "lofty piles" as they were often called during the era. With the wealth brought by the gold rush, Melbourne rapidly gained status as a major financial and commercial capital and many large banks and building societies erected impressive buildings. Most of the tall office buildings constructed during the 1880s boom have been [[Melbourne's Lost Victorian Landmarks|lost]] (including the prominent Federal Coffee Palace and [[APA Building, Melbourne|APA Building]]). Many other fine examples still stand today, most notably the collection of commercial gothic buildings on the corner of Collins and Queen Streets including the Australia & New Zealand Bank building known as the Gothic Bank (1883) due to its distinctive [[Venetian Gothic]] design by William Wardell<ref>{{cite VHD|733|ANZ Bank|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> as well its William Pitt designed neighbouring Old Stock Exchange (1887) and Safe Deposit building (1889).<ref>{{cite VHD|791|Safe Deposit Building|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Other surviving tall towers include [[Lombard Building]] (1889),<ref>{{cite VHD|789|Lombard Building|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> and Twentyman & Askew's 'high-rise' Stalbridge Chambers (1890).{{sfn|Goad|2012|pp=543}}  Smaller office buildings were also often elaborate. Elleker and Kilburn's Melbourne City Building (1888) is an unusual early Queen Anne design which forms a pair with the towered Colonial Bank Hotel (1888) across Balcombe Place.<ref>{{cite VHD|745|Melbourne City Building|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> William Pitt's vertical gothic styled Olderfleet Buildings (1888) the first commercial gothic office building listed with the National Trust,<ref>{{cite VHD|737|Olderfleet|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> New Zealand Chambers (1888),<ref>{{cite VHD|739|New Zealand Chambers|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Record Chambers (1887),<ref>{{cite VHD|738|Record Chambers|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Charles D'Ebro's Queen Anne styled Winfield Building (1891)<ref>{{cite VHD|742|Winfield Building|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> and William Pitt's highly detailed gothic revival Rialto Building (1888)<ref>{{cite VHD|743|Rialto Building|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> with their paired towers belong to what is now known as the [[Rialto building group, Melbourne|Rialto Group of Buildings]] and feature some of the most elaborate commercial gothic revival in Australia. The Nahum Barnet designed Austral Buildings (1890) continues the red brick Queen Anne theme.<ref>{{cite VHD|720|Austral Buildings|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Renaissance Revival of the gold rush period continued to be popular even with the larger banks and societies from the Smith and Johnson designed Melbourne Savage Club building (1884–1885)<ref>{{cite VHD|697|Savage Club|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> to the six storey Former Money Order Post Office (1890).<ref>{{cite VHD|781|Former Money Order Post Office|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> However academic classicism was often seen as too restrained for the boom style and architects sometimes gave them a more baroque flavour, as in Sum Kum Lee at Chinatown (1887–1888) by George De Lacy Evans<ref>{{cite VHD|779|Sum Kum Lee|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> and William Salway's design for the Collins Street Mercantile Bank (1888).<ref>{{cite VHD|732|Mercantile Bank|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Suburban offices, while rare, also took similar forms. Notable examples include the ES&A Bank in Hawthorn East (1885) with its unusual step gable gothic form combined with a slate roof.<ref>{{cite VHD|188|ES&A Bank |hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Another unusual commercial building is ANZ bank in North Fitzroy (1889),<ref>{{cite VHD|484|ANZ Bank|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> a miniature version of the now demolished Australian Building. The Kensington Property Exchange (1891–1892) is another heavily ornamented piece of suburban land boom Victoriana with its corner tower.<ref>{{cite VHD|4431|Kensington Property Exchange|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> The vaulted Banking Chamber (1891–1893) of the former Commercial Bank of Australia Limited by [[Lloyd Tayler]] and Alfred Dunn is one of the most spectacular Renaissance Revival interiors in the city.<ref>{{cite VHD|731|Former Commercial Bank of Australia Banking Chamber and Entrance|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Another impressive gothic office building is the Wright and Beaver designed Former National Mutual Life Association also known as A. C. Goode House (1891–1893) directly opposite Wardell's gothic bank.<ref>{{cite VHD|735|Former National Mutual Life Association|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref>

[[File:Leicester Place Flinders Lane.jpg|thumb|In the 1880s, multi-storey warehouses proliferated in [[Flinders Lane]], giving it a canyon-like appearance. Pictured: Leicester House, built in 1886.]]
Along with the advancements in rail, Melbourne during the land boom underwent a period of major industrialisation. Flinders Street had benefited from construction of the old docks and turning basin and Flinders Lane in particular was a growing centre for the [[rag trade]]. Fitzroy, Collingwood, Richmond, South Melbourne and [[Port Melbourne]] emerged as major industrial areas during the period. Among the architectural legacies of the industrial era are many red brick buildings constructed as warehouses. The Cordial Factory in Fitzroy (1882) is a polychrome brick set of warehouses a style which became popular with industrial architects.<ref>{{cite VHD|4555|Cordial Factory|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Leicester House (1886) four storey warehouses on Flinders Lane by T J Crouch incorporates florentine gothic arches in its upper storey and deep cornices into a familiar palazzo design.<ref>{{cite VHD|64932|Leicester House (NTAV list: Property No. B   )|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> The distinctive warehouses in Niagara Lane (1887) designed by George De Lacy Evans with their repetitive gables and supply cranes is one of Melbourne's laneway landmarks.<ref>{{cite VHD|788|Warehouses|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}ter]</ref> and five-storey James Bond Store (1888) is a landmark of the former South Melbourne industrial area.<ref>{{cite VHD|1064|James Bond Store|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> The former is noted for its facade featuring classical details while the latter is noted for its simplicity. [[Coop's Shot Tower]] (1889) preserved within the Melbourne Central shopping complex which unlike many more plain buildings incorporates a castellated design and a polychrome factory building at its base.<ref>{{cite VHD|768|Coop's Shot Tower|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Queen's Warehouse positioned near Victoria Dock (1890) is a landmark red brick warehouse at Docklands.<ref>{{cite VHD|3723|Queen's Warehouse|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Another industrial landmark of the era is the Former Richmond Power Station (1891) by Charles D'Ebro with its polychromatic brick and Italianate tower.<ref>{{cite VHD|982|Richmond Power Station|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref>

[[File:Tram and Omnibus Building, Bourke Street, Melbourne Australia (4589651289).jpg|thumb|upright|Tram and Omnibus Building, Bourke Street. Completed in 1891]]
[[File:67 Spencer Street Melbourne.jpg|thumb|left|Grand Hotel, 67 Spencer Street, the former head offices of the Victorian Railways, completed in 1893]]
Melbourne's tram and railway systems boomed during the period, resulting in many significant station and terminus buildings mostly constructed in red brick of the Queen Anne style. These included the former cable tram houses in Fitzroy (1886-1887),<ref>{{cite VHD|456|Former Cable Tram House Fitzroy|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Brunswick (1887),<ref>{{cite VHD|2155|Former Tram Substation|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}]</ref> Carlton (1889),<ref>{{cite VHD|245|Former Cable Tram Engine House|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}]</ref> North Melbourne (1890)<ref>{{cite VHD|4638|Former Cable Tramway Engine House|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> and Northcote.<ref>{{cite VHD|2148|Former Northcote Cable Tramways site|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> The former Melbourne Tramway and Omnibus Building (1891) in the gothic style by Twentyman and Askew is a prominent headquarters for administration of the growing transport system.<ref>{{cite VHD|708|Former Melbourne Cable Tramway and Omnibus Company Building|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Much of the railways had been built during earlier periods and many railway lines. Many stations have since been closed or converted to light rail. Nevertheless the land boom saw several impressive new buildings planned. Plans were drawn up for major railway hubs at [[Spencer Street Station]] and Flinders Street with an 1882 Spencer Street plan clearly modelled on [[St Pancras railway station]], however in 1883 more restrained neoclassical designs were chosen for both stations but not built, including yet another for Spencer Street in 1892 featuring a massive Italianate complex similar to the current [[Central railway station, Sydney]]. Instead funds were diverted to upgrade the suburban network which was experiencing a patronage boom. Prior to the land boom, some examples of High Victorian railway architecture include [[Hawthorn railway station, Melbourne|Hawthorn Railway Station]] (1882–1889),<ref>{{cite VHD|576|Hawthorn Railway Station|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> and [[Middle Brighton railway station]] (1882–1887),<ref>{{cite VHD|841|Middle Brighton Railway Station|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> [[South Melbourne light rail station]] (1883) signals the start of the boom's impact on railway building design with its striking Queen Anne design featuring tall chimneys, gable and polychromatic brick.<ref>{{cite VHD|1044|South Melbourne Railway Station|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> [[Jewell railway station]] (1884)<ref>{{cite VHD|2135|Former Coburg Railway Line|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> one of a template of similar station building designs which proved popular, [[Windsor railway station, Melbourne|Windsor Railway Station]] (1885–1886) a Queen Anne design in polychromatic brick which features Egyptian columns,<ref>{{cite VHD|1235|Windsor Railway Station|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> [[North Melbourne railway station]] (1886) which incorporates [[Filigree architecture#Victorian Filigree|Victorian Filigree]] into the design.<ref>{{cite VHD|889|North Melbourne Railway Complex|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> [[Newport Railway Workshops]] (1888) is known as one of the best preserved of its kind in the world with their gabled bays and Italianate clock tower.<ref>{{cite VHD|11566|Newport Railway Workshops|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Perhaps one of the most interesting of the land boom stations is the former Albert Park (now [[Albert Park light rail station]]) which features a highly detailed composition of bluestone, polychrome brick, cast iron corinthian columns and vaulted interiors of stained wood.<ref>{{cite VHD|12|Former Albert Park Railway Station|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> [[Brighton Beach railway station|Brighton Beach Railway Station]] (1889) the main building is another notable polychromatic brick construction featuring high archways and chimneys.<ref>{{cite VHD|163|Brighton Beach Railway Station|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Another interesting building is one of the few remaining old buildings in Melbourne Docklands, the [[No 2 Goods Shed]] (1889–1890) with its prominent second empire clock tower, and expansive covered railway platform featuring cast iron supports is a testament to the huge industrial impact of the Victorian railways.<ref>{{cite VHD|754|No. 2 Goods Shed|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> One of the largest buildings to come out of this era is the former [[67 Spencer Street|Former Victorian Railways Headquarters]] on Spencer Street (1893).<ref>{{cite VHD|800|Former Victorian Railways Headquarters|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> The expansive Renaissance Revival style building, later modified with an additional storey and distinctive domes, is substantially intact both inside and out.

[[File:Melbourne_Block_Arcade_2014.jpg|thumb|right|[[Block Arcade, Melbourne|Block Arcade]] on Collins Street became the most fashionable of the city's many shopping precincts from 1891]]
The retail sector was also growing exceptionally strongly and major department stores began to emerge centred along the ever expanding tramway network. Arcades and markets proliferated the city, while many have been demolished the most significant survivor is [[Block Arcade, Melbourne|The Block]] (1891–1893) with its magnificent arcade and baroque facades on Collins and Elizabeth Streets.<ref>{{cite VHD|730|Block Arcade|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> It became the most fashionable place to shop in the city.  The neoclassical inspired facade of Georges Department Store (1884) on Collins Street by [[John Harry Grainger]] is an earlier example of early department store architecture.<ref>{{cite VHD|64625|Former Georges Store (NTAV list: :Property No. B )|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Significant commercial buildings were also being built throughout the inner suburbs including large multi-storey shop buildings in several of the major shopping strips. Numerous boom style buildings, mostly double storey sprang up in the major retail strips such as Chapel Street South Yarra, Prahran, Windsor, Brunswick Street Fitzroy, Smith Street Collingwood and Clarendon Street South Melbourne among others. George de Lacy Evans design for Lygon Buildings (1888) are notable three storey palazzo shopfronts.<ref>{{cite VHD|225|Lygon Buildings|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Those designed by [[John Beswicke]] feature striking polychromatic brickwork including Beswicke Buildings in Fitzroy (1888)<ref>{{cite VHD|452|Shops|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> and 132–142 and 144–148 Victoria Street Auburn (1891). 313–315 Drummond Street Carlton is a particularly striking examples including kangaroo-gryphon gargoyles and polychromatic Florentine gothic arches.<ref>{{cite VHD|213|Shops and Residences|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> One of the largest and most spectacular landmarks, the Melbourne Fish Market (1889) was demolished in 1959 to make way for a carpark and road flyover. Retail arcades and markets were also popular in the suburbs. One of the largest markets from the era is the former Metropolitan Meat Market in North Melbourne (1880).<ref>{{cite VHD|882|Former Metropolitan Meat Market|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Prahran Arcade on Chapel Street (1890) though missing its original tall mansard roof makes a striking French Second Empire statement to the street.<ref>{{cite VHD|3556|Prahran Arcade|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref> Charles D'Ebro's [[Prahran Market]] (1891) is a prominent statement of Anglo-Dutch style with its large arched entry.<ref>{{cite VHD|66511|Prahran Market (NTAV list: Property No. B )|hr=|ho=|hi=|date=|access-date=}}</ref>
