{{Short description|Postmodern classical architectural movement}}
{{About|the contemporary movement|the historical style|Neoclassical architecture}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=June 2026}}
[[File:05 Ciudad Cayala Front View.jpg|thumb|Ciudad Cayalá in [[Guatemala City|Guatemala City, Guatemala]], 2011, by [[Léon Krier]]]]

'''New Classical architecture''', also known as '''New Classicism''' or '''Contemporary Classical architecture''',<ref>{{Cite book |title=Putting tradition into practice: heritage, place and design: proceedings of 5th INTBAU International Annual Event |date=2018 |editor=Giuseppe Amoruso |isbn=978-3-319-57937-5 |location=Cham |publisher=Springer |oclc=1000578629}}</ref> is a [[Contemporary architecture|contemporary]] movement that builds upon the principles of [[Classical architecture]]. It is sometimes considered the modern continuation of [[neoclassical architecture]],<ref>{{Cite web|last=Machalinski|first=Anne|title=Classical Contemporary Meets the Future|url=https://www.mansionglobal.com/articles/classical-contemporary-meets-the-future-212890|access-date=January 12, 2021|website=www.mansionglobal.com|date=March 16, 2020 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|author=Curl, James Stevens |title=A dictionary of architecture and landscape architecture|date=2006|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-280630-7|edition=2nd|location=Oxford [England]|oclc=64585874}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last1=Curl|first1=James Stevens|author-link1=James Stevens Curl|chapter=New Classicism|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4Lu6BwAAQBAJ|title=The Oxford Dictionary of Architecture|last2=Wilson|first2=Susan|date=2015|pages=520–522|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-967498-5|language=en}}</ref> even though other styles might be cited as well, such as [[Gothic architecture|Gothic]], [[Baroque architecture|Baroque]], [[Renaissance architecture|Renaissance]] or even non-[[Western culture|Western]] styles<ref>{{Cite web|date=April 19, 2015|title=6 Classical Buildings That Are Younger Than You Think|url=https://www.archdaily.com/621256/6-classical-buildings-that-are-younger-than-you-think|access-date=February 18, 2021|website=ArchDaily|language=en-US}}</ref> – often referenced and recreated from a [[Postmodern architecture|postmodern]] perspective rather than as strict [[Revivalism (architecture)|revivals]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Jencks|first=Charles|author-link=Charles Jencks|title=Post Modernism: The New Classicism in Art and Architecture|date=1987|pages=7–8|url=https://archive.org/details/postmodernismnew0000jenc/|location=New York|publisher=Rizzoli|isbn=0-85670-867-4|language=en}}</ref>

The design and construction of buildings in evolving classical styles continued throughout the 20th and 21st centuries, even as [[Modern architecture|modernist]] and other non-classical theories broke with the classical language of architecture. The New Classical movement is also tied to a resurgence in new [[traditional architecture]], which emphasizes craftsmanship rooted in local building traditions and materials.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.architecturaldigest.com/story/new-classical-architecture |title=Inside Architecture's New Classicism Boom |last=Quigley |first=Kathleen |website=[[Architectural Digest]] |date=August 7, 2018 |language=en |access-date=February 16, 2019}}</ref>

== Development ==
[[File:Schermerhorn.jpg|thumb|[[Schermerhorn Symphony Center]] in [[Nashville, Tennessee]], opened in 2006]]
During the 1950s and 1960s, a small group of architects in Europe continued designing classical buildings contrary to the prevailing fashion for [[Modern architecture|Modernist architecture]]. British architects [[Donald McMorran]], who designed several noteworthy neoclassical buildings such as the [[University of Nottingham Halls of Residence|Cripps Hall at the University of Nottingham]] and described the Modernist movement as "a dictatorship of taste",<ref>{{cite web |title=Central Criminal Court Extension, London – The Twentieth Century Society |url=https://c20society.org.uk/building-of-the-month/central-criminal-court-extension-london |access-date=December 9, 2021 |website=c20society.org.uk}}</ref><ref name="curl">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jIWr0IO9dYIC&dq=Donald+McMorran+architect&pg=PA466 |title=Oxford Dictionary of Architecture and Landscape Architecture |date=2006 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-860678-9 |editor1-last=Curl |editor1-first=James Stevens |pages=466–7 |language=en |access-date=December 3, 2021}}</ref> and [[Raymond Erith]], who mentored New Classical architect [[Quinlan Terry]] – Erith's pupil, employee, partner, and ultimately successor – were notable for their neoclassical works, including numerous civic buildings and housing estates. In mainland Europe, [[François Spoerry]] contributed to the [[European Urban Renaissance]] with his classical designs and by the late 1970s, architects like [[Léon Krier|Leon Krier]] and Maurice Culot began challenging modernist planning through publications and counter-projects,<ref>Leon Krier and Maurice Culot, "Counterprojets: Prefaces," (Brussels: Archives d'Architecture Moderne, 1980).</ref>  a movement further bolstered by the support of [[Charles III|King Charles III]] (then Prince of Wales) and initiatives such as [[INTBAU]] or [[The King's Foundation|The Prince's Foundation for Building Community]].<ref>Charles, Prince of Wales, "A Vision of Britain: A Personal View of Architecture," (New York: Doubleday, 1989)</ref> and, later, [[Create Streets]].

[[File:Darden School main UVa.jpg|thumb|[[Darden Graduate School of Business Administration]] at the [[University of Virginia]], 1992, by [[Robert A.M. Stern Architects]]]]

During the same period, [[postmodern architecture]] emerged as a critique to modernist architectural aesthetics.<ref name="McAlester">{{cite book |last=McAlester |first=Virginia Savage |title=A Field Guide to American Houses |publisher=Alfred A. Knopf |year=2013 |isbn=978-1-4000-4359-0 |pages=664–665, 668–669}}</ref> Influential architects inside this movement, such as [[Charles Moore (architect)|Charles Moore]], [[Robert Venturi]],<ref>Robert Venturi, "Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture," (New York: Museum of Modern Art, 1966).</ref> and [[Michael Graves]] used classical elements as ironic motifs to criticize modernism's sterility. A broad spectrum of more than two dozen architects, theorists, and historians also presented alternatives to modernism<ref>Andreas Papadakis and Harriet Watson, eds., "New Classicism: Omnibus Volume," (London: Academy Editions, 1990).</ref> and among them were several serious New Classical architects who viewed classicism as a legitimate mode of architectural expression, some of whom would later become [[Driehaus Architecture Prize|Driehaus Prize]] Laureates, including figures like [[Thomas H. Beeby|Thomas Beeby]] and [[Robert A. M. Stern|Robert A.M. Stern]], who practiced both postmodern and classical styles. Some postmodernist firms, such as Stern and Albert, Righter, & Tittman, outright transitioned from postmodern design to new interpretations of traditional architecture.<ref name="McAlester" /> 

On the education front, Thomas Gordon Smith, a Rome Prize laureate from the [[American Academy in Rome]], published ''Classical Architecture: Rule and Invention'' in 1988 and was appointed to chair the [[Notre Dame School of Architecture|University of Notre Dame's Department of Architecture]] a year later, structuring the curriculum around classical and traditional building practices.<ref>{{cite web |title=Many Canons, Many Conversions – |url=http://blogs.nd.edu/classicalarch/2012/09/28/many-canons-many-conversions/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029184453/http://blogs.nd.edu/classicalarch/2012/09/28/many-canons-many-conversions/ |archive-date=October 29, 2013 |access-date=May 3, 2018 |website=blogs.nd.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Gunts |first=Edward |date=July 1, 2021 |title=Notre Dame’s Thomas Gordon Smith, who led a revival in classical architecture, dies at 73 |url=https://www.archpaper.com/2021/07/thomas-gordon-smith-dies-at-73/ |access-date=December 26, 2024 |website=The Architect's Newspaper |language=en-US}}</ref> Today, programs that teach New Classical Architecture are offered at the [[University of Miami]], [[Judson University]], [[Andrews University]] and the Center for Advanced Research in Traditional Architecture in Traditional Architecture at the [[University of Colorado Denver]].<ref>{{cite web |title=College of Architecture and Planning at CU Denver |url=http://www.ucdenver.edu/academics/colleges/ArchitecturePlanning/Documents/Christine%20Franck%20appointment.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029191200/http://www.ucdenver.edu/academics/colleges/ArchitecturePlanning/Documents/Christine%20Franck%20appointment.pdf |archive-date=October 29, 2013 |access-date=October 26, 2013}}</ref>

The New Classical movement continues to develop at the professional and popular level, gaining momentum after the 1963 demolition of [[McKim, Mead & White]]'s [[New York Penn Station|Pennsylvania Railroad Station]] in New York City, which led to the formation of [[Classical America]]. Led by [[Henry Hope Reed Jr.|Henry Hope Reed, Jr.]],<ref>{{cite web |title=How Henry Hope Reed Saved Architecture |url=http://www.nysun.com/on-the-town/how-henry-hope-reed-saved-architecture/17877/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171020164252/http://www.nysun.com/on-the-town/how-henry-hope-reed-saved-architecture/17877 |archive-date=October 20, 2017 |access-date=May 3, 2018 |website=The New York Sun}}</ref> which advocated for the appreciation of classical architecture by teaching architects the classical orders and hosting various events and conferences.<ref>{{cite web |title=Books – Institute of Classical Architecture & Art |url=http://www.classicist.org/publications-and-bookshop/classical-america-series-in-art-and-architecture/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170620084212/http://www.classicist.org/publications-and-bookshop/classical-america-series-in-art-and-architecture/ |archive-date=June 20, 2017 |access-date=May 3, 2018 |website=www.classicist.org}}</ref> In 2002, the Institute of Classical Architecture merged with Classical America to form [[The Institute of Classical Architecture and Art]], which supports regional chapters in the United States that host awards programs,<ref>{{cite web |title=Articles – Institute of Classical Architecture & Art |url=http://blog.classicist.org/?cat=49 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101114024717/http://blog.classicist.org/?cat=49 |archive-date=November 14, 2010 |access-date=May 3, 2018 |website=blog.classicist.org}}</ref> publishes the peer-reviewed journal ''The Classicist'',<ref>{{cite web |title=Books – Institute of Classical Architecture & Art |url=http://www.classicist.org/publications-and-bookshop/the-classicist/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171010011101/http://www.classicist.org/publications-and-bookshop/the-classicist/ |archive-date=October 10, 2017 |access-date=May 3, 2018 |website=www.classicist.org}}</ref> and offers educational programs for professionals and the public.<ref>{{cite web |title=Calendar |url=http://www.classicist.org/programs/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171013011308/http://www.classicist.org/programs/ |archive-date=October 13, 2017 |access-date=May 3, 2018 |website=www.classicist.org}}</ref> The international expansion of the movement was catalyzed by the creation of the [[INTBAU|International Network for Traditional Building, Architecture & Urbanism]] in 2001,<ref>{{Cite news |author=Guardian Staff |date=February 11, 2002 |title=Hooked on classics: in praise of traditional architecture |url=https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2002/feb/11/artsfeatures |access-date=February 27, 2020 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> a global organization under the patronage of King Charles III,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Alexander |first=Michael |date=October 16, 2018 |title=United Kingdom: New crown coin celebrates the 70th birthday of HRH Charles, Prince of Wales |url=https://news.coinupdate.com/united-kingdom-new-crown-coin-celebrates-the-70th-birthday-of-hrh-charles-prince-of-wales/ |website=Coin Update}}</ref> focused on supporting traditional architecture and preserving local character.<ref>{{Cite web |title=About Us {{!}} INTBAU |url=https://www.intbau.org/info/about-us/ |access-date=February 27, 2020 |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2003, philanthropist [[Richard Driehaus|Richard H. Driehaus]] established the [[Driehaus Architecture Prize]], awarded by the [[Notre Dame School of Architecture|University of Notre Dame School of Architecture]], to honor architects whose work embodies classical and traditional principles in architecture and urbanism, seen as the alternative to the modernist [[Pritzker Architecture Prize|Pritzker Prize]], but with double the cash prize.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Thai Architect Wins Driehaus Prize – |url=https://www.world-architects.com/en/architecture-news/headlines/thai-architect-wins-driehaus-prize |access-date=December 26, 2024 |website=World-Architects |language=en}}</ref> It is awarded alongside the [[Henry Hope Reed Award|Reed Award]] which recognizes individuals outside architecture who support traditional city design through writing, planning, or promotion.<ref>{{cite web |title=Driehaus Prize Nomination Process |url=http://architecture.nd.edu/about/driehaus-prize/nomination-process/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130329102201/http://architecture.nd.edu/about/driehaus-prize/nomination-process/ |archive-date=March 29, 2013 |access-date=February 11, 2013 |publisher=University of Notre Dame School of Architecture}}</ref> Other notable classical architecture awards include the American [[Palladio Award]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Palladio Awards |url=http://www.palladioawards.com/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140406230208/http://palladioawards.com/ |archive-date=April 6, 2014 |access-date=April 10, 2014 |publisher=Active Interest Media}}</ref> the European Prize Philippe Rotthier,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Home |url=http://www.rotthierprize.be/index.php/en/ |access-date=January 5, 2022 |website=www.rotthierprize.be}}</ref> the Iberian [[Rafael Manzano Prize]],<ref>{{Cite web |date=February 28, 2018 |title=Premio Rafael Manzano de Nueva Arquitectura Tradicional |url=https://www.premiorafaelmanzano.com/en/ |access-date=February 11, 2020 |language=en-US |archive-date=October 26, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211026021858/https://www.premiorafaelmanzano.com/en/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>  the Edmund N. Bacon Prize,<ref>{{cite web |title=Edmund N. Bacon Prize |url=http://philadelphiacfa.org/lecture-bacon.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140413172007/http://philadelphiacfa.org/lecture-bacon.php |archive-date=April 13, 2014 |access-date=April 10, 2014 |publisher=Philadelphia Center for Architecture}}</ref> and the Rieger Graham Prize<ref>{{cite web |title=The Rieger Graham Prize |url=http://www.classicist.org/awards-and-prizes/rieger-graham-prize/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140413141627/http://www.classicist.org/awards-and-prizes/rieger-graham-prize/ |archive-date=April 13, 2014 |access-date=April 10, 2014 |publisher=Institute of Classical Architecture & Art in New York}}</ref> of [[The Institute of Classical Architecture and Art]] for architecture graduates.

Since 2014, movements such as the [[Architectural Uprising]], founded in Sweden, have advocated for traditional designs in new developments.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |date=August 1, 2023 |title=A Nordic Revolt Against 'Ugly' Modern Architecture |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2023-08-01/a-scandinavian-uprising-against-modern-architecture |access-date=December 25, 2023 |work=Bloomberg.com |language=en}}</ref> Originally a Facebook group, it has expanded to other Nordic countries and the rest of the world,<ref>{{Cite web |title=About (English) – Arkitekturupproret |url=https://www.arkitekturupproret.se/om-au/about-english/ |access-date=December 25, 2023 |language=sv-SE}}</ref> achieving moderate success in promoting traditional architecture.<ref name=":0" /> The movement's main goal is to "make architecture available to everyone"<ref name=":0" /> through social media and annual awards recognizing the best and worst new buildings in Sweden. 

Since the early 2020s, other groups such as Traditional Architecture Group, part of the [[Royal Institute of British Architects]] and 'The Nordic Symposium on Beauty in Architecture have gained prominence. In 2021, efforts to reintroduce New Classical architecture into urban planning were furthered in the U.S. by architect [[Nir Buras]],<ref>{{Cite news |last=Flanagan |first=Neil |date=October 14, 2009 |title=McMillan Two envisions a classical Anacostia |url=https://ggwash.org/view/3158/mcmillan-two-envisions-a-classical-anacostia |access-date=January 9, 2024 |work=Greater Greater Washington |language=en}}</ref> who founded the Classic Planning Institute (CPI). Based in Washington, D.C., the CPI focuses on research, practice, and education to incorporate New Classical principles into contemporary urban planning. The CPI also hosts the Traditional Architecture Gathering (TAG),<ref>{{Cite web |last=Brussat |first=David |date=March 2, 2021 |title=TAG 4: Classical gears up |url=https://architecturehereandthere.com/2021/03/02/tag-4-classical-gears-up/ |access-date=January 9, 2024 |website=Architecture Here and There |language=en}}</ref> an international conference that attracts hundred of architects and enthusiasts to discuss New Classical Architecture worldwide. As of 2025, ''Architectural Place'', the first openly pro-classical architecture magazine started operating.

== Philosophy ==
[[File:Selwyn3.jpg|thumb|Ann's Court, [[Selwyn College, Cambridge]], by [[Porphyrios Associates]]]]
[[File:Hillsdale Chapel Interior.jpg|thumb|Hillsdale Chapel, [[Hillsdale College]], by [[Duncan G. Stroik]]]]
{{See also|Sustainable architecture}}
New Classical professionals tend to work under the assumption that there is no such thing as purely original creation, and that innovation unavoidably occurs in an environment laden with suggestions, influences, a precedent of problems solved and, perhaps more importantly, mistakes to be avoided.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Callender |first=Jassen |date=July 28, 2017 |title=Architecture History and Theory in Reverse |doi=10.4324/9781315661315|isbn=978-1-315-66131-5 }}</ref>

Many New Classical architects believe in the importance of [[sustainability]], and aim to create long-lasting, well-crafted buildings of great quality, adapted to the context and with an efficient use of [[natural building|natural resources]].<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Sagharchi|first1=Alireza|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-9ZIAQAAIAAJ&q=classicism|title=New Palladians: Modernity and Sustainability for 21st Century Architecture|last2=Steil|first2=Lucien|date=2010|publisher=Artmedia|isbn=978-1-902889-12-2|language=en}}</ref>

While most universities worldwide teach modernist design principles, some institutions teach (solely, mainly, or partly) the principles of traditional and classical architecture and urban planning. Some of these are:<ref>[http://www.intbau.org/archive/academic.htm INTBAU] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150728131429/http://www.intbau.org/archive/academic.htm |date=July 28, 2015 }} – A guide to academic institutions/universities teaching New Urbanism and traditional/classical design. Retrieved March 10, 2015.</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Revivalism (architecture)
======================================================================

{{Short description|Architectural styles that echo the style of a previous architectural era}}
{{main category|Revival architectural styles}}
[[File:Clock Tower - Palace of Westminster, London - May 2007.jpg|thumb|One of the most famous [[Gothic Revival architecture|Gothic Revival]] structures, [[Elizabeth Tower]] (Big Ben) sits at the [[Palace of Westminster]] in London.]]

Architectural '''revivalism''' is the use of elements that echo the style of a [[Architectural style|previous architectural era]] that have or had fallen into disuse or abeyance between their heyday and period of revival. Revivalism, in a narrower sense, refers to the period of and movement within Western architectural history during which a succession of antecedent and reminiscent styles were taken to by architects, roughly from the mid-18th century, and which was itself succeeded by [[Modern architecture|Modernism]] around the late 19th and early 20th centuries.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://arthistoryteachingresources.org/lessons/european-and-american-architecture-1750-1900 | title=European and American Architecture (1750–1900) &#124; Art History Teaching Resources }}</ref> Notable revival styles include [[Neoclassical architecture]] (a revival of [[Classical architecture]]), and [[Gothic Revival architecture|Gothic Revival]] (a revival of [[Gothic architecture]]). Revivalism is related to [[Historicism (art)|historicism]].

Western architecture of the 19th century, including [[Victorian architecture]], is an example of Revivalism.

==History==

===Mid-18th–early 20th centuries===
[[File:Uspenski Cathedral Helsinki 2012.jpg|thumb|The [[Russian Revival architecture|Russian Revival]]-representing [[Uspenski Cathedral]] from 1868 in [[Katajanokka]], [[Helsinki, Finland]]]]
The idea that architecture might represent the glory of kingdoms can be traced to the dawn of civilisation, but the notion that architecture can bear the stamp of national character is a modern idea, that appeared in the historical and philosophical writing of the 18th century and was given political currency in the wake of the [[French Revolution]]. As the map of Europe was repeatedly changing, architecture was used to grant the aura of a glorious past to even the most recent of nations. In addition to the credo of universal Classicism, two new, and often contradictory, attitudes on historical styles existed in the early 19th century. Pluralism promoted the simultaneous use of the expanded range of style, while Revivalism held that a single historical model was appropriate for modern architecture. Associations between styles and building types appeared, for example: [[Egyptian Revival architecture|Egyptian]] for prisons, [[Gothic Revival architecture|Gothic]] for churches, or [[Renaissance Revival architecture|Renaissance Revival]] for banks and exchanges.{{citation-needed|date=May 2022}} These choices were the result of other associations: the [[pharaoh]]s with death and [[eternity]], the [[Middle Ages]] with Christianity, or the [[House of Medici|Medici family]] with the rise of banking and modern commerce.

Whether their choice was [[Neoclassical architecture|Classical]], medieval, or Renaissance, all Revivalists shared the strategy of advocating a particular style based on national history, one of the great enterprises of historians from the mid-18th to early 19th centuries. Only one historic period  was claimed to be the only one capable of providing models grounded in national traditions, institutions, or values. Issues of style became matters of state.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Bergdoll|first1=Barry|title=European Architecture 1750–1890|date=2000|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|isbn=978-0-19-284222-0|page=139, 140, 141|url=|language=en}}</ref> 

The most well-known Revivalist style is the [[Gothic Revival architecture|Gothic Revival]] one, that appeared in the mid-18th century in the houses of a number of wealthy antiquarians in England, a notable example being the [[Strawberry Hill House]]. German [[Romanticism|Romantic]] writers and architects were the first to promote Gothic as a powerful expression of national character, and in turn use it as a symbol of national identity in territories still divided. [[Johann Gottfried Herder]] posed the question 'Why should we always imitate foreigners, as if we were Greeks or Romans?'.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Bergdoll|first1=Barry|title=European Architecture 1750–1890|date=2000|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|isbn=978-0-19-284222-0|page=139, 140, 141, 142, 145|url=|language=en}}</ref>

===Mid-20th century–present===
Modern-day revival styles are frequently placed under the heading of [[New Classical architecture]].

==Styles==

===Mixed===
[[File:Leipzig Palais Roßbach.jpg|thumb|Typical historicist house: [[Gründerzeit]] building by [[Arwed Roßbach]] in Leipzig, Germany (built in 1892)]]

* [[Eclecticism in architecture|Eclecticism]] – Conscious mixing of disparate historical styles
* [[Historicism (art)|Historicism]] or Historism – mixed revivals that can include several older styles, combined with new elements
* [[Indo-Saracenic architecture]] (revival of [[Architecture of India|Indian architecture]] and [[Islamic architecture]])
* [[Mediterranean Revival architecture]] (revival of [[Renaissance architecture|Italian Renaissance architecture]] and [[Spanish Baroque architecture]])
* [[New Classical Architecture]] – an umbrella term for modern-day architecture following pre-modernist principles
* [[Russian Revival architecture]] – generic term for a number of different movements within Russian architecture that arose in second quarter of the 19th century.
* [[Traditionalist School (architecture)|Traditionalist School]] – revival of different regional traditional styles
* [[Vernacular architecture]] – umbrella term for regional architecture traditions continuing through the eras, also used and cited in revival architecture

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Architecture of Ghana
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}} <!-- "none" is usually preferred when the title is sufficiently descriptive by itself. See [[WP:SDNONE]] -->
{{Use British English|date=December 2024}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=December 2024}}
{{multiple image
|perrow = 1
|total_width = 240
|align = right
|image_style= border:none;
|image1 = A drone footage of Accra central, Ghana.jpg
|caption1 = [[Tower block|High-rise buildings]] in contemporary [[Accra]], the capital
|image2 = Pyramid House Ghaba.jpg
|caption2 = Pyramid House }}

The '''architecture of Ghana''' is influenced by a variety of historical, cultural, and environmental factors. Its architectural heritage consists of [[Vernacular architecture|traditional architectural]] styles, [[monumentalism|monumental]] and symbolic architecture, and historic buildings and neighbourhoods. Architecture found across the country can be classified into indigenous architecture of the various ethnic groups, architecture of the colonial era, the [[Tropical Modernism|tropical modernist]] style of the [[History of Ghana#Independence|independence era]], and architecture in contemporary times.

Traditional Ghanaian architecture is marked by the use of local materials such as [[mud]], wood, grass and [[thatching|thatch]], and is characterised by its adaptability to the local climate and environment. Indigenous structures, such as the [[Asante Traditional Buildings|Asante]] and Mole-Dagbani buildings were constructed using techniques like [[wattle and daub]], with decorative [[relief|bas-relief]] patterns, and features cultural symbols such as [[Adinkra symbols|Adinkra motifs]]. With the [[History of Ghana#Early European contact and the slave trade|arrival of the Europeans]] in the 15th century, architectural styles such as [[Gothic Revival architecture|Gothic Revival]] were introduced, influencing the design of churches, and [[Neoclassical architecture|Neoclassical elements]] became prominent in government buildings and residential structures. This fusion of European influences with traditional indigenous construction methods brought about a change in the country's architectural landscape.

From the late 1950s, the architectural scene of Ghana saw the rise of Tropical Modernism, which combined [[Modern architecture|modernist principles]] with the need for buildings adapted to the country's [[tropical climate]]. Characteristics of this style include the emphasis on natural ventilation, shading, and the use of locally sourced materials, with a focus on [[Sustainability in construction|sustainability]] and [[Functionalism (architecture)|functionality]].

In contemporary Ghana, architecture has evolved to incorporate a blend of traditional and modern elements. Locally available materials, energy-efficient designs, and construction methods adapted to the tropical climate influence building practices.

==Indigenous architecture==
{{multiple image
|perrow = 1
|total_width = 240
|align = right
|image_style= border:none;
|image1 = Mud room in northern Ghana.jpg
|caption1 = A room made of mud and roofed with dry grass.
|image2 = Traditional building.jpg
|caption2 = Locally designed buildings
|image 3 = A village house, Ghana.jpg
|caption3 = A village house in the [[Western region (Ghana)|Western Region]] of Ghana
}}

Traditional buildings in the northern, middle and southern zones vary in materials and techniques used for their construction. Common vernacular building materials that have been used over centuries include timber, [[bamboo]], [[laterite]], grass, thatch, and clay.{{sfn|Agyekum|Kissi|Danku|2020|pp=3–4}} In Pre-colonial Ghana, traditional buildings were primarily made from materials such as mud, wood and thatch, chosen for their availability, affordability, and climate adaptability.<ref name=":02">{{cite web |title=Architecture in Ghana: A Blend of Tradition and Modernity |url=https://greenviewsresidential.com/architecture-in-ghana/#:~:text=Ghana's%20architectural%20roots%20can%20be,sustainability%20of%20early%20Ghanaian%20communities |date=16 October 2024 |website=Green Views |access-date=9 December 2024 }}</ref> These materials were used to build durable structures, particularly in rural areas. The wattle and daub construction method was widely used by groups like the [[Asante Empire|Ashanti Empire]] and dates back to about 6000 years ago.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Shaffer |first=Gary D. |title=An Archaeomagnetic Study of a Wattle and Daub Building Collapse |journal=Journal of Field Archaeology |volume=20 |number=1 |date=Spring 1993 |pages=59–75 |doi=10.2307/530354 |jstor=530354}}</ref> This technique involved weaving wooden frames and filling them with a mixture of mud and [[straw]], which created a sturdy wall structure.

In the Southern coastal regions, timber-frame construction with palm-thatched roofs is prevalent, while in [[Nzema District|Nzema]], [[Stilt house|pile dwellings]] are built over water. The savanna regions of the north are characterised by dispersed homesteads and [[adobe]] compounds that blend with the landscape.<ref name=":04">{{cite journal |author=Faculty of Architecture, University of Science and Technology, Kumasi |title=Traditional Forms of Architecture in Ghana |journal=International Social Science Journal |volume=30 |issue=3 |year=1978 |pages=449–453 |publisher=UNESCO |series=Human Habitats: From Tradition to Modernism |issn=0020-8701 |url=https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000262190}}</ref> Historical influences, including European and Muslim penetration introduced elements like [[Jalousie window|louvered jalousies]] and [[Mudbrick|sun-dried bricks]], which were assimilated into Ghana's traditional architecture over time.<ref name=":04" />

{{multiple image
|perrow = 2
|total_width = 330
|align = left
|header = Murals
|image_style = border:none
|image1 = Wall Mural Ghana Library Authority Accra.jpg
|caption1 = An example of a wall mural, [[Ghana Library Authority]] Building
|image2 = Kingbu school.jpg
|caption2 = Depiction of mural decorations on the wall of Kingbu School.
|caption_align = center
|header_align = center
|footer_align = center
}}

[[Mural|Mural decoration]] is another important feature of Ghanaian indigenous architecture. In the northern regions like [[Kassena]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Painted earth architecture of the Kassena people |url=https://www.fieldstudyoftheworld.com/painted-earth-architecture-of-the-kassena-people/ |date=17 December 2018 |access-date=19 December 2024 |work=Field Study of the World}}</ref> it appears on nearly all buildings, both private and state-owned. In the southern regions, murals are primarily on chiefs' palaces and fetish houses. These decorations were not only for self-expression, but also served as a means of identifying and distinguishing individual structures.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Owusu |first=George W.A. |title=Mural Decoration on the Traditional Architecture of Northern Ghana |journal=Journal of the University of Science and Technology, Kumasi |volume=14 |number=2 |date=June 1994 |page=132 |url=https://www.ajol.info/index.php/just/article/view/244087/230854&ved=2ahUKEwi0ntLI17iKAxWKVkEAHflROBMQFnoECBkQAQ&usg=AOvVaw2Bc7rzPjXpBpCRPuScqM0s |format=PDF}}</ref>

A major characteristic of Ghana's indigenous style is its reliance on locally sourced materials, environmental adaptability, integration with nature, and cultural significance of building practices.<ref name=":02" />  Construction techniques and methods such as the timber framed, adobe construction, pile dwellings and [[rammed earth]] have been used for centuries, particularly in rural and semi-urban areas.<ref>{{cite web |title=Vernacular Architecture: Ghana |url=https://www.re-thinkingthefuture.com/architectural-styles/a5577-vernacular-architecture-ghana |website=Rethinking The Future |date=22 October 2021 |access-date=21 December 2024}}</ref>{{sfn|Agyekum|Kissi|Danku|2020|pp=4–6}}

===Ashanti Empire architecture===
[[File:Kentikrono Shrine (2).jpg|thumb|Front view of Kentikrono shrine, one of the traditional buildings of the Asante]]
[[File:Ashant architecture.jpg|thumb|Architecture of the Ashanti Empire drawn by [[Thomas Edward Bowdich]] in 1817]]
Traditional Ashanti buildings were primarily constructed using a wattle and daub method,<ref>{{cite web |title=Discover the History of Asante Traditional Buildings, Ghana, on Google Arts & Culture |url=https://www.wmf.org/journal-articles/discover-history-asante-traditional-buildings-ghana-google-arts-culture |publisher=World Monuments Fund |date=31 January 2023 |access-date=15 December 2024}}</ref> with a timber framework filled with clay and reinforced with bamboo, and had thatched roofs that were steeply pitched using [[raffia palm]].<ref name="sitesAtlas">{{cite web |title=Asante Kingdom Sites of Ghana |url=https://www.worldatlas.com/articles/asante-kingdom-sites-of-ghana.html |website=WorldAtlas |date=25 April 2017 |access-date=12 December 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Architecture of the Asante |url=https://artsandculture.google.com/story/1QWhwY4M1MccdQ |publisher=World Monuments Fund |website=Google Arts & Culture |access-date=22 December 2024}}</ref> This construction method utilised locally available materials, to adapt to the environment and resource availability.

Ashanti architecture is known for its 'fihankra' layout, where buildings are arranged around a central courtyard.<ref>{{cite book |last=Jectey-Nyarko |first=Mantey |title=Fihankra: The Concept of Communality and Security in Indigenous Asante Architecture |date=July 2020 |publisher=Independently published |chapter=Kaira Looro Architecture Competition: Emergency Operations Centre |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/351879323 |access-date=13 December 2024}}</ref> Typically, a compound would consist of four rectangular rooms surrounding the courtyard, with the inner corners connected by [[Splayed opening|splayed]] [[Spirit screen|screen walls]]. Three of these rooms were open to the courtyard, while the fourth was partially enclosed, serving functions such as ritual activities or housing shrines.<ref>{{cite web |title=Asante Traditional Buildings |url=https://gmmb.gov.gh/asante-traditional-buildings/ |publisher=Ghana Museums and Monuments Board |access-date=22 December 2024}}</ref>

{{multiple image
|perrow = 2
|total_width = 330
|align = left
|header = Adrinka symbols
|image_style = border:none
|image1 = Adinkra motifs Rattray 1927.jpg
|caption1 = Adrinka symbols by [[Robert Sutherland Rattray]]
|image2 = GhanaianEmbassyWashingtonDC.jpg
|caption2 = Adrinka symbols on the wall of the [[Embassy of Ghana, Washington, D.C.|Embassy of Ghana in the United States]]
|caption_align = center
|header_align = center
|footer_align = center
}}

The walls of Ashanti buildings were plastered with mud,<ref>{{cite book |title=Asante Traditional Buildings |publisher=Ghana Museums and Monuments Board |year=2021 |edition=2nd |page=12 |url=https://whc.unesco.org/uploads/news/documents/news-2348-2.pdf |access-date=11 December 2021 |series=World Heritage }}</ref> embellished with elaborate murals and bas-relief decorations featuring [[Pattern|geometric patterns]], animal motifs, and representations of plants.<ref>{{cite web |title=Asante Traditional Buildings: Preserving Ghana's cultural heritage |url=https://ghanaremembers.com/stories/culture/asante-traditional-buildings-preserving-ghanas-cultural-heritage.html |website=Ghana Remembers |access-date=22 December 2024}}</ref> These designs often incorporated Adrinka symbols, each carrying specific meanings related to Ashanti beliefs and proverbs.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Edwards |first=Amie |title=African Architecture and Identity: The Nineteenth Century Asante Palace of Kumase, Ghana |journal=School of Architecture Symposia |date=March 2023 |url=https://repository.gatech.edu/entities/publication/a9ed185b-de50-4165-bd1a-93e25eec176a |doi=10.35090/gatech/5978 |pages=62–64 |access-date=12 December 2024}}</ref> The upper walls displayed interlacing geometric designs, and was painted with white clay, while the lower sections which were painted in red laterite featured bodily modelled bas-reliefs polished to a dull shine.<ref name="sitesAtlas" /> This artistry serves both aesthetic and communicative purposes.

The [[Asante Traditional Buildings]] near [[Kumasi]], recognised as UNESCO World Heritage Sites, are the last surviving examples of this architectural style.<ref>{{cite web |title=Asante Traditional Buildings, UNESCO, Amansie Central, Ghana |url=https://heroesofadventure.com/listing/asante-traditional-buildings-unesco-amansie-central-ghana/ |access-date=22 December 2024}}</ref> This collection comprises 13 buildings located across ten sites. Much of the empire's architecture was destroyed during British raids in the 19th century, leaving these buildings as the last authentic remains of the Ashanti period.<ref>{{cite web |first=Edite |last=Strautmane |title=Asante Traditional Buildings |work=GhanaTRVL |url=https://ghanatrvl.com/places-to-see/historical/asante-traditional-buildings |date=5 May 2023 |access-date=27 December 2024}}</ref>

===Mole-Dagbani architecture===
The spatial organisation of Mole-Dagbani settlements were hierarchical, with the chief's hut centrally positioned,<ref>{{cite web |title=Mole-Dagbon people |url=https://www.101lasttribes.com/tribes/moledagbon.html |website=101 Last Tribes |access-date=26 December 2024}}</ref> and surrounded by the dwellings of family members and other community structures.<ref>{{cite web |title=Mole-Dagbon tribe: history, food, dance, languages, weapons, facts |url=https://yen.com.gh/173201-mole-dagbon-tribe-history-food-dance-languages-facts.html |author=Julian Mireri |date=15 April 2022 |access-date=24 December 2024}}</ref>

Symbols were important features in Mole-Dagbani architecture. Important structures, such as palaces, incorporated cultural symbols like the tortoise, lion, crocodile, and leopard, representing wisdom, strength, and fertility.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Abdulai |first1=Olivier Zakaria |last2=Glikpoe |first2=Noble Jesse | title=Cultural Significance of Some Symbols in Four Dagbon Palaces |journal=International Journal of Recent Research in Social Sciences and Humanities  |volume=10 |issue=4 |year= 2023 |pages=143–153 |issn=2349-7831 |doi=10.5281/zenodo.10078718}}</ref>

==Colonial architecture (15th – 20th century)==
Colonial architecture in Ghana emerged with the arrival of European powers, who introduced Western architectural styles in the 15th century.<ref name=":02" /> These merchants including the Portuguese, Dutch, Danish, and British, established [[Trading post|trade posts]], [[Fortification|forts]], and settlements along the [[Gold Coast (region)|Gold Coast]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Castles, Factories, and Forts |url=https://slaveryandremembrance.org/articles/article/?id=A0128 |website=Slavery and Remembrance |access-date=25 December 2024}}</ref><ref name="volta">{{cite web |title=Forts and Castles, Volta, Greater Accra, Central and Western Regions |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/34/ |work=UNESCO |access-date=17 December 2024}}</ref> This period spanning until the early 20th century,<ref>{{cite web |title=Ghana – Colonialism, Independence, Gold Coast |author=Ernest Boateng, John Fage |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Ghana/History |access-date=27 December 2024}}</ref> saw the introduction of European architectural styles that melded with local traditions, resulting in hybrid forms.

The construction of forts and castles was a main feature of early colonial architecture in Ghana. These forts and castles along Ghana's coast were constructed over a 300-year period between 1482 and 1786,<ref group="note">Most sources state that the forts and castles were constructed between 1482 and 1786, but a report by COMMARK Trust and the African World Heritage Fund gives the range as 1480 to 1790.</ref><ref name="awhf">{{cite report |title=Forts & Castles of Ghana: Situational Analysis, Report 4 |author=COMMARK Trust and African World Heritage Fund |publisher=African World Heritage Fund |date=2015}}</ref>{{rp|p=7}} and were occupied at different times by European traders from countries such as Portugal, Spain, Denmark, Sweden, Germany, and Britain.<ref>{{cite web |title=Ghana's Historic Coastal Forts And Castles |url=https://www.worldatlas.com/articles/historic-forts-and-castles-along-the-coast-of-ghana.html |website=WorldAtlas |date=25 April 2017 |access-date=24 December 2024}}</ref> Initially built to support the gold trade of European chartered companies, by the 17th and early 18th centuries, these structures later became central to the [[Atlantic slave trade|transatlantic slave trade]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Forts and Castles in Ghana |url=https://visitghana.com/attractions/all-forts-and-castles |website=Visit Ghana |access-date=18 December 2024}}</ref>  They linked trading routes, and acted as important market places for the gold and slave trades. By the 19th century, the efficiency of the forts began to decline as their functionality waned, and some were abandoned entirely.<ref name="awhf" />{{rp|pp=8–9}}

The [[Elmina Castle|Castle of St George]] at Elmina, built in 1482 by the Portuguese, stands as the oldest European stone structure [[Sub-Saharan Africa|south of the Sahara]], and was later expanded by the Dutch. This was followed by the construction of numerous forts, most of which were established in the 17th century when competition among European powers in the region intensified.<ref>{{cite web |title=Elmina Castle |url=https://everycastle.com/elmina-castle |website=everycastle |access-date=26 December 2024}}</ref>

[[Cape Coast Castle]], constructed by the [[Swedes]] in 1653, is one of the largest trade forts in West Africa. The British later took control of the castle in 1664. Initially a trade hub for gold, wood and textiles, it later became a centre for the slave trade, with added dungeons to accommodate more captives. After the [[Abolitionism in the United Kingdom|abolition of the slave trade in 1807]], the castle was repurposed as an educational and administrative centre.<ref>{{cite web |title=Cape Coast Castle |url=https://slaveryandremembrance.org/articles/article/?id=A0103 |website=Slavery and Remembrance |access-date=28 December 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Visit Ghana – Cape Coast Castle |url=https://visitghana.com/attractions/cape-coast-castle/ |website=Visit Ghana |access-date=28 December 2024}}</ref>

Architecturally, these forts were typically designed as large squares or rectangles, with outer components consisting of four [[bastion]]s or towers located at the corners. The inner-sections featured two or three-story buildings, some with additional towers, and often included enclosures, courtyards, or [[Spur (architecture)|spurs]]. These designs were periodically modified and expanded by successive European powers to suit new needs, and many forts bear traces of these adaptations. While some structures remain intact, others have fallen into ruins due to environmental pressures and lack of maintenance.<ref name="volta" /> Most of these sites remained as architectural landmarks, and in 1979 [[List of castles in Ghana#Coastal regions|designated as World Heritage Sites]] by UNESCO.

In the 19th century, European missionaries introduced new building typologies, including churches, schools, and training colleges. This included the Abetifi Presbyterian Church and Akropong Presbyterian Training College, constructed with local labour under European supervision.<ref name="op1">{{cite web |first=Samuel Opare |last=Larbi |title=Architectural History of Ghana |url=https://www.design233.com/articles/architectural-history-of-ghana |date=10 October 2020 |access-date=28 December 2024}}</ref> The latter is the second oldest higher educational institution in early modern West Africa.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://ptc.edu.gh/website/ |title=Presby - PTC COLLEGE OF EDUCATION |website=Presby |language=en-US |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180605144550/http://ptc.edu.gh/website/ |archive-date=5 June 2018}}</ref>  These buildings often used rammed earth, stone nog, and brick.

By the late 19th and early 20th centuries, colonial towns like [[Anomabu|Anomabo]] became centres of hybrid architecture, blending European and Ghanaian styles.<ref name="mimicry">{{cite journal |first=Courtnay |last=Micots |title=Status and Mimicry: African Colonial Period Architecture in Coastal Ghana |journal=The Journal of the Society of Architectural Historians |volume=74 |issue=1 |year=2015 |doi=10.1525/jsah.2015.74.1.41 |pages=41–43}}</ref> This hybridisation was particularly prominent in the homes of elite Africans, who used mimicry architecture to assert wealth, modernity, and resistance to colonial dominance. These homes often combined: European-inspired designs, such as [[Palladian architecture|Palladian symmetry]], arches, and verandas, and local construction methods using materials like laterite, rammed earth, and wattle and daub.<ref name="mimicry" /><ref>{{cite book |last=Micots |first=Courtnay |title=African Coastal Elite Architecture: Cultural Authentication during the Colonial Period in Anomabo, Ghana |date=2020 |publisher=University of Florida |type=thesis |url=https://openpublishing.psu.edu/ahd/content/african-coastal-elite-architecture-cultural-authentication-during-colonial-period-anomabo |access-date=28 December 2024 }}</ref>

Colonial administrators in the Gold Coast also constructed government offices, railways, and military barracks. Under Governor [[Gordon Guggisberg]] in the early 20th century, projects such as [[Takoradi Harbour]], [[Korle-Bu Teaching Hospital|Korle-Bu Hospital]], and [[Achimota School]] were established.<ref>{{cite web |first=Alex |last=Sarkodie |title=Governor Frederick Guggisberg, His Second Coming |url=https://www.modernghana.com/news/1356846/governor-frederick-guggisberg-his-second-coming.html |website=Modern Ghana |access-date=29 December 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Abbou |first=Tahar |title=The Ten Year Plan in the Gold Coast |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/333339199 |date=2019 |access-date=29 December 2024}}</ref> These projects predominantly employed European architects and engineers.<ref>{{cite web |last=Manful |first=Kuukuwa |title=On (Un)formalisation: The Regulation of Architecture in Ghana |url=https://kuukuwa.com/updates/h9ug7ejzrufwuj1a487kxo1bcyp3yp |access-date=26 December 2024}}</ref>

<gallery widths="180" heights="180">
File:Zcapecorse2.jpg|Cape Coast Castle in the 18th century by [[Jacques-Nicolas Bellin]]
File:Cape Coast Castle, Cape Coast, Ghana.JPG|Cape Coast Castle, [[Cape Coast]]

==Post-independence==
Following Ghana's independence in 1957, its first president, [[Kwame Nkrumah]] initiated various architectural projects. During this era, several monumental structures were commissioned. [[Black Star Square]], also known as Independence Square, in [[Accra]], is one of these projects. Designed by Ghanaian architect Victor Adegbite, the square was constructed on former colonial playing fields. It features the Independence Arch, consisting of three [[Parabolic arch|parabolic]] concrete arches that support a presidential platform, flanked by stands with a capacity of up to 30,000 spectators. The arch has been described as symbolising a "door of no return", signifying efforts to encourage the African diaspora to reconnect with their heritage and contribute to the country's development.<ref>{{cite news |last=Wainwright |first=Oliver |title=Post-colonial party pads! The architects who got Ghana back in the groove |url=https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign/2024/feb/26/post-colonial-party-pads-the-architects-who-got-ghana-back-in-the-groove |website=The Guardian |date=26 February 2024 |access-date=29 December 2024}}</ref>

Another project was the [[Ghana Trade Fair Center|International Trade Fair]] in Accra. The centrepiece of the fair, the African Pavilion, featured a circular design with an aluminium roof, inspired by the royal umbrellas of the [[Akan people|Akan]] chieftains and the [[Baobab|baobab tree]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Stanek|first=Łukasz|title=Architects from Socialist Countries in Ghana (1957-67): Modern Architecture and Mondialisation|url=https://www.academia.edu/19448876|journal=Journal of the Society of Architectural Historians|language=en|volume=74|issue=4|pages=416–442|doi=10.1525/jsah.2015.74.4.416 |issn=0037-9808}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Richardson |first=Ruth-Anne |last2=Stanek |first2=Łukasz |date=27 January 2021 |title=Accra's International Trade Fair Embodies Ghana's Complex Legacy of Pan-African Modernism |url=https://failedarchitecture.com/accras-international-trade-fair-embodies-ghanas-complex-legacy-of-pan-african-modernism/ |access-date=30 December 2024 |website=Failed Architecture}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Tropical Modernism: Ghana's architecture and independence |url=https://www.akadimagazine.com/post/tropical-modernism-ghana-s-architecture-and-independence |date=23 March 2024 |access-date=30 December 2024}}</ref>

Various public buildings such as the [[National Museum of Ghana|Ghana's National Museum]] and [[Job 600]], educational institutions like the [[University of Ghana#Academics#University of Ghana Campuses|University of Ghana's Legon Campus]], and infrastructure projects such as the Ghana International Trade Fair Centre were designed to incorporate modernist principles while integrating local cultural elements.

Around the same period, the first indigenous architectural firm in Ghana, Associated Consultants was founded by engineers and two Ghanaian architects, D.S.K. Kpodo-Tay and S.G.T Kofi, both graduates of [[Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology|KNUST]] with master's degree in architecture. Subsequently, other indigenous firms followed, such as, Plan Architects, which was established by E.O Adjettey, a KNUST graduate with postgraduate training in urban planning from [[Edinburgh]].<ref name="op1" />

Following the 1972 Aliens Compliance Order, which led to the departure of many expatriate architects, some remained in Ghana and collaborated with local professionals to foster architectural development in the country.<ref name="op1" />

===Tropical Modernism===
After Ghana gained independence, Tropical Modernism became a prominent architectural style in the country. It emerged as a response to the country's climatic conditions and socio-political context during the mid-20th century. This style combined modernist principles with designs suited to the tropical climate, incorporating features like [[brise soleil]], wide [[Overhang (architecture)|overhangs]], natural ventilation, and protective shade areas.{{sfn|Winterhalter|2017|pp=43–49}}<ref>{{cite web |title=Tropical Modernism: How To Incorporate This V&A Exhibition Into Your Interiors |author=Olivia Emily |date=5 March 2024 |url=https://www.countryandtownhouse.com/interiors/tropical-modernism/ |access-date=30 December 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=What is Tropical Modernism? |url=https://www.vam.ac.uk/articles/what-is-tropical-modernism?srsltid=AfmBOor1PrdgsLzfKe5GZaU019uOy5AKSz8gul59OdMt0CEkZqwCeHjd& |access-date=28 December 2024}}</ref>

One of the early examples of Tropical Modernism in Ghana is the Unity Hall at Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), designed by Ghanaian architect John Owusu Addo.<ref>{{cite web |title=Meet the Ghanaian architect who designed KNUST Unity Hall and Cedi House |work=GhanaWeb |url=https://mobile.ghanaweb.com/GhanaHomePage/entertainment/Meet-the-Ghanaian-architect-who-designed-KNUST-Unity-Hall-and-Cedi-House-1803374 |date=13 July 2023 |access-date=29 December 2024}}</ref> The building integrated climate-responsive features such as [[cross ventilation]] and [[Passive solar building design|shading devices]] while reflecting modernist aesthetics.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Kwabi |first=Prince Charles |date=2023-12-15 |title=Tropical Modern Architect: Prof. John Owusu Addo |journal=Docomomo Journal |issue=69 |pages=29–34 |doi=10.52200/docomomo.69.03 |issn=2773-1634|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Foreign architects also contributed to the development of this style in Ghana. British architects [[Maxwell Fry]] and [[Jane Drew]], influenced several public and private structures in Accra. They emphasised on adapting international modernist designs to the local environment, and helped to shape the architectural landscape of this era.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Jackson |first1=Iain |last2=Holland |first2=Jessica |title=The Architecture of Edwin Maxwell Fry and Jane Drew: Twentieth Century Architecture, Pioneer Modernism and the Tropics |year=2016 |doi=10.4324/9781315612492|isbn=978-1-317-04486-4 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=MAXWELL FRY (1899-1987) AND JANE DREW (1911-96) |url=https://www.commonwealthheritage.org/maxwell-fry-1899-1987-and-jane-drew-1911-96/ |website=The Commonwealth Heritage Forum |date=9 December 2022 |access-date=28 December 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Liscombe |first=Rhodri Windsor |title=Modernism in Late Imperial British West Africa: The Work of Maxwell Fry and Jane Drew, 1946-56 |journal=Journal of the Society of Architectural Historians |volume=65 |issue=2 |year=2006 |pages=188–215 |publisher=University of California Press |doi=10.2307/25068264 |jstor=25068264}}</ref>

Beyond functionality, Ghanaian Tropical Modernism also incorporated cultural elements and symbols. Local motifs and traditional construction methods were often integrated into the facades and interiors of buildings.  Public buildings such as the Ghana National Museum featured local materials and design motifs, for modernity and tradition. It also features faceted walls angled to allow for cross ventilation and a shallow [[dome]] made of [[reinforced concrete]] [[Cladding (construction)|clad]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Two African National Museums: National Identity Reflected in Modernist Design |author=Mohieldin Gamal |url=https://www.archdaily.com/1023950/two-african-national-museums-national-identity-reflected-in-modernist-design |date=26 November 2024 |website=Arch Daily |access-date=30 December 2024}}</ref>

Some Ghanaian architects adopted much of the architectural philosophy that "[[Form follows function]]", which defined much of the Ghanaian Tropical Modernist style, while other architects opted for a more expressive design philosophy, where form was influenced by, but not strictly bound to, function.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Journal |first=D. |title=Adaptive Reuse: The Modern Movement Towards the Future: 14th International docomomo Conference |journal=Docomomo Journal |volume=55 |url=https://docomomojournal.com/index.php/journal/article/view/392 |publisher=Docomomo International |year=2016 |pages=414–419}}</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Architecture of Iceland
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}}
<!-- "none" is preferred when the title is sufficiently descriptive; see [[WP:SDNONE]] -->
{{Use dmy dates|date=January 2024}}

{{Icelandic-people}}

The '''architecture of Iceland''' draws from [[Scandinavia]]n influences and traditionally was influenced by the lack of [[Indigenous (ecology)|native]] trees on the island. As a result, grass- and turf-covered houses were developed. Later on, the [[Swiss chalet style]] became a prevailing influence in Icelandic architecture as many timber buildings were constructed in this way. Stone and later [[concrete]] were popular building materials, the latter especially with the arrival of [[functionalism (architecture)|functionalism]] in the country. [[Contemporary architecture]] in Iceland is influenced by many sources, with styles varying greatly around the country.<ref name="-guide">{{cite book |title=A Guide to Icelandic Architecture |last=Jóhannesson |first=Dennis |author2=Kristjánsdóttir |publisher=The Association of Icelandic Architects |year=2000 |pages=9–15|first2=Málfríður}}</ref>

The architecture of Iceland is mainly low-rise, with many low tower blocks and two- or three-storey buildings with pitched roofs predominating. Houses and smaller municipal buildings were traditionally wooden-framed, and clad in [[wood]]en [[Lumber|plank]]s or corrugated metal. Often they were painted in traditional bright colours.<ref name="style">{{cite web|title=Iceland Architecture|url=http://www.blueshawk.info/texasflood/iceland_architecture.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070408000401/http://www.blueshawk.info/texasflood/iceland_architecture.htm|archive-date=8 April 2007|access-date=14 May 2007|website=www.blueshawk.info}}</ref> Many architectural influences can be seen, notably in the capital, such as the once-popular Swiss chalet style.

==Turf houses==
{{Main|Icelandic turf house}}
[[Image: Glaumbaer.jpg|thumb|Glaumbær at Skagafjordur Folk Museum]]
The original turf houses constructed by the [[Settlement of Iceland|original settlers]] of [[Iceland]] (from the west coast of [[Norway]]) were based on [[Vikings|Viking]] [[longhouse]]s ({{lang|is|langhús}}). The exterior turf walls were lined internally with a wooden frame, which was then paneled, with the roof resting on two rows of pillars dividing the internal space. The main room of the house was known as the {{lang|is|skáli}}, consisting of a central open [[hearth]] and two raised platforms, known as {{lang|is|set}}. Similar designs of longhouse have been found across Scandinavia, the [[Faroe Islands|Faroes]] and the [[List of islands of Scotland|Scottish isles]], as well as [[Greenland]].<ref name="grass houses-guide">{{Harvard citation|Jóhannesson|Kristjánsdóttir|2000|pages=9-10}}</ref>

There are many benefits and functionality to the turf houses. Turf houses provided thermal comfort to the cold, harsh climates that Iceland experiences. To prevent any cold from intruding into the house, cavities were filled with soil to add more insulation to the buildings. In addition, the turf houses required less resources, which Iceland was lacking in the late 9th century. Simple wood structures were used since wood was one of the few resources semi present. Other resources such as sod, twigs, moss, etc. were used to build the houses and further add to the thermal comfort of the houses.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=van Hoof |first1=Joost |last2=van Dijken |first2=Froukje |date=2008-06-01 |title=The historical turf farms of Iceland: Architecture, building technology and the indoor environment |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0360132307000984 |journal=Building and Environment |volume=43 |issue=6 |pages=1023–1030 |doi=10.1016/j.buildenv.2007.03.004 |bibcode=2008BuEnv..43.1023V |issn=0360-1323|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Later the houses included an additional living space, the {{lang|is|stofa}}, and would be accompanied by smaller outhouses.<ref name="grass houses-guide" /> This layout also incorporated a [[pantry]] and [[Toilet (room)|lavatory]].<ref name="grasshouses">{{cite web |url=http://www.iit.edu/~fordrob/ |title=Icelandic Turf Structures |access-date=14 May 2007 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080112104312/http://www.iit.edu/~fordrob/ | archive-date = 12 January 2008|website=www.iit.edu}}</ref> Over the years, the layout became more compartmentalised, eventually to include a {{lang|is|baðstofa}} (a heated [[sauna]] room). In response to the colder [[Climate of Iceland|Icelandic climate]], the sleeping area was eventually moved into the {{lang|is|baðstofa}}.<ref name="grasshouses" /> The design evolved as the entrance was moved between the living room and main room; all the rooms in the house were joined by a central passageway, this layout was known as a {{lang|is|gangabær}}. This was possibly in response to a deteriorating climate, and as timber supplies dwindled, people went back to living in the one-room {{lang|is|baðstofa}} layout.

Around 1791, under Danish interest, a [[gable]]-fronted design ({{lang|is|burstabær}}) was proposed by [[Guðlaugur Sveinsson]],<ref name="grasshouses"/> which became widespread in the south of Iceland where the climate is warmer. An example of this design is the Glaumbær turf farmhouse at [[Skagafjörður Folk Museum]] which was opened in 1952 at the Glaumbær Farm.<ref>{{Cite web |title=GLAUMBAER SKAGAFJORDUR FOLK MUSEUM |url=https://www.nat.is/Museums/glaumbaer_skagafj_folk_museum.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191118133843/https://www.nat.is/Museums/glaumbaer_skagafj_folk_museum.htm |archive-date=2019-11-18 |access-date=2026-06-15 |website=nat.is}}</ref>

By the 20th century, the design was evolving still, seeing such additions as the {{lang|is|framhús}}, a kind of timber porch at the front entrance of buildings.<ref name="grass houses-guide" /> Today grasshouses are no longer constructed in Iceland (construction stopped in the mid-20th century), and the few remaining examples are generally open to public as open-air museums.<ref name="grass houses-guide" /> There is some evidence to suggest a [[Celts|Celtic]] influence in early Icelandic architecture in the form of stone [[Roundhouse (dwelling)|roundhouse]]s and sheepcotes, however much of this is still shaded in obscurity.<ref name="grass houses-guide" />

== Styles and Influences ==
Like many other areas in the world, Iceland would often pull ideas from previous architectural styles, a method called historicism. Many of these styles can be seen in various buildings such as the gothic style in the churches and neoclassical style in commercial buildings such as banks. When it comes to residential buildings, a common theme seen is the simplicity in the designs, focusing more on functionality of the buildings rather than the ornamentation. Then, in the mid-18th century, there was some influence to the architecture from the Danish Government. One of the main stylistic changes seen in this time period is the transition from turf housing to stone housing.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Ultimate Guide to Architecture in Iceland |url=https://guidetoiceland.is/history-culture/icelandic-architecture |access-date=2024-11-10 |website=Guide to Iceland |language=en}}</ref>

== Stone buildings ==
Many high-quality stone buildings were erected in the 18th century, the first being a mansion on [[Viðey]], made completely out of Icelandic stone. These were some of the first buildings in Iceland to be constructed by architects, who were from Denmark, as these buildings were constructed for the Danish authorities. The craftsmen involved in the construction of these buildings were also foreign. Icelandic stone buildings from this period were inherently similar to those in Denmark, save the use of timber to clad the roofs instead of [[slate]]. This type of building was considered very expensive and is seen in many official buildings such as [[Bessastaðir]] (the presidential residence) and [[Alþingishúsið]] in [[Reykjavík]].

Many Icelanders learned the craft of [[masonry]] during the stone construction boom period, leading to the building of many stone houses which mimicked the design of Icelandic turf houses.<ref>{{Harvard citation|Jóhannesson|Kristjánsdóttir|2000|p=12}}</ref>

==Church buildings==
[[Image:Holakirkja.jpg|thumb|[[Hólar Cathedral]], in [[Hólar]], is the largest stone church constructed in the country.]]

With the arrival of [[Christianization of Iceland|Christianity in Iceland]] in 1000 AD, construction began on numerous impressive churches. A majority were probably constructed out of turf, but there were also numerous timber-framed churches, however not much remains of these buildings today. The first stone churches appeared in around in the 18th century, quite late considering the significant lack of timber on the island (even access to driftwood was not widespread).<ref>{{Harvard citation|Jóhannesson|Kristjánsdóttir|2000|p=11}}</ref>

In the oldest part of Reykjavik, the Eastern Hill, housed the Skólavörðuhol church. The Skólavörðuhol was designed by Guðjón Samúelsson, who built it with a romantic style originated in Scandinavia. It was designed with a Greek cross layout and contained a dome. In addition, over on the Western Hill, the Landakotskirkja church, also known as the Basilica of Christ the King, was built. This church was also designed by Guðjón Samúelsson but with a Neo-Gothic style. The Landakotskirkja was the largest church in Iceland in 1929. During this same time, Jón Helgason held a competition for the design of the Hallgrímskirkja church, which was to be built where the Skólavörðuhol once was. The Skólavörðuhol was to be built using the Gothic revival style and was designed by Águst Pálsson, who had won the competition.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Benárd |first=Aurél |date=2018 |title=A Late Example of Expressionist Church Architecture |url=https://intapi.sciendo.com/pdf/10.2478/jbe-2018-0006 |journal=Institute of Architecture|doi=10.2478/jbe-2018-0006 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Urbanization==
[[File:House in Reykjavik.jpg|thumb|A house in Reykjavík showing typical corrugated metal siding.]]
Urbanization began to appear around the 18th century, when Danish merchants set up permanent [[trading post]]s for themselves. The timber for constructing these residential and commercial premises was mostly [[prefabrication|prefabricated]] and imported. These timber-framed buildings had high [[Roof pitch|pitched roofs]] and low walls, and they were [[tar]]red on the outside making them dark in appearance.<ref name="urbanization-guide">{{Harvard citation|Jóhannesson|Kristjánsdóttir|2000|pages=11-12}}</ref>

With the movement towards independence from Denmark and the implementation of Icelandic free trade, more diverse architectural styles and influences were brought to the island.<ref name="20thc-guide">{{Harvard citation|Jóhannesson|Kristjánsdóttir|2000|pages=13–15}}</ref> Classical influences can be seen in timber buildings from the 19th century, these buildings were often two-storey and had higher walls. Details such as the layout of [[Window|fenestration]] on the building drew from classical traditions. A few buildings in this style remain today.<ref name="urbanization-guide"/>

As the 20th century dawned, [[Swiss chalet style]] architecture was brought indirectly to Iceland under Norwegian influence. Prefabricated houses were shipped and erected in settlements in the [[Eastern Region (Iceland)|Eastern Region]] and [[Westfjords]]. The buildings tended to be taller and with large windows, unlike anything of the styles that had prevailed in Iceland beforehand. Notable features of these buildings were the [[frieze]]s above doors and windows, and [[eaves]] which projected out above the walls. Here the distinctive Icelandic use of [[Corrugated galvanised iron|corrugated iron]] (imported from England), in place of external [[cladding (construction)|cladding]], was born. The Swiss chalet style was the dominant force in Icelandic architecture in the early 20th century.<ref name="urbanization-guide"/> The use of timber was banned in urban areas after great fires in Reykjavík and [[Akureyri]] around this time.<ref name="urbanization-guide"/>

Concrete was first used on a major scale as a building material in this period and became extremely popular as an easy and economical construction material. The material has shaped Icelandic architecture from this period. With the arrival of concrete came the first qualified Icelandic architect, [[Rögnvaldur Ólafsson]], who had at first designed in the Swiss chalet style but soon moved on to working in concrete. His first works in concrete resembled closely the stone buildings of earlier times.<ref name="20thc-guide" />

Characteristically urban buildings began to emerge, such as {{lang|is|Austurstræti}} 16 (designed by [[Guðjón Samúelsson]]) which were concrete constructions. Guðjón went on to become the leading Icelandic architect of the time. Referencing traditional Icelandic architectural styles, he revived the gable-fronted house design in concrete. This influence can be seen in stylised form in the [[National Theatre of Iceland]] building, for example. Guðjón Samúelsson was also the designer of [[Hallgrímskirkja]], one of the tallest structures in Iceland, which was modelled on cliff faces.<ref name="20thc-guide" />

==Contemporary architecture==

The [[Functionalism (architecture)|functionalist architectural style]] arrived in Iceland in the 1930s, brought by younger architects who would later have great influence on the [[urban planning]] of the country. Unusually, functionalism was not met with as much controversy as it was in other countries at the time. Early functionalist buildings in the country resembled those elsewhere in Europe, but conventional interior layouts being their differentiating feature. Many neighbourhoods were built up using the functionalist aesthetic as their guide. The buildings were made distinctively Icelandic with the use of local minerals and seashells as [[roughcast|dashing]]. Whole residential districts were dashed in this way. After World War II, larger houses with higher roofs began to appear, with a variety of decorative features marking a departure from the functionalist aesthetic.<ref name="20thc-guide" />

The next wave of architectural style to arrive was [[Modern architecture|modernism]], appearing after the country's gain of independence from Denmark. Influential architects created modernist buildings with low roofs and large windows and large, smooth expanses of colour (in contrast to the dashing style which was popular earlier). Modernist architecture commanded a modernist interior to boot, and so here began a strong furniture industry. New building techniques led to the construction of concrete high-rises in Reykjavík. Here new movements began to show up, such as an increase in popularity of [[open plan]] interiors.<ref name="20thc-guide" />

In addition to new styles and influences arriving, a sentiment for the conservation of existing older buildings was founded, with newfound interest in traditional handicrafts. Criticism of modern Icelandic architecture appeared at this time, pointing out [[Efficient energy use|energy-wasting]] designs and drawing from traditional building techniques such as steep pitched roofs to find solutions.<ref name="20thc-guide"/>

Many projects proposed during the boom period before the [[2008–2011 Icelandic financial crisis]], including Iceland's first skyscrapers, the [[Höfðatorg Tower 1|Höfðatorg]] and [[Smáratorg Tower|Smáratorg]] towers have been constructed.

Many of the taller buildings in the Reykjavík area look out of place when compared with their neighbours, for example traditional wooden houses neighbour the Höfðatorg Tower 1.

Other projects include the [[Harpa (concert hall)|Harpa]], completed in 2011, whose ambitious plans had originally included a [[World Trade Centers Association|world trade centre]]

Funding for the concert hall became insecure with the economic crisis, although the Icelandic government later promised that the project would be completed, with state funding.

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Architecture of India
======================================================================

'''Indian architecture''' is rooted in the [[History of India|history]], [[Culture of India|culture]], and [[Indian religions|religion]] of [[India]]. Among multiple architectural styles and traditions, the best-known include the many built in accordance to Indian religion and [[Indian philosophy|philosophy]] with [[Hindu temple architecture|Hindu]], [[Jain art#Architecture|Jain]], [[Buddhist architecture|Buddhist]], and [[Sikh architecture|Sikh]] styles of architecture being the most prevalent in India, with [[Indo-Islamic architecture]], [[Rajput architecture]], [[Mughal architecture]], [[Dravidian architecture|South Indian architecture]], and [[Indo-Saracenic architecture]] having a strong presence as well.

Early Indian architecture was made from wood, which did not survive due to rotting and instability in the structures. Instead, the earliest surviving examples of Indian architecture are [[Indian rock-cut architecture]], including many [[Buddhist temple|Buddhist]], [[Hindu temple|Hindu]], and [[Jain temple|Jain]] temples.

Hindu temple architecture is traditionally divided into two main architectural styles: the [[Dravidian architecture|Dravidian style]] of southern India and [[Nagara Style|Nagara style]] of northern India, with several regional variations that combine elements of both. Other regional styles, such as the [[Vesara|Vesara style]] of the [[Deccan Plateau|Deccan plateau]] and the [[Kalinga architecture|Kalinga style]] of eastern India, developed through local tastes. In addition to temple architecture, domestic housing styles in India also vary widely between regions, reflecting differences in climate, geography, building materials, and cultural traditions. 

The first major Islamic empire in India was the [[Delhi Sultanate]], which led to the development of [[Indo-Islamic architecture]], combining Indian and [[Islamic architecture|Islamic architectural features]]. The rule of the [[Mughal Empire]], when [[Mughal architecture]] evolved, is regarded as the zenith of Indo-Islamic architecture, with the [[Taj Mahal]] being the high point of their contribution. Indo-Islamic architecture got influenced by existing indigenous Hindu elements of style and later fused with [[Architecture of Rajasthan|Rajput]] and [[Sikh architecture|Sikh]] architecture as well.<ref>Petersen, Andrew (2002). Dictionary of Islamic Architecture. Routledge. pp. 115. {{ISBN|1-134-61366-0}} quote,"The most significant of these is the Hindu religion which was a highly developed culture well before the Muslim conquest and continues to be the major religion of the country. The effect of this on architecture means that Indian buildings have distinct design and building characteristics which distinguish them from Islamic buildings elsewhere. The most significant influence on architecture was the Hindu temple. Initially Hindu temples were destroyed and the remains were used to build mosques, such as the Quwwat al-Islam Mosque in Delhi which was built out of the remains of twenty-seven temples; later, however, Hindu features were copied for use in mosques and have now become characteristic of Indo-Islamic architecture. Examples of Hindu features incorporated into Islamic buildings include domed chatris, projecting chajjas and bulbous dome finials. Later on the influence of India can be seen in the mosques of south-east Asia, many of which are Indian in form."</ref>

During the [[British Raj|British colonial period]], European styles including [[Neoclassical architecture|Neoclassical]], [[Gothic Revival architecture|Gothic Revival]], and [[Baroque]] became prevalent across India. The amalgamation of Indo-Islamic and European styles led to a new style, known as the [[Indo-Saracenic architecture|Indo-Saracenic]] style. Following the events succeeding [[Indian independence movement|India's independence from Britain]], new [[Modern architecture|European modernist]] ideas spread amongst Indian architects as a means of progressing as a new republic. Swiss-French architect [[Le Corbusier]] was commissioned by the Indian government to design the city of [[Chandigarh]], which influenced a generation of architects towards modernism in the 20th century. The [[Economic liberalisation in India|continued economic reforms]] further bolstered modern architecture and the urban layout of India, as the country became more integrated with the world's economy.

==Neolithic period==
In South India, the [[Neolithic|Neolithic period]] began in 6500 BCE and lasted till around 1400 BCE when the [[Megalithic]] transition period began. The South Indian Neolithic period is characterized by ash mounds from 2500 BCE in the region of [[Karnataka]], which later expanded into [[Tamil Nadu]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Johansen |first=Peter G. |date=2014-02-01 |title=The politics of spatial renovation: Reconfiguring ritual places and practice in Iron Age and Early Historic South India |url=https://doi.org/10.1177/1469605313515976 |journal=Journal of Social Archaeology |language=EN |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=59–86 |doi=10.1177/1469605313515976 |issn=1469-6053|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Coningham |first=Robin |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/archaeology-of-south-asia/081F7A92EB62C2575E8BF3486B21080D |title=The Archaeology of South Asia: From the Indus to Asoka, c.6500 BCE–200 CE |last2=Young |first2=Ruth |date=2015 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-84697-4 |series=Cambridge World Archaeology |location=Cambridge}}</ref>
